message.content: I have 2 games that I started working on with the help of codex, those are the cpp shooting and the racing game. I now want to get a game where I can communicate with npcs and the npcs use a small llm, just smart enough for conversation. Of course not smart enough to do your taxes, write your code, or look up who run the dodgers game for you but something smart enough that it can pretend to be a blacksmith, lawyer, elf or a baker. Basically something just smart enough to roleplay, an llm that I can centralize and have multiple NPCs use it for their purposes, either as Jim the pharmecist, Jane the random pedestrian 47 or whatever. What are some good small LLMs that I can use entirely in house, and how can I get that? please help me plan out what llm to use, how to get it and how we can apply it to an npc. I will need to come up with the storyline later but I am thinking that a companion to talk to is a fun first thing to try.

content.text: Good — 6GB+ NVIDIA, sidecar now/embed later, cross-platform. Let me write the plan.

input.content:
# Plan: LLM-Powered NPC Companion Game

## Context

You have two completed C++ games (`cpp_shooter_game/`, `cpp_racing_game/`) and an empty `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/` directory waiting for content. The goal of this third project is a small game where the player can hold a conversation with NPCs whose dialogue is generated by a **single local LLM**, shared across every NPC. Each NPC contributes only a persona prompt and its own short conversation history; the LLM does the talking.

The first milestone is intentionally tiny: a single **companion** NPC you can chat with via a text box. Storyline, world, and other NPC personas come later, once the dialogue loop feels good.

Key constraints from our discussion:
- **Hardware:** 6GB+ NVIDIA VRAM — comfortable up to ~7-8B parameter models at 4-bit quantization.
- **Integration:** Start with **Ollama as a sidecar** (HTTP on localhost), plan a future migration to embedded `llama.cpp` once the design stabilizes.
- **Platform:** **Cross-platform from day one** (Linux + Windows). The existing games are MSYS2/Windows only, so this is a deliberate departure — we'll keep build scripts and paths portable.
- **No new dependencies** in the existing two games. All new deps live under `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/`.

---

## LLM choice

### Recommended starting model: **Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct** (`qwen2.5:3b-instruct`)
- ~2 GB on disk at Q4_K_M, ~3 GB VRAM at runtime — leaves plenty of headroom.
- Strong instruction-following at small size; good at staying in a persona when given a clear system prompt.
- Fast on a 6GB GPU (30+ tokens/sec typical), so replies feel snappy.
- Permissive license (Apache 2.0–compatible terms for the open weights).

### Honorable mentions (try after Qwen feels limiting)
- **Llama 3.2 3B Instruct** (`llama3.2:3b-instruct`) — comparable size, slightly different writing style. Easy A/B swap.
- **Nous Hermes 3 8B** (`hermes3:8b`) — 8B Llama-3.1 fine-tune explicitly tuned for roleplay and persona consistency. Fits your VRAM at Q4_K_M (~5 GB). This is the upgrade target once you want richer characters.
- **Phi-3.5 Mini 3.8B** (`phi3.5:3.8b-mini-instruct`) — Microsoft's small model; strong reasoning but somewhat stiffer dialogue. Worth trying for contrast.

What we are **not** picking and why:
- Anything under 1B (TinyLlama, SmolLM) — too prone to breaking character mid-reply.
- 13B+ models — overkill for "blacksmith small talk," and slower iteration during development.

### Why a sidecar via Ollama (for now)
- One install (`curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh` on Linux, installer on Windows) gives you model download, quantization, GPU acceleration, and a stable HTTP API.
- `ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct` is the entire "get the model" step.
- The C++ game just needs an HTTP client — no CMake gymnastics for CUDA/CMake/llama.cpp yet.
- You can swap models with one config line, with no rebuild.
- Migration path to embedded `llama.cpp` later is clean because the `LlmClient` interface will hide the transport.

---

## Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────────┐
│  cpp_game_with_llm_npcs      │  HTTP   │  Ollama (sidecar)      │
│  (SFML + OpenGL)             │ ──────► │  qwen2.5:3b-instruct   │
│                              │  JSON   │  localhost:11434       │
│  ┌────────────────────────┐  │         └────────────────────────┘
│  │ LlmClient (singleton)  │  │
│  │  - async request queue │  │
│  │  - HTTP via cpp-httplib│  │
│  └─────────▲──────────────┘  │
│            │                 │
│  ┌─────────┴──────────────┐  │
│  │ Npc                    │  │
│  │  - Persona (system     │  │
│  │    prompt template)    │  │
│  │  - ConversationHistory │  │
│  │  - askAsync(playerLine)│  │
│  └─────────▲──────────────┘  │
│            │                 │
│  ┌─────────┴──────────────┐  │
│  │ DialogUI (SFML)        │  │
│  │  - text input          │  │
│  │  - scrolling transcript│  │
│  │  - "thinking..." state │  │
│  └────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────┘
```

### Key design points
- **One `LlmClient` for the whole game.** NPCs don't each open their own connection — they all call `LlmClient::chat(personaSystemPrompt, history, userMsg, onReply)`. This matches your "centralized" intent.
- **Async by default.** The game loop never blocks on an LLM call. We use a worker thread + a thread-safe reply queue drained on the main thread (SFML is single-threaded for rendering).
- **Per-NPC history, capped.** Each `Npc` keeps its own conversation as a `vector<Turn>`. We cap it to N most-recent turns (e.g. 10) and prepend the persona system prompt every request. Simple, predictable token usage.
- **Persona template, not hardcoded NPCs.** `Persona { name, role, traits, speakingStyle, knowledgeBoundaries }` rendered into a system prompt string at construction. "Jim the pharmacist" and "Jane the random pedestrian #47" are two `Npc` instances built from the same template — exactly what you described.
- **Streaming optional.** Ollama supports streaming token-by-token; for the first milestone we ignore it and just wait for the full reply (simpler). Add streaming later if reply latency feels long.

---

## New C++ dependencies (only inside `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/`)

All header-only / vendored to keep cross-platform builds easy. No package manager required.

| Dep | Why | How to add |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **cpp-httplib** | Single-header HTTPS/HTTP client. POST to Ollama. | Vendor `httplib.h` into `external/` |
| **nlohmann/json** | Build/parse Ollama JSON requests and responses. | Vendor `json.hpp` into `external/` |
| **SFML 2.6** | Already used by the other games; reuse for window + text UI. | Same install path as existing games (apt / brew / vcpkg) |

No new runtime libs beyond what SFML already pulls in. Cross-platform "just works" because both vendored libs are header-only.

---

## Proposed directory layout

```
cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── README.md
├── config/
│   └── llm.cfg                 # ollama host, model name, temperature, max tokens
├── external/
│   ├── httplib.h
│   └── json.hpp
├── personas/
│   └── companion.txt           # system prompt template for the first NPC
├── src/
│   ├── main.cpp                # window + game loop + DialogUI glue
│   ├── LlmClient.hpp/.cpp      # HTTP + async queue
│   ├── Npc.hpp/.cpp            # persona + history + askAsync
│   ├── Persona.hpp             # struct + prompt renderer
│   └── DialogUI.hpp/.cpp       # SFML text box + transcript
└── run.sh / run.ps1            # cross-platform launch scripts
```

This mirrors the single-folder-per-game pattern of the other two but adds `src/` subfiles (the other games are single-file; we need more structure here because the LLM glue earns its own modules).

---

## First milestone: "the companion"

A vertical slice you can run end-to-end:

1. **Window** — single SFML window, 1280×720, dark background.
2. **The companion** — one `Npc` loaded from `personas/companion.txt`. Suggested starting persona: a curious traveling companion who knows nothing about real-world topics but lots about the (yet-undefined) game world. Keeps replies short (1-3 sentences).
3. **Dialog UI** — bottom-of-screen text input, scrolling transcript above. Press Enter to send; UI shows "*\<Companion\> is thinking...*" while the LLM call is in flight.
4. **Centralized client** — even with one NPC, the `LlmClient` is built as a singleton from day one so adding NPC #2, #3, etc. requires no refactor.
5. **No game world yet** — no 3D, no movement, no combat. Just the chat. This proves the dialogue loop in isolation before you wire it into anything more ambitious.

---

## Files to create (representative — not exhaustive)

- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/CMakeLists.txt` — finds SFML, adds `src/*.cpp`, includes `external/`. Same CMake 3.20+ baseline as your other games.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.hpp/.cpp` — public interface `chat(systemPrompt, history, userMsg, callback)`; internal worker thread and `std::queue<Reply>` drained from main thread.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Persona.hpp` — struct + `renderSystemPrompt()` that produces the final string Ollama receives.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Npc.hpp/.cpp` — owns a `Persona` and a bounded `vector<Turn>`; exposes `askAsync(playerLine, onReply)`.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/DialogUI.hpp/.cpp` — SFML text input + transcript rendering + "thinking" indicator.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp` — wires it all together; ~150 lines.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/config/llm.cfg` — key/value (same style as racing game's `track.cfg`): `host=localhost`, `port=11434`, `model=qwen2.5:3b-instruct`, `temperature=0.8`, `max_history_turns=10`.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/personas/companion.txt` — plain-text system prompt template.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/run.sh` and `run.ps1` — cross-platform launchers (check Ollama is running, build, run).

---

## Setup steps the user runs once

1. **Install Ollama** — Linux: `curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh`. Windows: installer from ollama.com.
2. **Pull the model** — `ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct` (~2 GB download).
3. **Confirm it runs** — `ollama run qwen2.5:3b-instruct "say hi"` should reply in a couple of seconds with GPU usage visible in `nvidia-smi`.
4. **Install SFML 2.6** — Linux: `sudo apt install libsfml-dev` (or distro equivalent). Windows: keep the existing MSYS2 path.
5. **Build** — `cmake -S cpp_game_with_llm_npcs -B cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/build && cmake --build cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/build`.
6. **Run** — `./cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/run.sh` (Ollama must be running; the script checks).

---

## Verification (manual test plan for milestone 1)

- `ollama list` shows `qwen2.5:3b-instruct`.
- `curl http://localhost:11434/api/chat -d '{"model":"qwen2.5:3b-instruct","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"stream":false}'` returns a JSON reply with a non-empty `message.content`.
- Game window opens, shows transcript area and input box.

---

## LLM choice

### Recommended starting model: **Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct** (`qwen2.5:3b-instruct`)
- ~2 GB on disk at Q4_K_M, ~3 GB VRAM at runtime — leaves plenty of headroom.
- Strong instruction-following at small size; good at staying in a persona when given a clear system prompt.
- Fast on a 6GB GPU (30+ tokens/sec typical), so replies feel snappy.
- Permissive license (Apache 2.0–compatible terms for the open weights).

### Honorable mentions (try after Qwen feels limiting)
- **Llama 3.2 3B Instruct** (`llama3.2:3b-instruct`) — comparable size, slightly different writing style. Easy A/B swap.
- **Nous Hermes 3 8B** (`hermes3:8b`) — 8B Llama-3.1 fine-tune explicitly tuned for roleplay and persona consistency. Fits your VRAM at Q4_K_M (~5 GB). This is the upgrade target once you want richer characters.
- **Phi-3.5 Mini 3.8B** (`phi3.5:3.8b-mini-instruct`) — Microsoft's small model; strong reasoning but somewhat stiffer dialogue. Worth trying for contrast.

What we are **not** picking and why:
- Anything under 1B (TinyLlama, SmolLM) — too prone to breaking character mid-reply.
- 13B+ models — overkill for "blacksmith small talk," and slower iteration during development.

- You can swap models with one config line, with no rebuild.
- Migration path to embedded `llama.cpp` later is clean because the `LlmClient` interface will hide the transport.

---

┌──────────────────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────────┐
│  cpp_game_with_llm_npcs      │  HTTP   │  Ollama (sidecar)      │

│                              │  JSON   │  localhost:11434       │
│  ┌────────────────────────┐  │         └────────────────────────┘

│  │  - async request queue │  │
│  │  - HTTP via cpp-httplib│  │
│  └─────────▲──────────────┘  │
│            │                 │

│  │  - Persona (system     │  │

│  │  - ConversationHistory │  │
│  │  - askAsync(playerLine)│  │

│  │  - scrolling transcript│  │
│  │  - "thinking..." state │  │
│  └────────────────────────┘  │

```
cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── README.md
├── config/
│   └── llm.cfg                 # ollama host, model name, temperature, max tokens

- Strong instruction-following at small size; good at staying in a persona when given a clear system prompt.
- Fast on a 6GB GPU (30+ tokens/sec typical), so replies feel snappy.
- Permissive license (Apache 2.0–compatible terms for the open weights).

- The C++ game just needs an HTTP client — no CMake gymnastics for CUDA/CMake/llama.cpp yet.

- Migration path to embedded `llama.cpp` later is clean because the `LlmClient` interface will hide the transport.

│                              │  JSON   │  localhost:11434       │
│  ┌────────────────────────┐  │         └────────────────────────┘
│  │ LlmClient (singleton)  │  │
│  │  - async request queue │  │
│  │  - HTTP via cpp-httplib│  │
│  └─────────▲──────────────┘  │
│            │                 │
│  ┌─────────┴──────────────┐  │

│  │  - Persona (system     │  │

| Dep | Why | How to add |
| --- | --- | --- |

```

├── README.md
├── config/
│   └── llm.cfg                 # ollama host, model name, temperature, max tokens
├── external/
│   ├── httplib.h
│   └── json.hpp
├── personas/
│   └── companion.txt           # system prompt template for the first NPC
├── src/
│   ├── main.cpp                # window + game loop + DialogUI glue

## Verification (manual test plan for milestone 1)

- `ollama list` shows `qwen2.5:3b-instruct`.
- `curl http://localhost:11434/api/chat -d '{"model":"qwen2.5:3b-instruct","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"stream":false}'` returns a JSON reply with a non-empty `message.content`.
- Game window opens, shows transcript area and input box.
- Typing "hi" and pressing Enter shows the user line in the transcript, then "*Companion is thinking...*", then the reply within a few seconds.
- The reply respects the persona (e.g., refuses to answer real-world questions in character; stays short).
- Sending 15+ messages exercises the history cap — no crash, no slowdown beyond steady state.
- Killing Ollama mid-game produces a graceful in-transcript error like *"\[Companion seems distracted...\]"* rather than a crash.
- Build runs cleanly on at least one Linux box (since cross-platform is a stated goal — if Windows is the only available test target, note that as a follow-up).

---

## Future work (explicitly out of scope for milestone 1)

- **Embed llama.cpp** — once dialogue feels right, swap `LlmClient`'s implementation from cpp-httplib → llama.cpp's C API. The public interface stays the same; only `LlmClient.cpp` changes.
- **Streaming replies** — show tokens as they arrive for a less "frozen" feel.
- **Multiple NPCs in a world** — the architecture already supports this; just instantiate more `Npc`s and add a way to choose who you're talking to (proximity, click, etc.).
- **Persistent memory** — write `vector<Turn>` per NPC to disk between sessions.
- **Game world** — once chat is fun on its own, layer it onto a 3D or 2D world (potentially borrowing rendering patterns from the shooter game).

input.content:
# cpp_game_with_llm_npcs

Milestone 1 of a small game where NPCs hold conversations powered by a single
local LLM. This first slice is just a chat window with one companion NPC named
**Wren**. No world, no movement, no combat — just dialogue. Later NPCs reuse
the same `LlmClient` by design.

## Architecture at a glance

- **One `LlmClient`** owns the only thread that talks to the LLM. Every NPC
  submits requests to it and gets replies back through a thread-safe queue
  drained on the main thread.
- **`Npc`** holds a `Persona` and a bounded conversation history. The history
  is capped at 10 round-trip turns so token usage stays predictable.
- **`Persona`** is a small struct rendered into a system prompt. "Jim the
  pharmacist" and "Jane the random pedestrian #47" are two `Persona` instances,
  not two classes.
- **Ollama** runs as a sidecar HTTP service. The C++ side just POSTs JSON to
  `localhost:11434/api/chat`. Vendored header-only deps (`cpp-httplib`,
  `nlohmann/json`) live in `external/`.

## One-time setup

### 1. Install Ollama

- **Linux:** `curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh`
- **Windows:** installer from <https://ollama.com>

### 2. Pull a model

```
ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct
```

About 2 GB. Runs comfortably on any 6 GB+ NVIDIA GPU. Swap to a different tag
later by editing `config/llm.cfg` — no rebuild needed. Suggested alternates:

- `llama3.2:3b-instruct` — comparable size, different voice.
- `hermes3:8b` — bigger, much better roleplay; needs ~5 GB VRAM at Q4_K_M.

### 3. Install SFML 2.6

- **Linux (Debian/Ubuntu):** `sudo apt install libsfml-dev`
- **Linux (Arch):** `sudo pacman -S sfml`
- **Windows:** MSYS2 UCRT64 — `pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-sfml`

## Build & run

Make sure `ollama serve` is running, then:

```
./run.sh         # Linux / macOS
./run.ps1        # Windows (PowerShell, MSYS2 UCRT64)
```

Either script verifies Ollama is reachable, configures CMake, builds, and
launches the game.

Or manually:

```
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build -j
./build/cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
```

## Talking to Wren

Type a line, press Enter. The input box dims while Wren is thinking; it
re-enables once the reply lands. Press Esc (or close the window) to quit.

## Where to look next

- `src/Persona.hpp` — add traits, change voice, or define new NPCs.
- `personas/companion.txt` — extra system-prompt directives, hot-reloaded on
  every launch (no rebuild).
- `config/llm.cfg` — host, port, model tag, temperature.

## Future milestones

- Multiple NPCs in one scene (architecture already supports it).
- Streaming token-by-token replies for a snappier feel.
- Persistent per-NPC memory across sessions.
- Embed `llama.cpp` directly to drop the Ollama dependency.

This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.

Based on the search results, here's information about the Ollama `/api/chat` endpoint request format for the messages parameter:

## Request Format

The endpoint accepts a POST request with a `model` field and a `messages` array. Here's the basic structure:

```json
{
  "model": "model-name",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": "your message here"
    }
  ]
}
```

## Messages Structure

The messages parameter is a list of messages, each message being an object with a `role` field. Possible values are: system, user, assistant, or tool.

Each message has the following fields: `role` (the role of the message), `content` (string), `images` (optional), and `tool_calls` (optional).

## Example

Here's an example with a user message: `{ "model": "llama3.2", "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "why is the sky blue?" } ] }`

## Additional Options

The request can also include other parameters like:
- `stream`: if false the response will be returned as a single response object, rather than a stream of objects
- `options`: additional model parameters such as temperature

Based on the search results, here's what I found about llama.cpp, embedding it in C++ applications, and GGUF integration:

## Overview

Llama.cpp is a library written in C/C++ for efficient inference of Large Language models. llama.cpp began development in March 2023 by Georgi Gerganov as an implementation of the Llama inference code in pure C/C++ with no dependencies.

## C++ Integration

For developers who want to embed local inference in a product rather than wrap an existing tool, llama.cpp is the layer to integrate against. The library provides a header file (`llama.h`) that you can include directly in your C++ applications for integration.

## GGUF Format

llama.cpp requires the model to be stored in the GGUF file format. GGUF focuses on quantization, the act of reducing precision in the model weights. This can lead to reduced memory usage and increased speed, albeit at the cost of reduced model accuracy.

## Game Development

Styled Lines is a proprietary licensed, async wrapper of inference part for game development in Unity3d with pre-built Mobile and Web platform wrappers and a model example. This suggests there are tools specifically designed for integrating llama.cpp into game applications.

## 2026 Status

As of May 2026, it has more than 109,000 stars on GitHub. Recent additions include full acceleration on Android and ChromeOS devices was introduced via a new GUI binding on December 17, 2025, which unlocks native app development beyond the previous approach of cross-compiling and running CLI in an adb shell.

Lesson 0001 · cpp_games / docs / learning

Embedded LLMs in Game Applications

Why this matters for cpp_game_with_llm_npcs: every line of dialogue your companion Wren says will come out of a model running on the player's machine. The architectural choices on this page are the architecture of your game.

1. The concept

An embedded LLM in a game is a language model whose output is consumed by the running game process — usually to generate NPC dialogue, narrate events, or interpret freeform player input. "Embedded" here doesn't necessarily mean the model lives inside the game's binary; it means the game itself drives inference rather than the user opening a chatbot in another window. There are three ways to plug one in, and the choice shapes everything else.

StyleWhat it isBest when
Cloud APIPOST to a remote service (OpenAI, Anthropic, Inworld, Convai).You want top quality and can require internet, payment, and trusting a third party with player prompts.
Sidecar processA separate local process (Ollama, LM Studio, llamafile) hosts the model and exposes HTTP on localhost.You want fully local with the smallest engineering cost. This is what we picked.
In-process libraryThe model lives in the game binary, called via a C/C++ API (llama.cpp, ONNX Runtime, candle, MLC-LLM).You're ready to ship to non-technical players and own GPU detection, quantization, and threading.

Why do this at all? Pre-LLM NPCs used dialogue trees: finite hand-authored graphs of "if player picks option B, NPC says line 47." Linear in writer-hours, canned by the second playthrough. LLM-driven NPCs trade authorial control for combinatorial breadth: the same blacksmith can answer a question no writer anticipated, in voice, because the persona prompt constrains how he talks rather than what he can say. The price is loss of guarantees — an unconstrained NPC might hallucinate a quest item, break character, or wander into real-world topics. The mitigations form a ladder of complexity:

  • Persona prompt + bounded history — cheapest, what we use. Just rules and recent context.
  • Structured output — force JSON with an allowed-action enum, validated with a grammar.
  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) — the NPC's "memory" is a searched knowledge base.

Industry footprint as of mid-2026: AI Dungeon (2019) pioneered the pattern with cloud calls. Suck Up! (2023) shipped with cloud LLM NPCs. Modders shipped Skyrim and Stardew Valley LLM-NPC mods using Ollama as a local sidecar. In 2026 we now have Gemma3NPC — a Gemma 3 fine-tune specifically for NPC roleplay — and Llama 4 Scout 9B as the low-VRAM darling. No AAA title has shipped with a fully embedded local LLM yet, mainly because consumer GPU VRAM is finite and competes with the rest of the game.

Our pick for milestone 1

Ollama sidecar serving qwen2.5:3b-instruct — small, fast, permissive license, and the same shape we'd swap to a 9B Gemma3NPC or Llama 4 Scout later with one config-line change.

2. A minimal standalone example

The sidecar technique in its entirety is 15 lines. The real game just wraps this in a worker thread and a reply queue.

#include "httplib.h"   // single-header HTTP client
#include "json.hpp"    // single-header JSON
using nlohmann::json;

int main() {
    // 1. Build the chat body. "system" = persona; "user" = player line.
    json body = {
        {"model", "qwen2.5:3b-instruct"},
        {"stream", false},
        {"messages", {
            {{"role", "system"}, {"content", "You are a gruff blacksmith. 1-2 sentences."}},
            {{"role", "user"},   {"content", "Have you seen any travelers today?"}},
        }},
    };

    // 2. POST to Ollama on localhost. No auth — it's local.
    httplib::Client cli("localhost", 11434);
    auto res = cli.Post("/api/chat", body.dump(), "application/json");

    // 3. Ollama replies with { "message": { "role", "content" }, ... }
    auto parsed = json::parse(res->body);
    std::cout << parsed["message"]["content"].get<std::string>() << "\n";
}

What this example doesn't show but a real game needs:

  • Async — that cli.Post() blocks for 1–3 seconds. A 60 fps game loop can't sit on it.
  • History — each NPC needs its own prior messages[] so context carries.
  • Bounding — history grows forever otherwise. Cap to N recent turns.
  • Failure handling — Ollama might not be running. Don't crash; surface it in character.

3. In this project

Each bullet above maps to a real file in your repo. The minimal example is what LlmClient::processOne() would look like with the production concerns ripped out.

Per-NPC history.../src/Npc.hppstd::vector<ChatTurn> history_
Bounded to 10 turns.../src/Npc.cpptrimHistory()

Non-blocking polling.../src/LlmClient.cppdrainReplies()
In-character failure.../src/main.cpp"[Wren seems distracted...]"

Walkthrough — the heart of LlmClient.cpp

This is the real function from your repo. Each comment block names the concept it implements.

// SIDECAR INTEGRATION — game talks to Ollama via plain HTTP.
ChatReply LlmClient::processOne(const ChatRequest& req) {
    ChatReply reply;
    reply.id = req.id;

    // PERSONA + HISTORY — system prompt, then prior turns, then user line.
    json messages = json::array();
    if (!req.systemPrompt.empty()) {
        messages.push_back({{"role", "system"}, {"content", req.systemPrompt}});
    }
    for (const auto& turn : req.history) {
        messages.push_back({{"role", turn.role}, {"content", turn.content}});
    }
    messages.push_back({{"role", "user"}, {"content", req.userMessage}});

    // stream=false → one reply at the end. Switch to true for streaming.
    json body = {
        {"model", config_.model},
        {"messages", messages},
        {"stream", false},
        {"options", {{"temperature", config_.temperature}}},
    };

    // FAILURE-FRIENDLY TRANSPORT — bounded timeouts so a hung Ollama
    // can't freeze the worker thread forever.
    httplib::Client cli(config_.host, config_.port);
    cli.set_read_timeout(config_.requestTimeoutSeconds, 0);
    cli.set_connection_timeout(5, 0);

    auto res = cli.Post("/api/chat", body.dump(), "application/json");
    if (!res) {
        reply.errorMessage = "could not reach Ollama";
        return reply;  // reply.ok stays false; UI handles it
    }
    // ... parse res->body into reply.content ...
    return reply;
}

Walkthrough — the async drain pattern

This is what lets a 60 fps game loop talk to a model that takes seconds to reply. Submit from the main thread, drain from the main thread, never block.

// MAIN THREAD, game loop frame N: submit and move on.
companion.ask("Have you seen any travelers?");
ui.setThinking(true);

// MAIN THREAD, every frame after: empty whatever has landed.
for (const auto& reply : client.drainReplies()) {
    auto text = companion.onReplyArrived(reply);
    if (text) ui.appendLine({Kind::Npc, "Wren", *text});
    ui.setThinking(false);
}

And the worker, the classic condition-variable consumer:

void LlmClient::workerLoop() {
    while (true) {
        ChatRequest req;
        {
            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(requestMutex_);
            requestCv_.wait(lock, [this] {
                return stop_.load() || !requests_.empty();
            });
            if (stop_.load() && requests_.empty()) return;
            req = std::move(requests_.front());
            requests_.pop();
        }
        ChatReply reply = processOne(req);  // the slow part
        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(replyMutex_);
            replies_.push_back(std::move(reply));
        }
    }
}

Two separate mutexes (one for the request queue, one for the reply list) is intentional: producer and consumer never contend, and the main thread can drain replies without ever blocking the worker mid-call.

4. Often confused with...

Sidecar process vs. embedded library

People hear "embedded LLM" and assume the model is linked into the binary. It might be (in-process), or it might be a separate program speaking HTTP (sidecar). Both qualify as "embedded in a game" the way we use the term — what matters is that your code drives inference. The line between them is which process holds the model in RAM.

 Sidecar (Ollama, what we use)In-process (llama.cpp linked in)
Who hosts the model?A separate process you startedYour game's own process
Player installThey must install Ollama tooOne executable, drop in
Switch modelsOne config lineRecompile or runtime model loader
Latency floor+localhost HTTP overhead (low)Function call (lowest)
Engineering costVendor cpp-httplib, you're doneOwn GPU/CUDA/quantization wiring

Concurrency vs. parallelism

Our worker thread gives us concurrency — the game loop and the LLM call are interleaved in time, both making progress — even on a single core. We get parallelism — literally executing simultaneously — only because modern CPUs have multiple cores. The architecture would work fine on a single-core machine; it would just be slower. Don't conflate "I added a thread" with "now it runs in parallel." You added concurrency; whether it's parallel depends on the hardware.

System prompt vs. RAG memory

Both supply context to the model. The system prompt is fixed identity ("you are Wren, a curious traveler"). Retrieval-augmented memory is dynamic recall ("look up what Wren learned about the player last session, paste the relevant bits into this turn's prompt"). Confusing the two is what produces NPCs that endlessly re-explain their own backstory: that's identity, it goes in the system prompt, not in retrieved memory.

5. Quiz

Click an answer; you'll see immediately whether it's right and why. The score badge in the corner tracks your progress.

Why does each Npc keep its own conversation history rather than the shared LlmClient keeping one history for the whole game?

  • Because keeping multiple histories saves on HTTP connection overhead.
  • So Jim the pharmacist's prior turns don't leak into Jane the pedestrian's prompts.
  • So we can have multiple LlmClient instances running in parallel.
  • Because the model itself already remembers previous chats with each character.

In the minimal example, cli.Post() blocks for 1–3 seconds. Which two pieces of machinery in our real code prevent the game from freezing?

  • setFramerateLimit(60) and a smaller temperature value.
  • Streaming responses and a shorter system prompt.
  • A worker thread doing the POST, and a thread-safe reply queue drained each frame.
  • A UDP socket and a callback registered with the OS.

What is the role of stream: false in the request body?

  • It makes the model's output deterministic.
  • It tells Ollama to return one complete reply at the end, not token-by-token.
  • It forces HTTPS so the reply is encrypted.
  • It disables the model's conversational memory.

You decide to ship your game to players who don't want to install Ollama. Which migration does our architecture already make cheap?

  • Switch every NPC to call OpenAI's API directly.
  • Replace processOne() with a call into linked llama.cpp, leaving the public LlmClient interface unchanged.
  • Convert all NPC dialogue back to a hand-authored dialogue tree.
  • Give each NPC its own dedicated worker thread.

A player asks Wren "what year is it in real life?" and she answers correctly with the current year. What is the most likely failure here?

  • The temperature in llm.cfg is too high.
  • We forgot to call trimHistory() often enough.
  • The persona's knowledgeBoundary and directives aren't strong enough to keep her in-frame.
  • Ollama is overriding our system prompt with its own.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

These are open-ended — jot down answers and we'll work through them. There's no auto-grader here on purpose; the goal is for you to explain it in your own words.

Scenario A. You add a second NPC, Jim the pharmacist. After a few turns Jim starts referring to "your friend Wren" by name. Where in the codebase is the bug, and what fix would you make?

Scenario B. Players complain that the 1–3 second "thinking..." delay feels dead. You don't want to change models. What single configuration change in the JSON body would help, and what code in LlmClient.cpp would you have to rewrite to take advantage of it?

Scenario C. You decide to swap to hermes3:8b. Walk through everywhere you have to touch — and everywhere you explicitly don't.

7. Track your progress

Tick these off as you go — resets when you reload (in-page only).

What is the role of stream: false in the request body?

  • It makes the model's output deterministic.
  • It tells Ollama to return one complete reply at the end, not token-by-token.
  • It forces HTTPS so the reply is encrypted.
  • It disables the model's conversational memory.

You decide to ship your game to players who don't want to install Ollama. Which migration does our architecture already make cheap?

  • Switch every NPC to call OpenAI's API directly.
  • Replace processOne() with a call into linked llama.cpp, leaving the public LlmClient interface unchanged.
  • Convert all NPC dialogue back to a hand-authored dialogue tree.
  • Give each NPC its own dedicated worker thread.

A player asks Wren "what year is it in real life?" and she answers correctly with the current year. What is the most likely failure here?

  • The temperature in llm.cfg is too high.
  • We forgot to call trimHistory() often enough.
  • The persona's knowledgeBoundary and directives aren't strong enough to keep her in-frame.
  • Ollama is overriding our system prompt with its own.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

These are open-ended — jot down answers and we'll work through them. There's no auto-grader here on purpose; the goal is for you to explain it in your own words.

Scenario A. You add a second NPC, Jim the pharmacist. After a few turns Jim starts referring to "your friend Wren" by name. Where in the codebase is the bug, and what fix would you make?

Scenario C. You decide to swap to hermes3:8b. Walk through everywhere you have to touch — and everywhere you explicitly don't.

input.content:
Quiz: 0 / 0
Lesson 0002 · cpp_games / docs / learning

std::vector vs. array

Why this matters: all three of your games pick between a fixed-size and a dynamic-size container every few hundred lines. Pick wrong and you either pay for heap allocation you didn't need (slow) or get memory corruption when the count grows past the bound you assumed (crash). This lesson is the rule for getting it right reliably.

1. The concept

C++ gives you three flavours of "a bunch of things in a row." They look similar in the source but differ enormously in where the storage lives, whether the size can change, and what you can hand to a function.

ContainerSizeStorageType carries size?
C-style array
T arr[N]		Fixed, set at declarationWherever the variable lives (stack, static, member)Yes — until it decays to a pointer.
std::array<T, N>Fixed at compile timeSame as above — usually the stackYes, permanently. Doesn't decay.
std::vector<T>Dynamic, grows and shrinks at runtimeHeap (the vector struct itself is on the stack; the data is heap-allocated)No — size is a runtime value you call .size() for.

The shortest possible decision rule:

Picking between them

Do you know the count at compile time? → std::array<T, N>.
Does the count change at runtime? → std::vector<T>.
Are you interoperating with C, or writing a tiny throwaway literal list? → C-style array is acceptable but not preferred.

The trap to know about: a C-style array decays to a pointer the moment you pass it to a function. void f(int arr[10]) looks like it knows the array is 10 long; it doesn't. The parameter is silently rewritten to int* arr and sizeof(arr) inside f is the size of a pointer, not the array. std::array never decays; std::array<int, 10>& stays exactly that.

The other thing to know: std::vector looks small — just three pointers on the stack — but every push that exceeds capacity triggers a heap reallocation and a copy/move of every element. Reserve up front when you know the count: v.reserve(1024). We'll see this in the shooter game shortly.

2. Minimal example — all three side by side

#include <array>
#include <vector>
#include <cstdio>

// Compile-time fixed size. Lives on the stack. Type loses size when passed.
void takesCArray(int arr[3]) {
    // printf("%zu", sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]));   // BUG: prints "2" on a 64-bit box.
    // arr decayed to int*; you have no way to ask "how many?".
}

// Compile-time fixed size. Type carries N forever. Pass by ref to avoid copy.
void takesArray(const std::array<int, 3>& arr) {
    std::printf("%zu\n", arr.size());  // always 3, known at compile time
}

// Runtime size. Storage is heap; the vector struct itself is small.
void takesVector(const std::vector<int>& v) {
    std::printf("%zu\n", v.size());  // whatever happens to be in there right now
}

int main() {
    int                  c[3] = {1, 2, 3};   // stack, fixed, decays
    std::array<int, 3>   a   = {1, 2, 3};   // stack, fixed, doesn't decay
    std::vector<int>     v   = {1, 2, 3};   // heap, can grow
    v.push_back(4);                          // fine; a and c cannot grow.

    takesCArray(c);
    takesArray(a);
    takesVector(v);
}

The interesting line is the commented-out sizeof(arr) inside takesCArray. That's the classic C bug C++'s std::array exists to eliminate.

3. In your games — the real code

Your three games together touch all three flavours. Here's the actual code, identified by which game it came from.

Fixed and small: use std::array

cpp_racing_game/src/main.cpp:943 
// A quad is, by definition, exactly four corners. The type guarantees that.
const std::array<sf::Vector2f, 4> outerQuad = {
    sf::Vector2f(kOuterX, kOuterY),
    sf::Vector2f(kOuterX + kOuterW, kOuterY),
    sf::Vector2f(kOuterX + kOuterW, kOuterY + kOuterH),
    sf::Vector2f(kOuterX, kOuterY + kOuterH),
};
cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:168 (and cpp_racing_game/src/main.cpp:597) 
// A 4x4 matrix is exactly 16 floats. Encoding that in the type
// stops you from ever accidentally building a 15-element "matrix".
const std::array<float, 16> matrix = { /* ... 16 entries ... */ };
cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:390 
// Three hardcoded font paths to try. Count is fixed; std::array advertises that.
const std::array<const char*, 3> candidates = {
    "C:/Windows/Fonts/arial.ttf",
    "C:/Windows/Fonts/segoeui.ttf",
    "C:/Windows/Fonts/tahoma.ttf",
};

Unknown until runtime: use std::vector

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:320 
struct GameState {
    Player player;
    std::vector<Projectile> projectiles;  // fired and consumed every frame
    std::vector<Enemy>      enemies;      // waves spawn variable counts
    std::vector<Pickup>     pickups;      // drop randomly, get picked up
    std::vector<ImpactEffect> impacts;    // born on hit, expire by timer
    // ...
};

None of those counts can be known at compile time. Every frame the shooter adds and removes entries from each of these. std::array would be wrong here because you cannot push or pop — the size is baked into the type.

cpp_racing_game/src/main.cpp:262 
// The number of points depends on cornerSegments — a runtime parameter.
std::vector<sf::Vector2f> buildRoundedRectLoop(float x, float y, float w, float h,
                                               float radius, int cornerSegments) {
    std::vector<sf::Vector2f> pts;
    // ... fill pts with up to ~4*cornerSegments points ...
    return pts;
}
cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:110 
// Size depends on the runtime `size` argument. Heap allocation is unavoidable.
std::vector<std::uint8_t> pixels(size * size * 4, 255);
cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Npc.hpp 
class Npc {
    // History grows turn by turn as the player chats. Cap is enforced
    // at runtime by trimHistory(), not by the type.
    std::vector<ChatTurn> history_;
};

The odd one out — a C-style array, in our newest code

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp:72 
const char* candidates[] = {
    "/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans.ttf",
    "/usr/share/fonts/dejavu/DejaVuSans.ttf",
    "C:/Windows/Fonts/segoeui.ttf",
    /* ... */
};
for (const char* c : candidates) { /* ... */ }

Compare with the shooter game's std::array<const char*, 3> candidates — same job, two different choices. Both compile. Both work. But:

  • The shooter version's type loudly states "there are exactly three of these." The new game's type doesn't — you'd have to count the lines.
  • If you ever pass the new game's array to a helper function, it'll decay to a pointer and the receiver loses the count.
  • Range-for (for (auto c : candidates)) works on both, which is why the C-style version doesn't bite us here.

So the C-style array isn't wrong in that exact spot — but the shooter's version is better style and would survive refactoring better. Replacing it with std::array<const char*, 6> would be a one-line improvement.

4. Often confused with...

C-style array vs. std::array

Same storage (typically stack), same access syntax, same iteration. The difference is what survives travel:

 int arr[3]std::array<int, 3>
.size()No method. Use sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) — brittle.arr.size(), always 3, constexpr.
Decay on function callYes — turns into int*, count is lost.No — size travels with the type.
Copy assignmentForbidden. a = b doesn't compile.Works. a = b copies all elements.
Returned from a functionForbidden directly.Works.
Bounds-checked accessNever.arr.at(i) throws on out-of-range. arr[i] doesn't.

std::array vs. std::vector

The biggest single-word difference is where:

 std::array<T, N>std::vector<T>
StorageInline — same memory as the variable itself. Typically stack.Heap — the vector holds 3 pointers and calls new/delete behind your back.
Size known when?Compile time. Baked into the type.Runtime. .size() is a counter.
Can grow?No. The type forbids it.Yes — push_back, resize, etc.
Allocation costZero — comes with the stack frame.At least one heap allocation; more on growth.
Best whenQuad corners, matrix entries, fixed lookup tables.Enemies, projectiles, chat history, anything dynamic.

std::vector vs. std::list (a trap worth naming)

Beginners reach for std::list when they hear "the middle of a vector is slow to delete from." It usually isn't, and std::list is almost always worse than a std::vector with erase — because vector's contiguous layout is so cache-friendly that even shifting elements often beats the pointer-chasing a linked list does. The shooter game's std::vector<Enemy> deletes mid-vector when enemies die; that's faster than the equivalent std::list<Enemy> would be on any modern CPU. Don't reach for std::list unless you've measured and have a specific reason.

5. Quiz

In the racing game, outerQuad is declared as std::array<sf::Vector2f, 4>. Why not std::vector<sf::Vector2f>?

  • A quad always has four corners; encoding that in the type prevents bugs and avoids a heap allocation.

Why this matters: all three of your games pick between a fixed-size and a dynamic-size container every few hundred lines. Pick wrong and you either pay for heap allocation you didn't need (slow) or get memory corruption when the count grows past the bound you assumed (crash). This lesson is the rule for getting it right reliably.

1. The concept

C++ gives you three flavours of "a bunch of things in a row." They look similar in the source but differ enormously in where the storage lives, whether the size can change, and what you can hand to a function.

ContainerSizeStorageType carries size?
C-style array
T arr[N]		Fixed, set at declarationWherever the variable lives (stack, static, member)Yes — until it decays to a pointer.
std::array<T, N>Fixed at compile timeSame as above — usually the stackYes, permanently. Doesn't decay.
std::vector<T>Dynamic, grows and shrinks at runtimeHeap (the vector struct itself is on the stack; the data is heap-allocated)No — size is a runtime value you call .size() for.

The shortest possible decision rule:

Picking between them

Do you know the count at compile time? → std::array<T, N>.
Does the count change at runtime? → std::vector<T>.
Are you interoperating with C, or writing a tiny throwaway literal list? → C-style array is acceptable but not preferred.

The trap to know about: a C-style array decays to a pointer the moment you pass it to a function. void f(int arr[10]) looks like it knows the array is 10 long; it doesn't. The parameter is silently rewritten to int* arr and sizeof(arr) inside f is the size of a pointer, not the array. std::array never decays; std::array<int, 10>& stays exactly that.

The other thing to know: std::vector looks small — just three pointers on the stack — but every push that exceeds capacity triggers a heap reallocation and a copy/move of every element. Reserve up front when you know the count: v.reserve(1024). We'll see this in the shooter game shortly.

2. Minimal example — all three side by side

#include <array>
#include <vector>
#include <cstdio>

// Compile-time fixed size. Lives on the stack. Type loses size when passed.
void takesCArray(int arr[3]) {
    // printf("%zu", sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]));   // BUG: prints "2" on a 64-bit box.
    // arr decayed to int*; you have no way to ask "how many?".
}

// Compile-time fixed size. Type carries N forever. Pass by ref to avoid copy.
void takesArray(const std::array<int, 3>& arr) {
    std::printf("%zu\n", arr.size());  // always 3, known at compile time
}

// Runtime size. Storage is heap; the vector struct itself is small.
void takesVector(const std::vector<int>& v) {
    std::printf("%zu\n", v.size());  // whatever happens to be in there right now
}

int main() {
    int                  c[3] = {1, 2, 3};   // stack, fixed, decays
    std::array<int, 3>   a   = {1, 2, 3};   // stack, fixed, doesn't decay
    std::vector<int>     v   = {1, 2, 3};   // heap, can grow
    v.push_back(4);                          // fine; a and c cannot grow.

    takesCArray(c);
    takesArray(a);
    takesVector(v);
}

The interesting line is the commented-out sizeof(arr) inside takesCArray. That's the classic C bug C++'s std::array exists to eliminate.

// A quad is, by definition, exactly four corners. The type guarantees that.
const std::array<sf::Vector2f, 4> outerQuad = {

    sf::Vector2f(kOuterX + kOuterW, kOuterY),
    sf::Vector2f(kOuterX + kOuterW, kOuterY + kOuterH),
    sf::Vector2f(kOuterX, kOuterY + kOuterH),
};
cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:168 (and cpp_racing_game/src/main.cpp:597) 
// A 4x4 matrix is exactly 16 floats. Encoding that in the type
// stops you from ever accidentally building a 15-element "matrix".

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:390

    "C:/Windows/Fonts/segoeui.ttf",
    "C:/Windows/Fonts/tahoma.ttf",

    Player player;

// Size depends on the runtime `size` argument. Heap allocation is unavoidable.

The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. ## Frame Budget Context
If a game engine runs at 60 FPS, you have ~16ms per frame to do all computations; saving even 1ms through optimization can accommodate more game logic or better graphics.

## Memory Allocation Best Practices

Most shared or larger resources get allocated on the heap through dynamic allocation using malloc or new, which requires a system call to expand the heap and introduces additional latency. Low-latency systems avoid this by pre-allocating memory segments at startup and building custom allocators on top of those segments to distribute memory during runtime, with the primary goal of eliminating all system calls from the hot path entirely.

Effective memory management is crucial for reducing latency in C++. Understanding the nuances of dynamic versus static allocation, as well as the differences between stack and heap usage, can profoundly impact performance. In many cases, stack allocation is faster as it is automatically managed.

## Key Techniques
- Use techniques like object pooling to reuse instances, reducing allocation costs.
- Use custom thread pools with only preallocated memory block pools.
- Pre-allocate arrays of things you need, run ring buffers on them if you have to use a varying number of things.

## Profiling-Driven Approach
Most optimization starts without profiling. Instead of measuring first and following the evidence, we guess.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of `emplace_back` vs `push_back` performance and best practices in modern C++:

## Key Performance Insights

The critical difference is that emplace_back excels at in-place construction from arguments (e.g., emplace_back(5, 'a') for std::string), while push_back(std::move) is designed for transferring ownership of existing objects.

Modern compilation and language rules make the optimized paths so similar that, in practice, there is often very little left to measure between them in these scenarios. This means that the performance advantage varies significantly depending on context.

## When to Use Each

**Use `push_back`:**
push_back is recommended for day-to-day use. Use push_back when you have an existing temporary object that you want to move into your std::vector, or more generally, when you want to move an existing object into your std::vector.

**Use `emplace_back`:**
Use emplace_back when you create a new temporary object. Use emplace_back where it is semantically significant to your algorithm (such as when the element type's move-constructor is absent or has been benchmarked as expensive).

## Important Caveats

A critical misconception exists about `emplace_back` and move semantics. You must explicitly mention std::move, so that the language understands that you're done using an object; emplace_back will never insert a move in a place you don't explicitly request one.

When implicit conversions are involved, emplace_back() can be somewhat faster than push_back(). However, the rule of thumb is that you should avoid "optimizations" that make the code less safe or less clear, unless the performance benefit is big enough to show up in your application benchmarks.

## Safety Considerations

Choosing push_back() is also safer: if you accidentally forget syntax in a nested container case with push_back() you'll get a compile error, but with emplace_back() the code will compile and you won't notice any problems until run-time.

content.text: I have current grounding. Building lesson 0003 around three rules — don't allocate, don't copy, don't pointer-chase — with real examples from the shooter game's per-frame update functions and the LlmClient I wrote. I'll also call out a genuine allocation-in-loop pattern hiding in `DialogUI::wrap()` for honest contrast.

input.content:
Quiz: 0 / 0
Lesson 0003 · cpp_games / docs / learning

Low-latency C++ for game loops

Why this matters: your three games each run an update-then-render loop 60 times a second. That gives you a 16.67 ms budget. Miss it once and you've stuttered. Most performance bugs in game code aren't algorithmic — they're the same three mistakes, repeated. This lesson is how to spot and avoid them in your own code.

1. The concept — the frame budget mindset

At 60 frames per second, you have 16.67 ms per frame. That budget pays for every game-loop step:

update (4ms)
AI / NPC (2ms)
render (6ms)
slack (4.67ms)

That slack — the dark bar — is your safety margin. A single 5 ms hiccup eats it. If your slack ever turns negative, the frame is dropped: the player sees a stutter even if your average is fine. Low-latency C++ is mostly about defending the slack against rare-but-large spikes, not chasing the last microsecond of average speed.

Three failure modes account for the overwhelming majority of game-loop hitches:

The ruleWhat it costs when you break itHow to spot it
Don't allocate in the hot loop.
new, malloc, vector growth, string concat.		A heap allocation is typically a few hundred nanoseconds — sometimes. Worst case it's a syscall and tens of microseconds. Multiplied by N entities, then N+1 next frame as the vector reallocates...Look inside for loops for push_back, std::string concatenation, make_unique, new. If the iteration count is unbounded, that's a smell.
Don't copy when you can move.
Returning vectors/strings by copy, passing big structs by value.		A copy of a std::vector<ChatTurn> with 20 entries means 20 string copies, each potentially a heap allocation. A copy of a std::string with 200 characters is one allocation.Look for big-typed function parameters or return values without const&, &&, or std::move.
Don't make the CPU wait on memory.
Pointer-chasing, scattered allocations, virtual calls in tight loops.		An L1 cache hit is ~1 ns. A main-memory fetch is ~100 ns. Iterating 1000 enemies stored in scattered heap memory can be 100× slower than 1000 in a contiguous std::vector.Look for std::list, std::map, std::vector<Enemy*>, or "components that all override a virtual update()."

The first rule of optimization

Measure before you change. Most performance "fixes" are guesses. Your slack today is comfortable — you don't have a problem yet. The point of learning this lesson is so that when you do profile and find a hot spot, you'll recognise which of these three patterns is causing it. Don't rewrite working code based on suspicion.

2. Minimal example — the same loop, twice

A toy "spawn particles" function in two styles. Same observable behaviour, very different per-frame cost.

// HOT-PATH HOSTILE — three mistakes in nine lines.
void spawnParticlesBad(int n) {
    std::vector<Particle> particles;                  // new vector every call
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        std::string name = "particle_" + std::to_string(i);  // alloc + alloc
        Particle p;                                   // fine, on stack
        p.label = name;                               // COPY of a heap string
        particles.push_back(p);                       // COPY into a growing vector
    }
    persist(particles);                               // passed by value — full COPY
}

// HOT-PATH FRIENDLY — same effect, no per-frame surprises.
void spawnParticlesGood(std::vector<Particle>& out, int n) {
    out.reserve(out.size() + n);                      // one allocation, at most
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        Particle p;
        p.labelId = i;                                // int instead of string — no alloc
        out.push_back(std::move(p));                  // move into the vector
    }
}  // caller already owns `out`; nothing copied across the boundary.

The bad version makes 2n + 2 allocations per call. The good version makes at most 1 (only if out's capacity wasn't enough). For n = 100 particles, that's ~202 vs ~1 allocations per frame. The bad version isn't algorithmically worse — it just leaks budget on every iteration.

3. In your games — the real code

The shooter game already does most of this right

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:318 — GameState owns its vectors 
struct GameState {
    Player player;
    std::vector<Projectile> projectiles;
    std::vector<Enemy>      enemies;
    std::vector<Pickup>     pickups;
    std::vector<ImpactEffect> impacts;
    // ...
};

The vectors are members of GameState, not locals reborn every frame. Across frames their capacity grows once and stays. Each frame's push_back after warmup is just a write to an already-allocated slot — no allocation. That's rule 1 followed by accident: just by giving the vectors a long-lived home, you've avoided the worst trap.

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:686 — erase-remove for cleanup 
game.projectiles.erase(
    std::remove_if(game.projectiles.begin(), game.projectiles.end(),
                   [](const Projectile& p) {
                       return p.lifetime <= 0.0f;
                   }),
    game.projectiles.end());

This is the classic erase-remove idiom. remove_if shifts the surviving elements toward the front in O(n) of cache-friendly contiguous writes; erase then just adjusts size. The capacity stays put — no shrink, no free, no realloc. Next frame's push_back reuses the freed slots.

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:639 — the update loop 
void updateProjectiles(GameState& game, float dt) {
    for (auto& projectile : game.projectiles) {   // reference, no copy
        projectile.pos += projectile.velocity * dt;
        projectile.lifetime -= dt;
    }
    // ... collision pass over the same contiguous vector ...
}

Three things to notice:

  • auto& — we iterate by reference. auto alone would copy each Projectile every iteration. With 500 projectiles per frame that adds up.
  • GameState& game — the whole game state passes by reference. Passing by value would copy every vector every frame: a catastrophic mistake the type system would let you make silently.
  • The data being iterated is contiguous (std::vector). The prefetcher loves this. Each iteration's memory fetch overlaps the previous iteration's arithmetic.

The LLM client — rule 2 in action

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:21 
std::uint64_t LlmClient::submit(std::string systemPrompt,
                                std::vector<ChatTurn> history,
                                std::string userMessage) {
    ChatRequest req;
    req.id = nextId_.fetch_add(1);
    req.systemPrompt = std::move(systemPrompt);   // move, not copy
    req.history      = std::move(history);
    req.userMessage  = std::move(userMessage);
    // ...
    requests_.push(std::move(req));               // move into the queue
}

The parameters are by-value on purpose. The caller decides whether to give us a copy or a move; once they're our locals, we treat them as such and std::move them deeper. A history with 20 turns goes from caller → submit → requests_ with zero element copies. If we'd written req.history = history;, every ChatTurn would be deep-copied.

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:42 — drainReplies() 
std::vector<ChatReply> LlmClient::drainReplies() {
    std::vector<ChatReply> out;
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(replyMutex_);
    out.swap(replies_);   // O(1): swap three pointers, no element work
    return out;             // NRVO — no return copy either
}

swap on two std::vectors exchanges their internal pointers in constant time, regardless of how many elements they hold. We hold the mutex for only the swap, not for any element copying. The return uses Named Return Value Optimization: the compiler builds out directly in the caller's slot, no copy or move.

A real allocation-in-loop bug, in my own code

Look what I left in DialogUI.cpp...

Honesty: lesson 0003 wouldn't be worth much if I only showed you fixed code. Here's a per-frame allocation pattern in code I wrote for you. It's fine right now because the budget is comfortable, but the next lesson on profiling will surface it.

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/DialogUI.cpp:109 — render(), called every frame 
void DialogUI::render(sf::RenderTarget& target) const {
    // ... compute layout ...
    struct RenderedLine { std::string text; sf::Color color; };
    std::vector<RenderedLine> rendered;                // 1) fresh vector every frame

    for (auto it = transcript_.rbegin(); it != transcript_.rend(); ++it) {
        const auto& line = *it;
        std::string prefix = line.speaker.empty() ? "" : line.speaker + ": ";  // 2) string alloc
        auto wrapped = wrap(prefix + line.text, wrapChars);                       // 3) more allocs
        // ...
    }
    // ... and inside render():
    for (const auto& rl : rendered) {
        sf::Text t(rl.text, font_, kFontSize);        // 4) sf::Text constructor allocates
        target.draw(t);
    }
}

Every frame, on every transcript line that fits on screen, this:

  1. Allocates a fresh rendered vector and reallocates as it grows.
  2. Builds a prefix string via concatenation — one allocation per line.
  3. Calls wrap(), which builds yet more strings.
  4. Constructs an sf::Text per line, which sets up internal glyph state.

For 20 transcript lines this might be 50–100 small allocations per frame — well under the budget on a modern PC, but a textbook violation of rule 1. The fix is not to rewrite it now; the fix is to recognise it when a profiler eventually points here. The good news is you've seen the bad pattern from inside your own repo, which is the version most likely to stick.

4. Often confused with...

Latency vs. throughput

A web server cares about throughput — total requests per second across many users. A game cares about latency — how long the single in-flight frame takes. A doubling of throughput at the cost of an occasional 30 ms spike is a great deal for a server and a disaster for a game. When you read "low latency" advice written for trading systems or game engines, that's the lens: keeping the worst-case single operation small, not maximising overall work done.

Stack allocation vs. heap allocation

A local Projectile p; "allocates" too — on the stack. Stack allocation is just a register decrement; it costs nothing measurable. Heap allocation (new, malloc, vector growth) is the slow one. When we say "don't allocate in the hot loop," we mean don't heap-allocate. Locals are free.

std::move vs. copy — and when std::move is a copy

std::move doesn't move anything by itself — it's a cast. It tells the compiler "this object's value can be stolen from." Whether anything is actually stolen depends on the destination's move constructor. For std::string and std::vector, that move steals the heap buffer in O(1). For an int or a Vec3 of three floats, there's nothing on the heap to steal — the "move" copies the bytes. That's fine; it just means std::move on small trivial types is free but not magic. Don't expect it to make POD operations faster.

push_back(std::move(x)) vs. emplace_back(...)

Common online advice says "always prefer emplace_back." The current consensus is more nuanced: use push_back when you have an existing object to put in (it's safer and just as fast after move); use emplace_back when you'd otherwise construct a temporary just to immediately copy/move it. In your code, lines like history_.push_back({"user", std::move(line)}); are fine — an emplace_back("user", std::move(line)) would be equivalent on a modern compiler.

5. Quiz

You add a feature where every frame the shooter game scans for nearby enemies. The new code is std::vector<Enemy*> nearby; for (auto& e : game.enemies) if (close(e)) nearby.push_back(&e);. Frame time spikes randomly. Which rule is being broken?

  • Rule 3 (cache) — storing pointers instead of values.
  • Rule 1 (don't allocate) — nearby is local, so it allocates and grows every frame.
  • Rule 2 (don't copy) — push_back copies the enemy.
  • None of the rules — std::vector itself is the problem.

In LlmClient::submit the parameters are std::string systemPrompt, std::vector<ChatTurn> history, std::string userMessage — passed by value. Why isn't that always wasteful?

  • The compiler always elides parameter copies, so by-value is free.
  • The caller decides whether to copy or move into the parameter; inside submit we std::move the parameter deeper, so it costs at most one move.
  • Pass-by-value allocates a fresh buffer, which we then re-use.
  • Pass-by-value is required for thread-safety with the worker thread.

Why does LlmClient::drainReplies() use out.swap(replies_) instead of out = replies_; replies_.clear();?

  • The assignment form wouldn't compile because replies_ is a member.
  • swap keeps replies in arrival order; assignment would reorder them.
  • swap is O(1) and runs while we hold the mutex; assignment would deep-copy every reply and keep the worker thread blocked longer.
  • Assignment is unsafe under the mutex; swap is the only thread-safe operation.

A new feature pings the shooter game's update loop: for (auto& e : game.enemies) e.name = "enemy_" + std::to_string(e.id);. Why is this a low-latency landmine?

  • It won't compile — you can't assign to a string member through a reference.
  • It allocates 1 GB of memory per frame.
  • Every frame, every enemy does at least two heap allocations — for to_string and the + — even though the name never changes.
  • Iteration order over std::vector isn't guaranteed, so names will drift.

Your average frame is 8 ms with occasional 22 ms spikes that cause visible stutter. Which kind of fix should you reach for first?

  • Find an algorithmic improvement that drops the 8 ms average to 4 ms.
  • Profile the 22 ms frames specifically — spikes are almost always allocation or sync events, not the average path.
  • Raise setFramerateLimit to 120 so each frame has half as much work to skip.
  • Move all update functions to a worker thread.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. You're adding a debug overlay to the racing game that prints "speed: 142 kph" in the corner each frame. Sketch the version of this that would break rule 1, and the version that wouldn't. (Hint: the difference is where the std::string lives.)

Scenario B. Look at DialogUI::render() at cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/DialogUI.cpp:109. Without writing the fix, list two distinct per-frame allocations you'd target if a profiler said this function was hot. For each, name the rule it breaks.

Scenario C. In the shooter game, suppose a player triggers a "screen-clearing super-bomb" that should despawn every projectile and every enemy at once. Walk through what happens to the four vectors in GameState — do they shrink? Do they free memory? Should they? Reason from the rules.

7. Track your progress
