That slack — the dark bar — is your safety margin. A single 5 ms hiccup eats it. If your slack ever turns negative, the frame is dropped: the player sees a stutter even if your average is fine. Low-latency C++ is mostly about defending the slack against rare-but-large spikes, not chasing the last microsecond of average speed.

Three failure modes account for the overwhelming majority of game-loop hitches:

The ruleWhat it costs when you break itHow to spot it
Don't allocate in the hot loop.
new, malloc, vector growth, string concat.		A heap allocation is typically a few hundred nanoseconds — sometimes. Worst case it's a syscall and tens of microseconds. Multiplied by N entities, then N+1 next frame as the vector reallocates...Look inside for loops for push_back, std::string concatenation, make_unique, new. If the iteration count is unbounded, that's a smell.
Don't copy when you can move.
Returning vectors/strings by copy, passing big structs by value.		A copy of a std::vector<ChatTurn> with 20 entries means 20 string copies, each potentially a heap allocation. A copy of a std::string with 200 characters is one allocation.Look for big-typed function parameters or return values without const&, &&, or std::move.
Don't make the CPU wait on memory.
Pointer-chasing, scattered allocations, virtual calls in tight loops.		An L1 cache hit is ~1 ns. A main-memory fetch is ~100 ns. Iterating 1000 enemies stored in scattered heap memory can be 100× slower than 1000 in a contiguous std::vector.Look for std::list, std::map, std::vector<Enemy*>, or "components that all override a virtual update()."

The first rule of optimization

Measure before you change. Most performance "fixes" are guesses. Your slack today is comfortable — you don't have a problem yet. The point of learning this lesson is so that when you do profile and find a hot spot, you'll recognise which of these three patterns is causing it. Don't rewrite working code based on suspicion.

2. Minimal example — the same loop, twice

A toy "spawn particles" function in two styles. Same observable behaviour, very different per-frame cost.

// HOT-PATH HOSTILE — three mistakes in nine lines.
void spawnParticlesBad(int n) {
    std::vector<Particle> particles;                  // new vector every call
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        std::string name = "particle_" + std::to_string(i);  // alloc + alloc
        Particle p;                                   // fine, on stack
        p.label = name;                               // COPY of a heap string
        particles.push_back(p);                       // COPY into a growing vector
    }
    persist(particles);                               // passed by value — full COPY
}

// HOT-PATH FRIENDLY — same effect, no per-frame surprises.
void spawnParticlesGood(std::vector<Particle>& out, int n) {
    out.reserve(out.size() + n);                      // one allocation, at most
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        Particle p;
        p.labelId = i;                                // int instead of string — no alloc
        out.push_back(std::move(p));                  // move into the vector
    }
}  // caller already owns `out`; nothing copied across the boundary.

The bad version makes 2n + 2 allocations per call. The good version makes at most 1 (only if out's capacity wasn't enough). For n = 100 particles, that's ~202 vs ~1 allocations per frame. The bad version isn't algorithmically worse — it just leaks budget on every iteration.

3. In your games — the real code

The shooter game already does most of this right

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:318 — GameState owns its vectors 
struct GameState {
    Player player;
    std::vector<Projectile> projectiles;
    std::vector<Enemy>      enemies;
    std::vector<Pickup>     pickups;
    std::vector<ImpactEffect> impacts;
    // ...
};

The vectors are members of GameState, not locals reborn every frame. Across frames their capacity grows once and stays. Each frame's push_back after warmup is just a write to an already-allocated slot — no allocation. That's rule 1 followed by accident: just by giving the vectors a long-lived home, you've avoided the worst trap.

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:686 — erase-remove for cleanup 
game.projectiles.erase(
    std::remove_if(game.projectiles.begin(), game.projectiles.end(),
                   [](const Projectile& p) {
                       return p.lifetime <= 0.0f;
                   }),
    game.projectiles.end());

This is the classic erase-remove idiom. remove_if shifts the surviving elements toward the front in O(n) of cache-friendly contiguous writes; erase then just adjusts size. The capacity stays put — no shrink, no free, no realloc. Next frame's push_back reuses the freed slots.

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:639 — the update loop 
void updateProjectiles(GameState& game, float dt) {
    for (auto& projectile : game.projectiles) {   // reference, no copy
        projectile.pos += projectile.velocity * dt;
        projectile.lifetime -= dt;
    }
    // ... collision pass over the same contiguous vector ...
}

Three things to notice:

  • auto& — we iterate by reference. auto alone would copy each Projectile every iteration. With 500 projectiles per frame that adds up.
  • GameState& game — the whole game state passes by reference. Passing by value would copy every vector every frame: a catastrophic mistake the type system would let you make silently.
  • The data being iterated is contiguous (std::vector). The prefetcher loves this. Each iteration's memory fetch overlaps the previous iteration's arithmetic.

The LLM client — rule 2 in action

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:21 
std::uint64_t LlmClient::submit(std::string systemPrompt,
                                std::vector<ChatTurn> history,
                                std::string userMessage) {
    ChatRequest req;
    req.id = nextId_.fetch_add(1);
    req.systemPrompt = std::move(systemPrompt);   // move, not copy
    req.history      = std::move(history);
    req.userMessage  = std::move(userMessage);
    // ...
    requests_.push(std::move(req));               // move into the queue
}

The parameters are by-value on purpose. The caller decides whether to give us a copy or a move; once they're our locals, we treat them as such and std::move them deeper. A history with 20 turns goes from caller → submit → requests_ with zero element copies. If we'd written req.history = history;, every ChatTurn would be deep-copied.

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:42 — drainReplies() 
std::vector<ChatReply> LlmClient::drainReplies() {
    std::vector<ChatReply> out;
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(replyMutex_);
    out.swap(replies_);   // O(1): swap three pointers, no element work
    return out;             // NRVO — no return copy either
}

swap on two std::vectors exchanges their internal pointers in constant time, regardless of how many elements they hold. We hold the mutex for only the swap, not for any element copying. The return uses Named Return Value Optimization: the compiler builds out directly in the caller's slot, no copy or move.

A real allocation-in-loop bug, in my own code

Look what I left in DialogUI.cpp...

Honesty: lesson 0003 wouldn't be worth much if I only showed you fixed code. Here's a per-frame allocation pattern in code I wrote for you. It's fine right now because the budget is comfortable, but the next lesson on profiling will surface it.

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/DialogUI.cpp:109 — render(), called every frame 
void DialogUI::render(sf::RenderTarget& target) const {
    // ... compute layout ...
    struct RenderedLine { std::string text; sf::Color color; };
    std::vector<RenderedLine> rendered;                // 1) fresh vector every frame

    for (auto it = transcript_.rbegin(); it != transcript_.rend(); ++it) {
        const auto& line = *it;
        std::string prefix = line.speaker.empty() ? "" : line.speaker + ": ";  // 2) string alloc
        auto wrapped = wrap(prefix + line.text, wrapChars);                       // 3) more allocs
        // ...
    }
    // ... and inside render():
    for (const auto& rl : rendered) {
        sf::Text t(rl.text, font_, kFontSize);        // 4) sf::Text constructor allocates
        target.draw(t);
    }
}

Every frame, on every transcript line that fits on screen, this:

  1. Allocates a fresh rendered vector and reallocates as it grows.
  2. Builds a prefix string via concatenation — one allocation per line.
  3. Calls wrap(), which builds yet more strings.
  4. Constructs an sf::Text per line, which sets up internal glyph state.

For 20 transcript lines this might be 50–100 small allocations per frame — well under the budget on a modern PC, but a textbook violation of rule 1. The fix is not to rewrite it now; the fix is to recognise it when a profiler eventually points here. The good news is you've seen the bad pattern from inside your own repo, which is the version most likely to stick.

4. Often confused with...

Latency vs. throughput

A web server cares about throughput — total requests per second across many users. A game cares about latency — how long the single in-flight frame takes. A doubling of throughput at the cost of an occasional 30 ms spike is a great deal for a server and a disaster for a game. When you read "low latency" advice written for trading systems or game engines, that's the lens: keeping the worst-case single operation small, not maximising overall work done.

Stack allocation vs. heap allocation

A local Projectile p; "allocates" too — on the stack. Stack allocation is just a register decrement; it costs nothing measurable. Heap allocation (new, malloc, vector growth) is the slow one. When we say "don't allocate in the hot loop," we mean don't heap-allocate. Locals are free.

std::move vs. copy — and when std::move is a copy

std::move doesn't move anything by itself — it's a cast. It tells the compiler "this object's value can be stolen from." Whether anything is actually stolen depends on the destination's move constructor. For std::string and std::vector, that move steals the heap buffer in O(1). For an int or a Vec3 of three floats, there's nothing on the heap to steal — the "move" copies the bytes. That's fine; it just means std::move on small trivial types is free but not magic. Don't expect it to make POD operations faster.

push_back(std::move(x)) vs. emplace_back(...)

Common online advice says "always prefer emplace_back." The current consensus is more nuanced: use push_back when you have an existing object to put in (it's safer and just as fast after move); use emplace_back when you'd otherwise construct a temporary just to immediately copy/move it. In your code, lines like history_.push_back({"user", std::move(line)}); are fine — an emplace_back("user", std::move(line)) would be equivalent on a modern compiler.

5. Quiz

You add a feature where every frame the shooter game scans for nearby enemies. The new code is std::vector<Enemy*> nearby; for (auto& e : game.enemies) if (close(e)) nearby.push_back(&e);. Frame time spikes randomly. Which rule is being broken?

  • Rule 3 (cache) — storing pointers instead of values.
  • Rule 1 (don't allocate) — nearby is local, so it allocates and grows every frame.
  • Rule 2 (don't copy) — push_back copies the enemy.
  • None of the rules — std::vector itself is the problem.

In LlmClient::submit the parameters are std::string systemPrompt, std::vector<ChatTurn> history, std::string userMessage — passed by value. Why isn't that always wasteful?

  • The compiler always elides parameter copies, so by-value is free.
  • The caller decides whether to copy or move into the parameter; inside submit we std::move the parameter deeper, so it costs at most one move.
  • Pass-by-value allocates a fresh buffer, which we then re-use.
  • Pass-by-value is required for thread-safety with the worker thread.

Why does LlmClient::drainReplies() use out.swap(replies_) instead of out = replies_; replies_.clear();?

  • The assignment form wouldn't compile because replies_ is a member.
  • swap keeps replies in arrival order; assignment would reorder them.
  • swap is O(1) and runs while we hold the mutex; assignment would deep-copy every reply and keep the worker thread blocked longer.
  • Assignment is unsafe under the mutex; swap is the only thread-safe operation.

A new feature pings the shooter game's update loop: for (auto& e : game.enemies) e.name = "enemy_" + std::to_string(e.id);. Why is this a low-latency landmine?

  • It won't compile — you can't assign to a string member through a reference.
  • It allocates 1 GB of memory per frame.
  • Every frame, every enemy does at least two heap allocations — for to_string and the + — even though the name never changes.
  • Iteration order over std::vector isn't guaranteed, so names will drift.

Your average frame is 8 ms with occasional 22 ms spikes that cause visible stutter. Which kind of fix should you reach for first?

  • Find an algorithmic improvement that drops the 8 ms average to 4 ms.
  • Profile the 22 ms frames specifically — spikes are almost always allocation or sync events, not the average path.
  • Raise setFramerateLimit to 120 so each frame has half as much work to skip.
  • Move all update functions to a worker thread.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. You're adding a debug overlay to the racing game that prints "speed: 142 kph" in the corner each frame. Sketch the version of this that would break rule 1, and the version that wouldn't. (Hint: the difference is where the std::string lives.)

Scenario B. Look at DialogUI::render() at cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/DialogUI.cpp:109. Without writing the fix, list two distinct per-frame allocations you'd target if a profiler said this function was hot. For each, name the rule it breaks.

Scenario C. In the shooter game, suppose a player triggers a "screen-clearing super-bomb" that should despawn every projectile and every enemy at once. Walk through what happens to the four vectors in GameState — do they shrink? Do they free memory? Should they? Reason from the rules.

## H

- **Hot loop / hot path** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Code that runs many times per frame — per-entity update loops,
  per-line render code. Allocations and copies that would be invisible
  elsewhere are budget-eaters here.

## L

- **Latency vs throughput** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Latency = time for a single operation (a game frame). Throughput =
  total operations per second (requests). Games optimize for worst-case
  latency, not average throughput.

## M

- **`std::move`** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  A cast that marks a value as "you may steal from this." Whether
  anything is actually stolen depends on the destination's move
  constructor. For `std::string`/`std::vector` it steals the heap buffer
  in O(1); for trivial types it falls back to a copy.

## N

- **NRVO (Named Return Value Optimization)** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Compiler optimization that builds a returned local directly in the
  caller's slot, eliminating the return copy/move entirely.
  `LlmClient::drainReplies()` relies on this.

Lesson 0003 is in place. To open it on Linux:

```
xdg-open /home/node/work/normal_work/cpp_games/docs/learning/lessons/0003-low-latency-cpp-game-loops.html
```

## What's in lesson 0003

- **§1 The concept** — the **16.67 ms frame budget** illustrated as a flex-box bar (update/AI/render/slack), then the three rules: *don't allocate, don't copy, don't pointer-chase*.
- **§2 Minimal example** — the same `spawnParticles` function in two styles, side by side, with the bad version's three mistakes highlighted in red and the good version in green.
- **§3 In your games** — real code from all three projects:
  - **Shooter `GameState`** (`main.cpp:318`) — vectors as long-lived members, capacity grows once.
  - **Shooter `updateProjectiles`** (`main.cpp:639`) — `auto&` iteration, `GameState&` parameter, contiguous-vector cache friendliness.
  - **Shooter erase-remove** (`main.cpp:686`) — cleanup that doesn't shrink capacity.
  - **`LlmClient::submit`** — by-value parameters + deep `std::move` (caller decides cost).
  - **`LlmClient::drainReplies`** — O(1) `swap` under the mutex + NRVO on return.
  - **An honest bug call-out in my own `DialogUI::render()`** (`DialogUI.cpp:109`) — per-frame string concat and vector growth. Flagged as a "wait for the profiler" item rather than a fix.
- **§4 Often confused with** — latency vs throughput, stack vs heap, what `std::move` actually is (and when it's just a copy), `push_back(std::move(x))` vs `emplace_back(...)` with the *current* consensus (push_back is fine and safer).
- **§5 Quiz** — 5 shuffled multiple-choice questions, including one direct stab-the-spike-with-a-profiler item.
- **§6 Scenarios** — 3 open-ended, including a direct task to walk through your shooter game's `GameState` vectors under a "super-bomb."

## Workspace state

- **PROGRESS.md** — lesson 0003 logged; new suggested-next is **profiling with `std::chrono::steady_clock`** so the `DialogUI` callout from this lesson gets paid off with evidence, not speculation.
- **GLOSSARY.md** — promoted: *erase-remove idiom*, *frame budget*, *hot loop*, *latency vs throughput*, *`std::move`*, *NRVO*. Eleven still pending promotion until you use them correctly.

## Knowledge check (let's talk through these)

Three questions to make sure the concepts landed:

1. **Why is `setFramerateLimit(60)` in your racing/shooter games not actually "low-latency"?** It limits frames you can produce, not how long each one takes. What does that mean for how you should *use* spare budget when you have it?

2. **Look at your `Npc::onReplyArrived`** (`cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Npc.cpp:23`). It does `history_.push_back({"user", std::move(pendingUserLine_)});`. What does the `std::move` save? What would change if I'd written `pendingUserLine_` without it?

3. **Suppose you run the shooter and see a *consistent* 11 ms per frame, no spikes.** Is rule 1 still relevant? Should you go optimize the per-frame allocations anyway? Defend your answer.

Take a swing. I'll correct gently and update PROGRESS/GLOSSARY based on how the answers land — especially anything that turns out shaky.

This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. I've found comprehensive information about FPGA basics for beginners. Here's a summary of key concepts:

## What is an FPGA?

An FPGA (Field Programmable Gate Array) is essentially a huge array of gates that can be programmed and reconfigured any time anywhere. You decide how the chip behaves by programming the logic itself.

## Key Advantages

Developers can change functionality as needed, even in the field, which makes prototyping faster and field updates possible. Additionally, parallelism is built in—different logic blocks work simultaneously, enabling massive throughput for image processing, audio filtering, and streaming data.

## Programming Languages

For FPGA programming, Verilog and VHDL remain dominant, as they describe digital systems at the logic level. Some developers use High-Level Synthesis (HLS) to write FPGA logic in C or C++, and these tools convert high-level code into HDL.

## Design and Implementation Process

Once you've written your HDL, you simulate it and check for logic errors and timing issues, then use a tool to synthesize the design and turn your HDL into a "bitstream"—a file that configures the actual FPGA.

## Getting Started

Real understanding comes from learning the basics—signals, timing, logic gates, which is the foundation.

Lesson 0004 · cpp_games / docs / learning

FPGAs, calling them from C++, and running LLMs on them

Why this matters: your cpp_game_with_llm_npcs already uses a sidecar for inference. Researchers are now putting that same inference workload on FPGAs, and getting 1.1–3.3× the speed of a GPU at 3–6× less energy. This lesson is the conceptual bridge from "Ollama on a GPU" to "what if Wren's brain were a programmable chip instead?"

1. What an FPGA actually is

An FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array) is a chip whose wiring is programmable. A CPU has a fixed circuit that fetches instructions and runs them. An FPGA ships with a sea of generic logic blocks and wires, and at boot you load a configuration that becomes a specific custom circuit. You're not running software on hardware — you're describing hardware that the chip then is.

inside an FPGA, every cell is one of these: +----+----+----+----+ LUT = a tiny 4- or 6-input lookup table |LUT |LUT |LUT |LUT | that you fill in to implement |----+ FF +----+ FF | any boolean function |LUT | |LUT | | FF = a flip-flop (one bit of state) +----+----+----+----+ DSP = a dedicated multiplier-accumulator |LUT |LUT |DSP |LUT | BRAM = a small on-chip RAM block |----+ FF | | FF | |LUT | | | | Routing fabric (the lines between) +----+----+----+----+ is itself programmable. |BRAM|BRAM|LUT |LUT | | | |----+ FF | You "program" an FPGA by deciding which | | |LUT | | cells light up and how they're wired +----+----+----+----+ together. The result is a circuit.

You describe what you want using a hardware description language — Verilog or VHDL — or with High-Level Synthesis (HLS), where you write C/C++ and a compiler produces the HDL for you. A synthesizer reduces your description to LUTs/FFs/DSPs, a placer assigns them to physical cells, a router connects them, and the final output is a bitstream: a file that, when loaded into the chip, rewires it to be the circuit you described.

The one-sentence mental model

An FPGA is a chip where you specify the schematic at boot time, then run signals through it — not instructions through a fixed CPU.

2. FPGA vs. CPU vs. GPU

All three are silicon. They diverge on what they're optimized to do.

CPU (your game loop)

  • Few (4–16) very smart cores
  • Branch prediction, deep caches, out-of-order execution
  • Optimized for latency on serial code with unpredictable control flow
  • Programmed in C++/Rust/etc.

GPU (Ollama, today)

  • Thousands of small cores, ganged into "warps"
  • Massive memory bandwidth, simple cache
  • Optimized for throughput on regular parallel math (matrices, pixels)
  • Programmed in CUDA/Vulkan/OpenCL

FPGA

  • Sea of LUTs/FFs/DSPs wired to your spec
  • You build a deep custom pipeline; throughput = 1 result per clock
  • Optimized for determinism + efficiency on a single fixed workload
  • Programmed in Verilog/VHDL/HLS
QuestionCPUGPUFPGA
"What's it good at?"Irregular code, branches, single-threaded latencyLots of identical math in parallelOne specific dataflow done with minimal energy
"How do I program it?"Write code, compile, runWrite a kernel, dispatch from hostDescribe a circuit, synthesize, load bitstream
"Time from idea to running"Seconds (compile)Seconds (compile)Hours (synth + place & route)
"Change behaviour at runtime?"Trivially — new codeTrivially — new kernelPossible (reload bitstream) but heavy
"Energy efficiency"Worst — lots of silicon never usedBetter on its workloadBest — only the circuit you needed exists
"Cost to get started"You have oneYou have one$500 dev board → $40k data-center card

The takeaway: an FPGA shines when you have one workload you'll run millions of times and you care about energy and tail latency. That's not a game loop — game logic branches too much. But it is an LLM doing matrix-multiply after matrix-multiply.

3. How a C++ program "calls" an FPGA

This is the part that maps cleanly onto what you've already built. From a C++ program's point of view, an FPGA is an accelerator at the other end of a bus — usually PCIe. You don't "call a function" on it the way you call printf. You move data into its memory, kick off a kernel, and wait for the result.

your C++ host the bus the FPGA card +---------------+ +--------+ +--------------------+ | game / driver | ===> | PCIe | ===> | bitstream is your | | OpenCL/XRT API| | (or | | custom circuit: | | | <=== | HBM | <=== | matrix multiply, | +---------------+ | link) | | attention kernel, | +--------+ | whatever you need | +--------------------+ data flow: 1. host allocates a buffer (host RAM, mapped to FPGA card via OpenCL) 2. host writes input data into it 3. host enqueues the kernel (a one-line API call) 4. FPGA does the work (everything runs in parallel inside) 5. host waits, then reads the output buffer

Here is the same pattern in C++ using AMD's XRT (the Xilinx Runtime, which lives behind the Vitis HLS toolchain). It looks deceptively like our LlmClient:

#include <xrt/xrt_device.h>
#include <xrt/xrt_kernel.h>
#include <xrt/xrt_bo.h>

int main() {
    // 1. Open the FPGA card and load the bitstream — analogous to
    //    "ollama serve starting up with a model loaded".
    auto device = xrt::device(0);
    auto uuid   = device.load_xclbin("matmul_kernel.xclbin");
    auto kernel = xrt::kernel(device, uuid, "matmul");

    // 2. Allocate device buffers and fill them — like building a JSON body.
    auto A = xrt::bo(device, N*N*sizeof(float), kernel.group_id(0));
    auto B = xrt::bo(device, N*N*sizeof(float), kernel.group_id(1));
    auto C = xrt::bo(device, N*N*sizeof(float), kernel.group_id(2));
    A.write(matrixA); A.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_TO_DEVICE);
    B.write(matrixB); B.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_TO_DEVICE);

    // 3. Launch the kernel — like cli.Post("/api/chat", ...) in LlmClient.cpp.
    auto run = kernel(A, B, C, N);

    // 4. Wait for it (blocking) — or .start()/.wait() async like our worker thread does.
    run.wait();

    // 5. Read result back to host RAM — like parsing res->body into reply.content.
    C.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_FROM_DEVICE);
    C.read(resultMatrix);
}

Notice the five-step shape: set up → ship inputs → launch → wait → read outputs. That's structurally identical to a network call to Ollama. The only difference is what's on the other side: instead of a process talking HTTP, it's a circuit talking memory.

4. LLMs on FPGAs — the exciting part

Until recently the idea of running a language model on an FPGA was a research curiosity. As of 2026 it's real, and the results are interesting enough that AMD and a couple of startups are pouring money into it.

Real 2026 numbers

The LUT-LLM paper (Nov 2025) implemented Qwen 3 1.7B — not a toy — on an AMD Alveo V80 FPGA. On the generation step it reported 1.10–3.29× faster than a GPU, and 3.05–6.60× better energy efficiency. A Versal/Alveo system running Mamba2-2.7B hit ~93 tokens/s on the prefill, ~200 tokens/s in decode on an Alveo U280, and ~333 tokens/s in decode on a VHK158.

Why does an FPGA win on LLM inference at all? Three reasons:

  1. The arithmetic is regular and quantized. Modern LLM inference is mostly multiplying weight matrices by activation vectors at 4- or 8-bit precision. That's the workload where an FPGA's dedicated DSPs and customizable bit widths beat a GPU's fixed FP16/BF16 lanes.
  2. You can build the exact dataflow. A GPU has fixed-size warps and a fixed cache hierarchy. An FPGA lets you wire one layer's output straight into the next layer's input on chip, without round-tripping through HBM. That's where the energy savings come from.
  3. Lookup-table tricks like LUT-LLM. A 2025 insight: at very low bit-width, you can replace some multiplies with pre-baked table lookups in the FPGA's BRAM. CPUs and GPUs can't do that cheaply; FPGAs absolutely can — LUTs are their native unit.

The catches, in plain English:

  • An Alveo V80 is several thousand dollars; a VHK158 is tens of thousands. For a hobby game, you'd use a GPU.
  • "Programming" the FPGA means an HLS or HDL flow, a multi-hour synthesis run, and probably $1k+ of Vitis tooling (or its open-source approximations).
  • You target one model at a time. Switching from Qwen 3 to Llama 3 means reloading a different bitstream — potentially recompiling it.

5. In your project (hypothetically)

Your game doesn't have an FPGA in it. But here's the punchline: your LlmClient wouldn't care if you added one. The whole reason we made processOne() the only place that knows about Ollama is precisely so we could replace it later. Here's what would change — and what wouldn't.

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:67 — today 
// Sidecar implementation, HTTP to Ollama.
ChatReply LlmClient::processOne(const ChatRequest& req) {
    httplib::Client cli(config_.host, config_.port);
    auto res = cli.Post("/api/chat", buildJson(req), "application/json");
    // ... parse and return ...
}
cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:67 — hypothetical FPGA backend 
// Same signature, different transport — XRT call to a Qwen kernel on Alveo.
ChatReply LlmClient::processOne(const ChatRequest& req) {
    auto tokens = tokenize(req);                            // CPU
    inputBuf_.write(tokens.data());
    inputBuf_.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_TO_DEVICE);                // PCIe -> FPGA
    auto run = qwenKernel_(inputBuf_, outputBuf_, tokens.size());
    run.wait();                                              // FPGA does the work
    outputBuf_.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_FROM_DEVICE);             // FPGA -> PCIe
    ChatReply reply;
    reply.id = req.id;
    reply.ok = true;
    reply.content = detokenize(outputBuf_);                  // CPU
    return reply;
}

The function body changes completely. But nothing else in the codebase moves:

  • LlmClient::submit(), drainReplies(), workerLoop() — unchanged.
  • Npc, Persona, history-trimming — unchanged.
  • DialogUI, main.cpp — unchanged.
  • Your async drain pattern, your thread-safe queues — unchanged.

That's the whole reward for the encapsulation we did in lesson 0001. From the game's point of view, "Wren's brain is on an FPGA" and "Wren's brain is in a Python process down the hall" are indistinguishable as long as processOne() turns a request into a reply.

6. Often confused with...

FPGA vs. ASIC

An ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) is a chip designed and fabricated for one job — an NVIDIA H100 is an ASIC, your phone's neural engine is an ASIC. It's faster and more power-efficient than the same design on an FPGA, but the design is frozen in silicon. FPGA is the reprogrammable cousin: you give up some efficiency in exchange for being able to ship a new bitstream tomorrow. Most chips that ship to consumers in volume are ASICs; FPGAs dominate prototyping, niche workloads, and any case where the workload mutates faster than chip fab cycles (years).

FPGA vs. GPU

Both are massively parallel and live on PCIe. The difference is rigidity. A GPU's parallelism is fixed: 32-wide warps, fixed-size caches, a fixed instruction set. You write a kernel that maps your problem onto that grid. An FPGA's parallelism is whatever you wire up: 17-wide pipelines, 12-bit arithmetic, on-chip RAM blocks placed where you need them. GPUs are easier to program and have better tooling; FPGAs are more efficient when your workload is regular and you're willing to spend weeks tuning.

FPGA vs. microcontroller

A microcontroller (Arduino, STM32) is a tiny CPU. An FPGA can contain a microcontroller as one circuit among many — that's called a "soft core" — but the FPGA itself is fundamentally different: customizable wiring, not fixed CPU logic. People sometimes use FPGAs because they need both a tiny CPU and a hardware pipeline next to it.

FPGA on a board vs. eFPGA inside an SoC

Modern AMD Versal chips put a small FPGA fabric inside the same package as ARM CPU cores and a GPU. This is an embedded FPGA (eFPGA). From a programmer's view it's still "configurable hardware you call from C++"; from a hardware view it lives on the same die as everything else, so the PCIe step disappears. The LLM-on-FPGA work increasingly targets Versal AI Edge SoCs for exactly this reason.

7. Quiz

You "program" an FPGA. What does that actually mean at the chip level?

  • You write machine instructions to a small instruction memory and the chip executes them in order.
  • You load a bitstream that configures which logic blocks are active and how they're wired into a circuit.
  • You upload a kernel that runs across thousands of parallel threads on a fixed instruction set.
  • You permanently etch a custom design into the silicon during the fabrication process.

Why is an FPGA not a good fit for your game's main loop (the SFML/OpenGL update-and-render code in cpp_shooter_game or cpp_racing_game)?

  • FPGAs can only do integer math, and game physics needs floats.
  • Game-loop code is branchy and irregular — the FPGA strength is regular dataflow, not unpredictable control flow.
  • SFML doesn't have FPGA bindings.
  • An FPGA doesn't have enough memory to hold the game state.

In the hypothetical FPGA backend for LlmClient::processOne(), the host C++ code calls inputBuf_.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_TO_DEVICE). What is this doing, and why is it necessary?

  • Loading a fresh bitstream into the FPGA so it knows what model to run.
  • Copying the buffer contents over PCIe from host RAM to the FPGA's on-card memory so the kernel can read them.
  • Allocating a new buffer on the FPGA each time.
  • Acquiring a mutex so the worker thread doesn't read while the FPGA writes.

Why do FPGAs win on energy efficiency for LLM inference (~3–6× a GPU in the LUT-LLM result)?

  • FPGAs run at a much lower temperature, so their transistors switch with less leakage.
  • FPGAs clock higher than GPUs, so each operation takes fewer joules.
  • The bitstream only lights up the circuit the workload actually uses, at the bit-widths it actually uses, and routes data on-chip instead of through HBM.

  • LlmClient::processOne() in LlmClient.cpp, and the CMakeLists.txt to link XRT instead of httplib.
  • All of them — you'd rewrite the codebase against XRT from scratch.

Lesson 0004 · cpp_games / docs / learning

FPGAs, calling them from C++, and running LLMs on them

Why this matters: your cpp_game_with_llm_npcs already uses a sidecar for inference. Researchers are now putting that same inference workload on FPGAs, and getting 1.1–3.3× the speed of a GPU at 3–6× less energy. This lesson is the conceptual bridge from "Ollama on a GPU" to "what if Wren's brain were a programmable chip instead?"

1. What an FPGA actually is

An FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array) is a chip whose wiring is programmable. A CPU has a fixed circuit that fetches instructions and runs them. An FPGA ships with a sea of generic logic blocks and wires, and at boot you load a configuration that becomes a specific custom circuit. You're not running software on hardware — you're describing hardware that the chip then is.

inside an FPGA, every cell is one of these: +----+----+----+----+ LUT = a tiny 4- or 6-input lookup table |LUT |LUT |LUT |LUT | that you fill in to implement |----+ FF +----+ FF | any boolean function |LUT | |LUT | | FF = a flip-flop (one bit of state) +----+----+----+----+ DSP = a dedicated multiplier-accumulator |LUT |LUT |DSP |LUT | BRAM = a small on-chip RAM block |----+ FF | | FF | |LUT | | | | Routing fabric (the lines between) +----+----+----+----+ is itself programmable. |BRAM|BRAM|LUT |LUT | | | |----+ FF | You "program" an FPGA by deciding which | | |LUT | | cells light up and how they're wired +----+----+----+----+ together. The result is a circuit.

You describe what you want using a hardware description language — Verilog or VHDL — or with High-Level Synthesis (HLS), where you write C/C++ and a compiler produces the HDL for you. A synthesizer reduces your description to LUTs/FFs/DSPs, a placer assigns them to physical cells, a router connects them, and the final output is a bitstream: a file that, when loaded into the chip, rewires it to be the circuit you described.

The one-sentence mental model

An FPGA is a chip where you specify the schematic at boot time, then run signals through it — not instructions through a fixed CPU.

2. FPGA vs. CPU vs. GPU

All three are silicon. They diverge on what they're optimized to do.

CPU (your game loop)

  • Few (4–16) very smart cores
  • Branch prediction, deep caches, out-of-order execution
  • Optimized for latency on serial code with unpredictable control flow
  • Programmed in C++/Rust/etc.

GPU (Ollama, today)

  • Thousands of small cores, ganged into "warps"
  • Massive memory bandwidth, simple cache
  • Optimized for throughput on regular parallel math (matrices, pixels)
  • Programmed in CUDA/Vulkan/OpenCL

FPGA

  • Sea of LUTs/FFs/DSPs wired to your spec
  • You build a deep custom pipeline; throughput = 1 result per clock
  • Optimized for determinism + efficiency on a single fixed workload
  • Programmed in Verilog/VHDL/HLS
QuestionCPUGPUFPGA
"What's it good at?"Irregular code, branches, single-threaded latencyLots of identical math in parallelOne specific dataflow done with minimal energy
"How do I program it?"Write code, compile, runWrite a kernel, dispatch from hostDescribe a circuit, synthesize, load bitstream
"Time from idea to running"Seconds (compile)Seconds (compile)Hours (synth + place & route)
"Change behaviour at runtime?"Trivially — new codeTrivially — new kernelPossible (reload bitstream) but heavy
"Energy efficiency"Worst — lots of silicon never usedBetter on its workloadBest — only the circuit you needed exists
"Cost to get started"You have oneYou have one$500 dev board → $40k data-center card

The takeaway: an FPGA shines when you have one workload you'll run millions of times and you care about energy and tail latency. That's not a game loop — game logic branches too much. But it is an LLM doing matrix-multiply after matrix-multiply.

3. How a C++ program "calls" an FPGA

This is the part that maps cleanly onto what you've already built. From a C++ program's point of view, an FPGA is an accelerator at the other end of a bus — usually PCIe. You don't "call a function" on it the way you call printf. You move data into its memory, kick off a kernel, and wait for the result.

your C++ host the bus the FPGA card +---------------+ +--------+ +--------------------+ | game / driver | ===> | PCIe | ===> | bitstream is your | | OpenCL/XRT API| | (or | | custom circuit: | | | <=== | HBM | <=== | matrix multiply, | +---------------+ | link) | | attention kernel, | +--------+ | whatever you need | +--------------------+ data flow: 1. host allocates a buffer (host RAM, mapped to FPGA card via OpenCL) 2. host writes input data into it 3. host enqueues the kernel (a one-line API call) 4. FPGA does the work (everything runs in parallel inside) 5. host waits, then reads the output buffer

Here is the same pattern in C++ using AMD's XRT (the Xilinx Runtime, which lives behind the Vitis HLS toolchain). It looks deceptively like our LlmClient:

#include <xrt/xrt_device.h>
#include <xrt/xrt_kernel.h>
#include <xrt/xrt_bo.h>

int main() {
    // 1. Open the FPGA card and load the bitstream — analogous to
    //    "ollama serve starting up with a model loaded".
    auto device = xrt::device(0);
    auto uuid   = device.load_xclbin("matmul_kernel.xclbin");
    auto kernel = xrt::kernel(device, uuid, "matmul");

    // 2. Allocate device buffers and fill them — like building a JSON body.
    auto A = xrt::bo(device, N*N*sizeof(float), kernel.group_id(0));
    auto B = xrt::bo(device, N*N*sizeof(float), kernel.group_id(1));
    auto C = xrt::bo(device, N*N*sizeof(float), kernel.group_id(2));
    A.write(matrixA); A.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_TO_DEVICE);
    B.write(matrixB); B.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_TO_DEVICE);

    // 3. Launch the kernel — like cli.Post("/api/chat", ...) in LlmClient.cpp.
    auto run = kernel(A, B, C, N);

    // 4. Wait for it (blocking) — or .start()/.wait() async like our worker thread does.
    run.wait();

    // 5. Read result back to host RAM — like parsing res->body into reply.content.
    C.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_FROM_DEVICE);
    C.read(resultMatrix);
}

Notice the five-step shape: set up → ship inputs → launch → wait → read outputs. That's structurally identical to a network call to Ollama. The only difference is what's on the other side: instead of a process talking HTTP, it's a circuit talking memory.

4. LLMs on FPGAs — the exciting part

Until recently the idea of running a language model on an FPGA was a research curiosity. As of 2026 it's real, and the results are interesting enough that AMD and a couple of startups are pouring money into it.

Real 2026 numbers

The LUT-LLM paper (Nov 2025) implemented Qwen 3 1.7B — not a toy — on an AMD Alveo V80 FPGA. On the generation step it reported 1.10–3.29× faster than a GPU, and 3.05–6.60× better energy efficiency. A Versal/Alveo system running Mamba2-2.7B hit ~93 tokens/s on the prefill, ~200 tokens/s in decode on an Alveo U280, and ~333 tokens/s in decode on a VHK158.

Why does an FPGA win on LLM inference at all? Three reasons:

  1. The arithmetic is regular and quantized. Modern LLM inference is mostly multiplying weight matrices by activation vectors at 4- or 8-bit precision. That's the workload where an FPGA's dedicated DSPs and customizable bit widths beat a GPU's fixed FP16/BF16 lanes.
  2. You can build the exact dataflow. A GPU has fixed-size warps and a fixed cache hierarchy. An FPGA lets you wire one layer's output straight into the next layer's input on chip, without round-tripping through HBM. That's where the energy savings come from.
  3. Lookup-table tricks like LUT-LLM. A 2025 insight: at very low bit-width, you can replace some multiplies with pre-baked table lookups in the FPGA's BRAM. CPUs and GPUs can't do that cheaply; FPGAs absolutely can — LUTs are their native unit.

The catches, in plain English:

  • An Alveo V80 is several thousand dollars; a VHK158 is tens of thousands. For a hobby game, you'd use a GPU.
  • "Programming" the FPGA means an HLS or HDL flow, a multi-hour synthesis run, and probably $1k+ of Vitis tooling (or its open-source approximations).
  • You target one model at a time. Switching from Qwen 3 to Llama 3 means reloading a different bitstream — potentially recompiling it.

5. In your project (hypothetically)

Your game doesn't have an FPGA in it. But here's the punchline: your LlmClient wouldn't care if you added one. The whole reason we made processOne() the only place that knows about Ollama is precisely so we could replace it later. Here's what would change — and what wouldn't.

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:67 — today 
// Sidecar implementation, HTTP to Ollama.
ChatReply LlmClient::processOne(const ChatRequest& req) {
    httplib::Client cli(config_.host, config_.port);
    auto res = cli.Post("/api/chat", buildJson(req), "application/json");
    // ... parse and return ...
}
cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:67 — hypothetical FPGA backend 
// Same signature, different transport — XRT call to a Qwen kernel on Alveo.
ChatReply LlmClient::processOne(const ChatRequest& req) {
    auto tokens = tokenize(req);                            // CPU
    inputBuf_.write(tokens.data());
    inputBuf_.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_TO_DEVICE);                // PCIe -> FPGA
    auto run = qwenKernel_(inputBuf_, outputBuf_, tokens.size());
    run.wait();                                              // FPGA does the work
    outputBuf_.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_FROM_DEVICE);             // FPGA -> PCIe
    ChatReply reply;
    reply.id = req.id;
    reply.ok = true;
    reply.content = detokenize(outputBuf_);                  // CPU
    return reply;
}

The function body changes completely. But nothing else in the codebase moves:

  • LlmClient::submit(), drainReplies(), workerLoop() — unchanged.
  • Npc, Persona, history-trimming — unchanged.
  • DialogUI, main.cpp — unchanged.
  • Your async drain pattern, your thread-safe queues — unchanged.

That's the whole reward for the encapsulation we did in lesson 0001. From the game's point of view, "Wren's brain is on an FPGA" and "Wren's brain is in a Python process down the hall" are indistinguishable as long as processOne() turns a request into a reply.

6. Often confused with...

FPGA vs. ASIC

An ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) is a chip designed and fabricated for one job — an NVIDIA H100 is an ASIC, your phone's neural engine is an ASIC. It's faster and more power-efficient than the same design on an FPGA, but the design is frozen in silicon. FPGA is the reprogrammable cousin: you give up some efficiency in exchange for being able to ship a new bitstream tomorrow. Most chips that ship to consumers in volume are ASICs; FPGAs dominate prototyping, niche workloads, and any case where the workload mutates faster than chip fab cycles (years).

FPGA vs. GPU

Both are massively parallel and live on PCIe. The difference is rigidity. A GPU's parallelism is fixed: 32-wide warps, fixed-size caches, a fixed instruction set. You write a kernel that maps your problem onto that grid. An FPGA's parallelism is whatever you wire up: 17-wide pipelines, 12-bit arithmetic, on-chip RAM blocks placed where you need them. GPUs are easier to program and have better tooling; FPGAs are more efficient when your workload is regular and you're willing to spend weeks tuning.

FPGA vs. microcontroller

A microcontroller (Arduino, STM32) is a tiny CPU. An FPGA can contain a microcontroller as one circuit among many — that's called a "soft core" — but the FPGA itself is fundamentally different: customizable wiring, not fixed CPU logic. People sometimes use FPGAs because they need both a tiny CPU and a hardware pipeline next to it.

FPGA on a board vs. eFPGA inside an SoC

Modern AMD Versal chips put a small FPGA fabric inside the same package as ARM CPU cores and a GPU. This is an embedded FPGA (eFPGA). From a programmer's view it's still "configurable hardware you call from C++"; from a hardware view it lives on the same die as everything else, so the PCIe step disappears. The LLM-on-FPGA work increasingly targets Versal AI Edge SoCs for exactly this reason.

7. Quiz

You "program" an FPGA. What does that actually mean at the chip level?

  • You write machine instructions to a small instruction memory and the chip executes them in order.
  • You load a bitstream that configures which logic blocks are active and how they're wired into a circuit.
  • You upload a kernel that runs across thousands of parallel threads on a fixed instruction set.
  • You permanently etch a custom design into the silicon during the fabrication process.

Why is an FPGA not a good fit for your game's main loop (the SFML/OpenGL update-and-render code in cpp_shooter_game or cpp_racing_game)?

  • FPGAs can only do integer math, and game physics needs floats.
  • Game-loop code is branchy and irregular — the FPGA strength is regular dataflow, not unpredictable control flow.
  • SFML doesn't have FPGA bindings.
  • An FPGA doesn't have enough memory to hold the game state.

In the hypothetical FPGA backend for LlmClient::processOne(), the host C++ code calls inputBuf_.sync(XCL_BO_SYNC_BO_TO_DEVICE). What is this doing, and why is it necessary?

  • Loading a fresh bitstream into the FPGA so it knows what model to run.
  • Copying the buffer contents over PCIe from host RAM to the FPGA's on-card memory so the kernel can read them.
  • Allocating a new buffer on the FPGA each time.
  • Acquiring a mutex so the worker thread doesn't read while the FPGA writes.

Why do FPGAs win on energy efficiency for LLM inference (~3–6× a GPU in the LUT-LLM result)?

  • FPGAs run at a much lower temperature, so their transistors switch with less leakage.
  • FPGAs clock higher than GPUs, so each operation takes fewer joules.
  • The bitstream only lights up the circuit the workload actually uses, at the bit-widths it actually uses, and routes data on-chip instead of through HBM.
  • FPGAs don't use any memory hierarchy — the weights are baked into the gates.

You decide one day to swap Ollama for an FPGA-hosted Qwen kernel. Which of the following files will you have to change?

  • Persona.hpp, Npc.cpp, and DialogUI.cpp.
  • Mostly main.cpp, plus a new CMake target.
  • LlmClient::processOne() in LlmClient.cpp, and the CMakeLists.txt to link XRT instead of httplib.
  • All of them — you'd rewrite the codebase against XRT from scratch.

## Concepts demonstrated in the project but not yet formally taught

These are concepts the user has *seen* in the code I wrote but hasn't yet

- **Filesystem path walking with `std::filesystem`** — how `main.cpp`

# Glossary

> Terms the user has demonstrably grasped. Each entry: short definition,
> the lesson it was introduced in, and where it lives in the codebase.
> Only promote a term here once the user has used it correctly in
> conversation or aced the quiz item about it.

> Status legend:
> `taught` = explained in a lesson  ·
> `firm` = used correctly unprompted  ·
> `shaky` = needs revisit

## A

- **Array decay** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When a C-style array is passed to a function, the parameter is silently
  rewritten to a pointer, losing its size. `void f(int arr[10])` becomes
  `void f(int* arr)`. `std::array` does not decay.

## C

- **C-style array** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Raw `T arr[N]` from C. Fixed size, stack storage, decays to pointer on
  function call. Still appears at
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp:72`.

## E

- **Erase-remove idiom** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Pattern for deleting elements from a `std::vector` that match a
  predicate without shrinking capacity. `v.erase(std::remove_if(b, e,
  pred), e)`. Used in `cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:686` to clean up
  dead projectiles per frame.

## F

- **Frame budget** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  The wall-clock time available for one game-loop iteration before the
  next vsync. 16.67 ms at 60 Hz, 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. Exceeding it once
  produces visible stutter regardless of average speed.

## G

- **Embedded LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  A language model whose output is consumed by the running game process,
  regardless of whether the model lives in the same binary or in a sidecar
  process on `localhost`.

## I

- **In-process LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  Model linked into the game binary, called via a C/C++ API (e.g.
  `llama.cpp`). Contrast: **sidecar process**.

## P

- **Persona prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  Static system-prompt text rendered from a `Persona` struct, prepended to
  every chat request to keep the NPC in character. See
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Persona.hpp::renderSystemPrompt`.

## H

- **Hot loop / hot path** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Code that runs many times per frame — per-entity update loops,
  per-line render code. Allocations and copies that would be invisible
  elsewhere are budget-eaters here.

## L

- **Latency vs throughput** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Latency = time for a single operation (a game frame). Throughput =
  total operations per second (requests). Games optimize for worst-case
  latency, not average throughput.

## M

- **`std::move`** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  A cast that marks a value as "you may steal from this." Whether
  anything is actually stolen depends on the destination's move
  constructor. For `std::string`/`std::vector` it steals the heap buffer
  in O(1); for trivial types it falls back to a copy.

## N

- **NRVO (Named Return Value Optimization)** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Compiler optimization that builds a returned local directly in the
  caller's slot, eliminating the return copy/move entirely.
  `LlmClient::drainReplies()` relies on this.

## R

- **Reallocation (vector growth)** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When `std::vector::push_back` exceeds capacity, a new heap buffer is
  allocated, all existing elements are moved/copied across, and the old
  buffer is freed. `reserve()` ahead of time avoids the storm.

## S

- **`std::array<T, N>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Fixed-size, compile-time-known array wrapper. Stack-allocated, doesn't
  decay, carries its size in the type. Used in the racing/shooter games
  for quad corners, matrices, and font candidate lists.

- **`std::vector<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Dynamic-size, heap-backed sequence container. Use when count varies at
  runtime. Used throughout: shooter `projectiles`/`enemies`/`pickups`/
  `impacts`, racing's `buildRoundedRectLoop` return, NPC `history_`.

- **Sidecar process** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  A separate local process (Ollama, LM Studio, llamafile) that hosts the
  model and exposes an HTTP API the game POSTs to. Contrast:
  **in-process LLM**.

- **System prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  The `role: "system"` message in a chat request. Fixed identity, applied
  before any user turn.

## Pending promotion

(Terms used in the lesson but not yet confirmed grasped in conversation —
once the user demonstrates understanding, move them above.)

- Async drain pattern (worker thread + thread-safe reply queue)
- Bounded conversation history
- Dialogue tree (the pre-LLM baseline being contrasted)
- GGUF (quantized model file format)
- llama.cpp (the embedded-inference library)
- Ollama (the sidecar we're using)
- Quantization
- RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
- Streaming inference (`"stream": true`)
- Structured output (grammar-constrained JSON)
- Concurrency vs parallelism

# Glossary

> Terms the user has demonstrably grasped. Each entry: short definition,
> the lesson it was introduced in, and where it lives in the codebase.
> Only promote a term here once the user has used it correctly in
> conversation or aced the quiz item about it.

> Status legend:
> `taught` = explained in a lesson  ·
> `firm` = used correctly unprompted  ·
> `shaky` = needs revisit

## A

- **Array decay** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When a C-style array is passed to a function, the parameter is silently
  rewritten to a pointer, losing its size. `void f(int arr[10])` becomes
  `void f(int* arr)`. `std::array` does not decay.

- **ASIC** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. A chip fabricated for one
  fixed job (e.g. NVIDIA H100, phone neural engine). Faster and more
  efficient than the same design on an FPGA, but unchangeable once
  shipped. FPGA is the reprogrammable cousin.

## C

- **C-style array** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Raw `T arr[N]` from C. Fixed size, stack storage, decays to pointer on
  function call. Still appears at
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp:72`.

## E

- **Erase-remove idiom** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Pattern for deleting elements from a `std::vector` that match a
  predicate without shrinking capacity. `v.erase(std::remove_if(b, e,
  pred), e)`. Used in `cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:686` to clean up
  dead projectiles per frame.

## F

- **Frame budget** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  The wall-clock time available for one game-loop iteration before the
  next vsync. 16.67 ms at 60 Hz, 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. Exceeding it once
  produces visible stutter regardless of average speed.

## G

- **Embedded LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  A language model whose output is consumed by the running game process,
  regardless of whether the model lives in the same binary or in a sidecar
  process on `localhost`.

## I

- **In-process LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  Model linked into the game binary, called via a C/C++ API (e.g.
  `llama.cpp`). Contrast: **sidecar process**.

## P

- **Persona prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  Static system-prompt text rendered from a `Persona` struct, prepended to
  every chat request to keep the NPC in character. See
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Persona.hpp::renderSystemPrompt`.

## H

- **Hot loop / hot path** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Code that runs many times per frame — per-entity update loops,
  per-line render code. Allocations and copies that would be invisible
  elsewhere are budget-eaters here.

## L

- **Latency vs throughput** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Latency = time for a single operation (a game frame). Throughput =
  total operations per second (requests). Games optimize for worst-case
  latency, not average throughput.

## M

- **`std::move`** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  A cast that marks a value as "you may steal from this." Whether
  anything is actually stolen depends on the destination's move
  constructor. For `std::string`/`std::vector` it steals the heap buffer
  in O(1); for trivial types it falls back to a copy.

## N

- **NRVO (Named Return Value Optimization)** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Compiler optimization that builds a returned local directly in the
  caller's slot, eliminating the return copy/move entirely.
  `LlmClient::drainReplies()` relies on this.

## R

- **Reallocation (vector growth)** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When `std::vector::push_back` exceeds capacity, a new heap buffer is
  allocated, all existing elements are moved/copied across, and the old
  buffer is freed. `reserve()` ahead of time avoids the storm.

## S

- **`std::array<T, N>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Fixed-size, compile-time-known array wrapper. Stack-allocated, doesn't
  decay, carries its size in the type. Used in the racing/shooter games
  for quad corners, matrices, and font candidate lists.

- **`std::vector<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Dynamic-size, heap-backed sequence container. Use when count varies at
  runtime. Used throughout: shooter `projectiles`/`enemies`/`pickups`/
  `impacts`, racing's `buildRoundedRectLoop` return, NPC `history_`.

- **Sidecar process** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  A separate local process (Ollama, LM Studio, llamafile) that hosts the
  model and exposes an HTTP API the game POSTs to. Contrast:
  **in-process LLM**.

- **System prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  The `role: "system"` message in a chat request. Fixed identity, applied
  before any user turn.

## Pending promotion

(Terms used in the lesson but not yet confirmed grasped in conversation —
once the user demonstrates understanding, move them above.)

- Async drain pattern (worker thread + thread-safe reply queue)
- Bounded conversation history
- Dialogue tree (the pre-LLM baseline being contrasted)

- Ollama (the sidecar we're using)
- Quantization

- Streaming inference (`"stream": true`)
- Structured output (grammar-constrained JSON)
- Concurrency vs parallelism

# Glossary

> Terms the user has demonstrably grasped. Each entry: short definition,
> the lesson it was introduced in, and where it lives in the codebase.
> Only promote a term here once the user has used it correctly in
> conversation or aced the quiz item about it.

> Status legend:
> `taught` = explained in a lesson  ·
> `firm` = used correctly unprompted  ·
> `shaky` = needs revisit

## A

- **Array decay** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When a C-style array is passed to a function, the parameter is silently
  rewritten to a pointer, losing its size. `void f(int arr[10])` becomes
  `void f(int* arr)`. `std::array` does not decay.

- **ASIC** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. A chip fabricated for one
  fixed job (e.g. NVIDIA H100, phone neural engine). Faster and more
  efficient than the same design on an FPGA, but unchangeable once
  shipped. FPGA is the reprogrammable cousin.

## C

- **C-style array** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Raw `T arr[N]` from C. Fixed size, stack storage, decays to pointer on
  function call. Still appears at
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp:72`.

## E

- **Erase-remove idiom** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Pattern for deleting elements from a `std::vector` that match a
  predicate without shrinking capacity. `v.erase(std::remove_if(b, e,
  pred), e)`. Used in `cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:686` to clean up
  dead projectiles per frame.

## F

- **Frame budget** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  The wall-clock time available for one game-loop iteration before the
  next vsync. 16.67 ms at 60 Hz, 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. Exceeding it once
  produces visible stutter regardless of average speed.

## G

- **Embedded LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  A language model whose output is consumed by the running game process,
  regardless of whether the model lives in the same binary or in a sidecar
  process on `localhost`.

## I

- **In-process LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  Model linked into the game binary, called via a C/C++ API (e.g.
  `llama.cpp`). Contrast: **sidecar process**.

## P

- **Persona prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  Static system-prompt text rendered from a `Persona` struct, prepended to
  every chat request to keep the NPC in character. See
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Persona.hpp::renderSystemPrompt`.

## H

- **Hot loop / hot path** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Code that runs many times per frame — per-entity update loops,
  per-line render code. Allocations and copies that would be invisible
  elsewhere are budget-eaters here.

## L

- **Latency vs throughput** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Latency = time for a single operation (a game frame). Throughput =
  total operations per second (requests). Games optimize for worst-case
  latency, not average throughput.

## M

- **`std::move`** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  A cast that marks a value as "you may steal from this." Whether
  anything is actually stolen depends on the destination's move
  constructor. For `std::string`/`std::vector` it steals the heap buffer
  in O(1); for trivial types it falls back to a copy.

## N

- **NRVO (Named Return Value Optimization)** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Compiler optimization that builds a returned local directly in the
  caller's slot, eliminating the return copy/move entirely.
  `LlmClient::drainReplies()` relies on this.

## R

- **Reallocation (vector growth)** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When `std::vector::push_back` exceeds capacity, a new heap buffer is
  allocated, all existing elements are moved/copied across, and the old
  buffer is freed. `reserve()` ahead of time avoids the storm.

## S

- **`std::array<T, N>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Fixed-size, compile-time-known array wrapper. Stack-allocated, doesn't
  decay, carries its size in the type. Used in the racing/shooter games
  for quad corners, matrices, and font candidate lists.

- **`std::vector<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Dynamic-size, heap-backed sequence container. Use when count varies at
  runtime. Used throughout: shooter `projectiles`/`enemies`/`pickups`/
  `impacts`, racing's `buildRoundedRectLoop` return, NPC `history_`.

- **Sidecar process** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  A separate local process (Ollama, LM Studio, llamafile) that hosts the
  model and exposes an HTTP API the game POSTs to. Contrast:
  **in-process LLM**.

- **System prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  The `role: "system"` message in a chat request. Fixed identity, applied
  before any user turn.

## Process vs. Thread Virtual Address Space

A process has a full complement of private state including program registers, condition codes, virtual address space, and kernel-managed resources like file descriptors. In contrast, a thread has a limited complement of private state, primarily just program registers and condition codes.

Multiple threads generated in a single process share the same virtual address space. More specifically, when the CLONE_VM flag is set in Linux, the child shares the parent's virtual memory space, which is fundamental to thread creation because it enables multiple execution contexts to operate within the same address space.

## System Calls and Address Space

When a process thread makes a system call, the kernel, which executes in the context of this thread, can access the process memory efficiently.

## Localhost and Virtual Loopback

Regarding localhost and loopback addresses, the Citrix virtual loopback feature allows you to configure applications that depend on communications with localhost (127.0.0.1 by default) to use a unique virtual loopback address in the localhost range.

## Spurious Wakeup and Predicates

Spurious wakeups occur when threads that are waiting for condition variables become unblocked without appropriate notifications. A predicate can be optionally provided to detect spurious wakeup.

## How wait() Works

The wait() function causes the current thread to block until the condition variable is notified or a spurious wakeup occurs. The thread will be unblocked when notify_all() or notify_one() is executed, or it may also be unblocked spuriously.

## Using Predicates to Handle Spurious Wakeups

The predicate overload may be used to ignore spurious awakenings while waiting for a specific condition to become true. You can use wait(unique_lock<mutex>& lock, Predicate pred) to perform this loop automatically for you.

The predicate approach is recommended because the wait() function must be invoked from a loop that checks whether a condition predicate holds.

The effects of notify_one()/notify_all() and the atomic parts of wait() take place in a single total order that makes it impossible for notify_one() to be delayed and unblock a thread that started waiting just after the call to notify_one() was made.

This modern C++ approach with condition variables ensures thread-safe synchronization when used with proper predicates.
