Lesson 0005 · cpp_games / docs / learning

Multithreading and shared resources

Why this matters: your LlmClient already runs two threads (the game loop and a worker) and they pass data through shared memory. Every primitive in this lesson is sitting in LlmClient.cpp right now — mutex, condition variable, atomic, joinable thread. This lesson is the why behind what you already have.

1. The concept — what threads share, and what goes wrong

A thread is an independent stream of execution. When you start one inside your program, it runs alongside the main thread on a different CPU core (most of the time). They can both be doing useful work simultaneously. And — this is the part that gets you in trouble — they share the same memory.

What's shared between threads in one process?What's private to each thread?
The heap. std::vector, std::queue, any object reachable through a pointer or reference.The stack. Local variables and the call chain that produced them.
Global and static variables.CPU registers, including the program counter (where in the code this thread is).
Open file descriptors, sockets, anything kernel-tracked.Whatever's currently in this thread's registers.

Shared mutable state is the source of every multithreading bug. The classic disaster:

time --> Thread A: read counter (= 5) ... add 1 ... write counter (= 6) Thread B: read counter (= 5) ... add 1 ... write counter (= 6) Two increments happened. The counter is 6 instead of 7. That's a race condition.

The fix is synchronisation — tools that force threads to take turns where it matters. Modern C++ gives you three you'll meet today:

PrimitiveWhat it doesUse when
std::mutexOnly one thread at a time can hold the lock. Others wait at the door.Protecting a non-trivial data structure (a queue, a vector, a struct with multiple fields).
std::condition_variableLets a thread sleep cheaply until another thread says "wake up, the thing you were waiting for is ready.""Wait until the queue has work" / "wait until shutdown is signalled."
std::atomic<T>A single variable whose read/modify/write is uninterruptible by another thread. Hardware-supported.One simple value: a counter, a flag, a pointer swap.

The rule of thumb

Use atomic for a single variable. Use mutex for anything bigger. Use a condition variable on top of a mutex when one thread needs to wait for a state change rather than poll.

2. Minimal example — the same counter, three ways

Two threads each try to increment a counter a million times. We expect 2,000,000.

// (1) NO SYNC — race condition. Final value is unpredictable, usually low.
int counter = 0;
auto worker = [&] { for (int i = 0; i < 1'000'000; ++i) ++counter; };
std::thread t1(worker), t2(worker);
t1.join(); t2.join();
std::cout << counter;   // e.g. 1,437,221. Different every run. Wrong.

// (2) MUTEX — correct, ~50× slower for this trivial workload.
int counter = 0;
std::mutex m;
auto worker = [&] {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1'000'000; ++i) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);  // take lock
        ++counter;                            // safe
    }                                         // lock released here
};

// (3) ATOMIC — correct, near native speed. The right tool here.
std::atomic<int> counter{0};
auto worker = [&] {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1'000'000; ++i) {
        counter.fetch_add(1);                // uninterruptible RMW
    }
};

Three things to take away from this example:

  • "It works on my machine" is meaningless for thread bugs. Version 1 will sometimes print 2,000,000 by sheer luck. Race conditions are not deterministic.
  • The mutex is correct but wasteful here. We're locking and unlocking a million times to protect a single int. That's what atomics exist for.
  • The atomic version isn't free. fetch_add compiles to a special CPU instruction (e.g. LOCK XADD on x86). It's much faster than a mutex but still ~10× slower than a plain ++.

3. In your project — the four primitives in LlmClient

Open cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.hpp. The bottom of the class is a small museum of every concept above.

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.hpp:74 
private:
    // ATOMIC FLAGS — single bools read/written from both threads.
    std::atomic<bool> stop_{false};
    std::atomic<bool> inFlight_{false};

    // MUTEX + CV + QUEUE — main thread submits, worker dequeues.
    std::mutex requestMutex_;
    std::condition_variable requestCv_;
    std::queue<ChatRequest> requests_;

    // SECOND MUTEX — protects the reply list independently.
    std::mutex replyMutex_;
    std::vector<ChatReply> replies_;

    // ATOMIC COUNTER — generating unique request IDs without a mutex.
    std::atomic<std::uint64_t> nextId_{1};

    std::thread worker_;

The thread itself: RAII lifetime

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:13 
LlmClient::LlmClient(LlmConfig config) : config_(std::move(config)) {
    worker_ = std::thread(&LlmClient::workerLoop, this);   // start
}

LlmClient::~LlmClient() {
    stop_.store(true);          // signal: time to leave
    requestCv_.notify_all();    // wake worker if it's sleeping
    if (worker_.joinable()) worker_.join();   // wait for it to finish
}

The thread is owned by the object. Constructor starts it, destructor joins it. If we forgot the join(), the program would std::terminate() when the thread object went out of scope while still running. RAII for thread lifetime is just as important as RAII for memory.

Producer side: submit a request

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:21 
std::uint64_t LlmClient::submit(std::string systemPrompt,
                                std::vector<ChatTurn> history,
                                std::string userMessage) {
    ChatRequest req;
    req.id = nextId_.fetch_add(1);   // ATOMIC: no mutex needed
    // ... move parameters into req ...

    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(requestMutex_);  // MUTEX: take lock
        requests_.push(std::move(req));                   // modify shared queue
    }                                                     // release at scope end
    requestCv_.notify_one();   // CV: wake up one waiter (the worker)
    return req.id;
}

Two synchronisation primitives in one function. nextId_ is atomic because incrementing a counter is the textbook atomic use case — cheaper than a mutex. The queue is mutex-protected because it's a non-trivial data structure with multiple pointers being shuffled around inside push(). The notify wakes the worker if it was asleep waiting for work.

Consumer side: the worker waits properly

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:48 
void LlmClient::workerLoop() {
    while (true) {
        ChatRequest req;
        {
            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(requestMutex_);

            // CV WITH PREDICATE — sleeps if predicate is false,
            // re-checks every wakeup, ignores spurious wakeups for free.
            requestCv_.wait(lock, [this] {
                return stop_.load() || !requests_.empty();
            });

            if (stop_.load() && requests_.empty()) return;
            req = std::move(requests_.front());
            requests_.pop();
        }   // release lock before doing slow work

        ChatReply reply = processOne(req);  // no lock held — others can submit

        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(replyMutex_);
            replies_.push_back(std::move(reply));
        }
    }
}

Four design decisions to notice:

  1. The CV uses the predicate form of wait. The version without a predicate is a trap — OS-level CVs are allowed to wake threads spuriously (no notify happened, the thread just woke up anyway). With a predicate, the standard library re-checks the condition and goes back to sleep if it wasn't really ready. We don't have to write that loop ourselves.
  2. The predicate checks two things. stop_ OR !requests_.empty(). So the worker wakes on either "shutdown" or "new work". One CV handles both.
  3. The lock is released before processOne(). Otherwise the worker would hold requestMutex_ for the entire 1-3 second HTTP call to Ollama, and any thread calling submit() would block. The scope of the lock is exactly "manipulate the queue" — not "do the actual work."
  4. The reply uses a different mutex. The worker doesn't need requestMutex_ while writing to replies_, and the main thread (calling drainReplies()) doesn't need replyMutex_ while calling submit(). Two independent locks = no false sharing of contention.

Why two mutexes and not one

Imagine if both vectors lived under a single stateMutex_. Every submit() would briefly contend with every drainReplies() even though they touch different data. With two mutexes:

Single mutex: main thread |--submit--||--drain--| worker :----wait-----: |--push-result--| Two mutexes: main thread |--submit--||--drain--| worker :wait: |---http call (no lock)---| |push-result| The worker can hold replyMutex_ to write a result *while* the main thread is holding requestMutex_ to submit a new request. They don't block each other.

4. Often confused with...

Mutex vs. atomic

People reach for atomics because they sound faster. They are — for one variable. The moment you need to update two fields together ("subtract from account A and add to account B"), atomic stops being correct on its own; you'd need a mutex around both updates so they appear atomic together. Atomic is for single values that can be read/modified/written in one CPU instruction. Mutex is for anything bigger or any case where invariants span multiple variables.

Race condition vs. deadlock

A race condition is two threads stepping on each other's data because neither waited. The program runs but produces wrong results. A deadlock is two threads each holding a lock the other one needs; they wait forever. The program freezes producing nothing. Different failure modes, different fixes: more synchronisation prevents races; less or smarter synchronisation prevents deadlocks. The cardinal rule for avoiding deadlocks is: always acquire locks in the same order. Our LlmClient never holds both mutexes at once, so deadlock is impossible there.

notify_one vs. notify_all

Our submit() calls notify_one — there's only one worker, so waking one is exactly right. notify_all is for when you've changed the state in a way multiple waiters might care about (e.g. "the connection is now open; everyone who was waiting can proceed"). Using notify_all when notify_one would do creates a thundering herd: every waiter wakes, contends for the mutex, finds nothing to do, and goes back to sleep. The destructor uses notify_all in case we ever add a second worker; with only one waiter today it's equivalent.

CV vs. polling with sleep

A tempting alternative for the worker loop is while(!hasWork) sleep_for(1ms);. It would even work. But the worker is awake every millisecond doing nothing — burning CPU and battery, and adding up to a millisecond of latency when work arrives mid-sleep. The CV version is asleep — the OS removes it from the scheduler entirely. It wakes only when notified. Lower latency, lower power, less code.

Threads vs. processes

Lesson 0004 mentioned this in passing. Threads share memory; processes don't. Your game and Ollama are two processes — they can't even see each other's std::queue, which is why we need HTTP to communicate. Your main thread and worker thread are inside one process — they share requests_ directly, no serialisation, no syscall. That's why threading is the right tool for the producer/consumer pattern inside LlmClient, and processes are the right tool for talking to a totally separate program like Ollama.

5. Quiz

You add a debug counter int requestsSubmitted to LlmClient and bump it inside submit(). The class is now multithread-buggy. What's the smallest correct fix?

  • Wrap the increment in a std::lock_guard<std::mutex>.
  • Change the type to std::atomic<int> and use fetch_add(1).
  • Mark it volatile int.
  • Move it to a static variable so only one thread can write it.

Why does the worker in workerLoop() release requestMutex_ before calling processOne()?

  • processOne needs the mutex internally, so holding it from outside would deadlock.
  • So that other threads calling submit() can keep enqueueing while the slow HTTP call is happening.
  • Because the compiler will optimize away the mutex if it sees the call.
  • To allow the mutex's internal timer to expire and avoid a deadlock.

The worker loop's wait line is requestCv_.wait(lock, [this] { return stop_.load() || !requests_.empty(); });. Why include the predicate and not just wait(lock)?

  • Predicates are syntactic sugar that lets notify_one work without a lambda.
  • Condition variables can wake spuriously (with no notify). The predicate re-checks and goes back to sleep if the wakeup was bogus.
  • The predicate form is faster than the plain form on modern CPUs.
  • You need a separate CV for shutdown vs work; the predicate ties them together.

A junior dev "simplifies" LlmClient by replacing both mutexes with one stateMutex_. The code still compiles and passes its tests. What real-world behaviour is now worse?

  • Memory use roughly doubles — one big mutex is larger than two small ones.
  • The class is now susceptible to deadlock.
  • submit() and drainReplies() now contend on the same lock even though they touch different data.
  • Race conditions become more likely because one lock has to cover more code.

A new feature lets multiple NPCs talk in parallel by spawning multiple worker threads, all calling processOne. submit() still does notify_one. Is anything wrong?

  • Nothing's wrong. notify_one wakes any single waiter, which is what we want when handing work to a worker pool.
  • You must switch to notify_all or only the first worker will ever do work.
  • You need one CV per worker; sharing a CV among workers is undefined behaviour.
  • Each worker needs its own std::shared_ptr<ChatRequest> to avoid use-after-free.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. Imagine I'd written stop_ as a plain bool instead of a std::atomic<bool>. Describe a sequence where the worker thread misses the shutdown signal and runs forever. Two threads, three or four steps each. (Hint: there's no mutex on stop_.)

Scenario B. The destructor calls requestCv_.notify_all() after setting stop_. Why is the order (set, then notify) important? What goes wrong if you flip them?

Scenario C. You decide to give each Npc its own dedicated worker thread (a worker per NPC, not one shared worker). Argue both sides: what's the case for it (one paragraph), what's the case against it for your game specifically (one paragraph)? Use lesson 0003's concepts where they apply.

7. Track your progress

A tempting alternative for the worker loop is while(!hasWork) sleep_for(1ms);. It would even work. But the worker is awake every millisecond doing nothing — burning CPU and battery, and adding up to a millisecond of latency when work arrives mid-sleep. The CV version is asleep — the OS removes it from the scheduler entirely. It wakes only when notified. Lower latency, lower power, less code.

Threads vs. processes

Lesson 0004 mentioned this in passing. Threads share memory; processes don't. Your game and Ollama are two processes — they can't even see each other's std::queue, which is why we need HTTP to communicate. Your main thread and worker thread are inside one process — they share requests_ directly, no serialisation, no syscall. That's why threading is the right tool for the producer/consumer pattern inside LlmClient, and processes are the right tool for talking to a totally separate program like Ollama.

5. Quiz

You add a debug counter int requestsSubmitted to LlmClient and bump it inside submit(). The class is now multithread-buggy. What's the smallest correct fix?

  • Wrap the increment in a std::lock_guard<std::mutex>.
  • Change the type to std::atomic<int> and use fetch_add(1).
  • Mark it volatile int.
  • Move it to a static variable so only one thread can write it.

Why does the worker in workerLoop() release requestMutex_ before calling processOne()?

  • processOne needs the mutex internally, so holding it from outside would deadlock.
  • So that other threads calling submit() can keep enqueueing while the slow HTTP call is happening.
  • Because the compiler will optimize away the mutex if it sees the call.
  • To allow the mutex's internal timer to expire and avoid a deadlock.

The worker loop's wait line is requestCv_.wait(lock, [this] { return stop_.load() || !requests_.empty(); });. Why include the predicate and not just wait(lock)?

  • Predicates are syntactic sugar that lets notify_one work without a lambda.
  • Condition variables can wake spuriously (with no notify). The predicate re-checks and goes back to sleep if the wakeup was bogus.
  • The predicate form is faster than the plain form on modern CPUs.
  • You need a separate CV for shutdown vs work; the predicate ties them together.

A junior dev "simplifies" LlmClient by replacing both mutexes with one stateMutex_. The code still compiles and passes its tests. What real-world behaviour is now worse?

  • Memory use roughly doubles — one big mutex is larger than two small ones.
  • The class is now susceptible to deadlock.
  • submit() and drainReplies() now contend on the same lock even though they touch different data.
  • Race conditions become more likely because one lock has to cover more code.

A new feature lets multiple NPCs talk in parallel by spawning multiple worker threads, all calling processOne. submit() still does notify_one. Is anything wrong?

  • Nothing's wrong. notify_one wakes any single waiter, which is what we want when handing work to a worker pool.
  • You must switch to notify_all or only the first worker will ever do work.
  • You need one CV per worker; sharing a CV among workers is undefined behaviour.
  • Each worker needs its own std::shared_ptr<ChatRequest> to avoid use-after-free.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. Imagine I'd written stop_ as a plain bool instead of a std::atomic<bool>. Describe a sequence where the worker thread misses the shutdown signal and runs forever. Two threads, three or four steps each. (Hint: there's no mutex on stop_.)

Scenario B. The destructor calls requestCv_.notify_all() after setting stop_. Why is the order (set, then notify) important? What goes wrong if you flip them?

Scenario C. You decide to give each Npc its own dedicated worker thread (a worker per NPC, not one shared worker). Argue both sides: what's the case for it (one paragraph), what's the case against it for your game specifically (one paragraph)? Use lesson 0003's concepts where they apply.

7. Track your progress

   FPGA step. Note: requires the Vitis toolchain, which is a big install —

# Glossary

> Terms the user has demonstrably grasped. Each entry: short definition,
> the lesson it was introduced in, and where it lives in the codebase.
> Only promote a term here once the user has used it correctly in
> conversation or aced the quiz item about it.

> Status legend:
> `taught` = explained in a lesson  ·
> `firm` = used correctly unprompted  ·
> `shaky` = needs revisit

## A

- **Array decay** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When a C-style array is passed to a function, the parameter is silently
  rewritten to a pointer, losing its size. `void f(int arr[10])` becomes
  `void f(int* arr)`. `std::array` does not decay.

- **ASIC** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. A chip fabricated for one
  fixed job (e.g. NVIDIA H100, phone neural engine). Faster and more
  efficient than the same design on an FPGA, but unchangeable once
  shipped. FPGA is the reprogrammable cousin.

## B

- **Bitstream** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  The binary file that programs an FPGA. Produced by synthesizing an
  HDL/HLS design through place-and-route. Loading a different bitstream
  reconfigures the chip into a different circuit.

## C

- **C-style array** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Raw `T arr[N]` from C. Fixed size, stack storage, decays to pointer on
  function call. Still appears at
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp:72`.

## E

- **Embedded LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  A language model whose output is consumed by the running game process,
  regardless of whether the model lives in the same binary or in a sidecar
  process on `localhost`.

- **Erase-remove idiom** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Pattern for deleting elements from a `std::vector` that match a
  predicate without shrinking capacity. `v.erase(std::remove_if(b, e,
  pred), e)`. Used in `cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:686` to clean up
  dead projectiles per frame.

## F

- **FPGA** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  Field-Programmable Gate Array. A chip whose internal wiring is
  reconfigured at boot by loading a bitstream — the chip *becomes* the
  custom circuit you described, rather than executing instructions on a
  fixed circuit.

- **Frame budget** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  The wall-clock time available for one game-loop iteration before the
  next vsync. 16.67 ms at 60 Hz, 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. Exceeding it once
  produces visible stutter regardless of average speed.

## H

- **HLS (High-Level Synthesis)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  A flow that lets you write FPGA logic in C/C++ instead of Verilog/VHDL.
  Vitis HLS is the current AMD/Xilinx tool. The compiler converts your
  C++ kernel into HDL, then through synthesis into a bitstream.

- **Hot loop / hot path** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Code that runs many times per frame — per-entity update loops,
  per-line render code. Allocations and copies that would be invisible
  elsewhere are budget-eaters here.

## I

- **In-process LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  Model linked into the game binary, called via a C/C++ API (e.g.
  `llama.cpp`). Contrast: **sidecar process**.

## L

- **Latency vs throughput** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Latency = time for a single operation (a game frame). Throughput =
  total operations per second (requests). Games optimize for worst-case
  latency, not average throughput.

- **LUT (Look-Up Table)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  The fundamental cell of an FPGA. A 4- or 6-input table you fill in to
  implement any boolean function. Combined with flip-flops, DSPs, and
  BRAM blocks via programmable routing, LUTs build the user's circuit.

## M

- **`std::move`** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  A cast that marks a value as "you may steal from this." Whether
  anything is actually stolen depends on the destination's move
  constructor. For `std::string`/`std::vector` it steals the heap buffer
  in O(1); for trivial types it falls back to a copy.

## N

- **NRVO (Named Return Value Optimization)** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Compiler optimization that builds a returned local directly in the
  caller's slot, eliminating the return copy/move entirely.
  `LlmClient::drainReplies()` relies on this.

## P

- **Persona prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  Static system-prompt text rendered from a `Persona` struct, prepended to
  every chat request to keep the NPC in character. See
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Persona.hpp::renderSystemPrompt`.

## R

- **Reallocation (vector growth)** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When `std::vector::push_back` exceeds capacity, a new heap buffer is
  allocated, all existing elements are moved/copied across, and the old
  buffer is freed. `reserve()` ahead of time avoids the storm.

## S

- **`std::array<T, N>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Fixed-size, compile-time-known array wrapper. Stack-allocated, doesn't
  decay, carries its size in the type. Used in the racing/shooter games
  for quad corners, matrices, and font candidate lists.

- **`std::vector<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Dynamic-size, heap-backed sequence container. Use when count varies at
  runtime. Used throughout: shooter `projectiles`/`enemies`/`pickups`/
  `impacts`, racing's `buildRoundedRectLoop` return, NPC `history_`.

- **Sidecar process** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  A separate local process (Ollama, LM Studio, llamafile) that hosts the
  model and exposes an HTTP API the game POSTs to. Contrast:
  **in-process LLM**.

- **System prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  The `role: "system"` message in a chat request. Fixed identity, applied
  before any user turn.

## X

- **XRT (Xilinx Runtime)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  The host-side C++ API for talking to an FPGA over PCIe. Provides
  `xrt::device`, `xrt::kernel`, `xrt::bo` (buffer object). The
  five-step pattern: load xclbin → allocate BOs → write inputs + sync to
  device → launch kernel → sync output back. Structurally identical to
  the LlmClient HTTP pattern.

## Pending promotion

(Terms used in lessons but not yet confirmed grasped in conversation —
once the user demonstrates understanding, move them above.)

- Async drain pattern (worker thread + thread-safe reply queue)
- Bounded conversation history
- Dialogue tree (the pre-LLM baseline being contrasted)
- GGUF (quantized model file format)
- llama.cpp (the embedded-inference library)
- Ollama (the sidecar we're using)
- Quantization
- RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
- Streaming inference (`"stream": true`)
- Structured output (grammar-constrained JSON)
- Concurrency vs parallelism
- eFPGA / soft core (FPGA fabric inside an SoC; CPU built from LUTs)
- HBM (high-bandwidth memory on FPGA cards like VHK158, VCU128)
- Vitis HLS / Verilog / VHDL (the FPGA programming toolchain)
- LUT-LLM (the 2025 paper that put Qwen 3 1.7B on an Alveo V80)

## A

- **Array decay** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When a C-style array is passed to a function, the parameter is silently
  rewritten to a pointer, losing its size. `void f(int arr[10])` becomes
  `void f(int* arr)`. `std::array` does not decay.

- **ASIC** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. A chip fabricated for one
  fixed job (e.g. NVIDIA H100, phone neural engine). Faster and more
  efficient than the same design on an FPGA, but unchangeable once
  shipped. FPGA is the reprogrammable cousin.

## B

- **Bitstream** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  The binary file that programs an FPGA. Produced by synthesizing an
  HDL/HLS design through place-and-route. Loading a different bitstream
  reconfigures the chip into a different circuit.

## C

- **C-style array** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Raw `T arr[N]` from C. Fixed size, stack storage, decays to pointer on
  function call. Still appears at
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp:72`.

- **Condition variable (`std::condition_variable`)** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
  Synchronisation primitive that lets a thread sleep cheaply until
  another thread signals state change. Always paired with a mutex and a
  predicate (`cv.wait(lock, pred)`) so spurious wakeups are handled
  automatically. Used at
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:52`.

## D

- **Deadlock** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
  Two threads each holding a lock the other needs; both wait forever.
  Cardinal prevention rule: always acquire multiple locks in the same
  order. `LlmClient` avoids the risk by never holding both mutexes
  simultaneously.

## E

- **Embedded LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  A language model whose output is consumed by the running game process,
  regardless of whether the model lives in the same binary or in a sidecar
  process on `localhost`.

- **Erase-remove idiom** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Pattern for deleting elements from a `std::vector` that match a
  predicate without shrinking capacity. `v.erase(std::remove_if(b, e,
  pred), e)`. Used in `cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:686` to clean up
  dead projectiles per frame.

## F

- **FPGA** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  Field-Programmable Gate Array. A chip whose internal wiring is
  reconfigured at boot by loading a bitstream — the chip *becomes* the
  custom circuit you described, rather than executing instructions on a
  fixed circuit.

- **Frame budget** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  The wall-clock time available for one game-loop iteration before the
  next vsync. 16.67 ms at 60 Hz, 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. Exceeding it once
  produces visible stutter regardless of average speed.

## H

- **HLS (High-Level Synthesis)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  A flow that lets you write FPGA logic in C/C++ instead of Verilog/VHDL.
  Vitis HLS is the current AMD/Xilinx tool. The compiler converts your
  C++ kernel into HDL, then through synthesis into a bitstream.

- **Hot loop / hot path** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Code that runs many times per frame — per-entity update loops,
  per-line render code. Allocations and copies that would be invisible
  elsewhere are budget-eaters here.

## I

- **In-process LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  Model linked into the game binary, called via a C/C++ API (e.g.
  `llama.cpp`). Contrast: **sidecar process**.

## L

- **Latency vs throughput** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Latency = time for a single operation (a game frame). Throughput =
  total operations per second (requests). Games optimize for worst-case
  latency, not average throughput.

- **LUT (Look-Up Table)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  The fundamental cell of an FPGA. A 4- or 6-input table you fill in to
  implement any boolean function. Combined with flip-flops, DSPs, and
  BRAM blocks via programmable routing, LUTs build the user's circuit.

## M

- **Mutex (`std::mutex`)** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*

  release is automatic. `LlmClient` uses two independent mutexes

  contend on unrelated data.

- **`std::move`** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  A cast that marks a value as "you may steal from this." Whether
  anything is actually stolen depends on the destination's move
  constructor. For `std::string`/`std::vector` it steals the heap buffer
  in O(1); for trivial types it falls back to a copy.

- **NRVO (Named Return Value Optimization)** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Compiler optimization that builds a returned local directly in the
  caller's slot, eliminating the return copy/move entirely.
  `LlmClient::drainReplies()` relies on this.

- **Persona prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*

  the no-predicate form. Used at `LlmClient.cpp:52`.

## R

- **Race condition** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
  Two or more threads accessing the same data without synchronisation,
  with at least one writer. Behaviour becomes nondeterministic and
  usually wrong. Not the same as a deadlock — race conditions produce
  bad data, deadlocks freeze.

- **Reallocation (vector growth)** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When `std::vector::push_back` exceeds capacity, a new heap buffer is
  allocated, all existing elements are moved/copied across, and the old
  buffer is freed. `reserve()` ahead of time avoids the storm.

- **`std::array<T, N>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Fixed-size, compile-time-known array wrapper. Stack-allocated, doesn't
  decay, carries its size in the type. Used in the racing/shooter games
  for quad corners, matrices, and font candidate lists.

- **`std::vector<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Dynamic-size, heap-backed sequence container. Use when count varies at
  runtime. Used throughout: shooter `projectiles`/`enemies`/`pickups`/

  A separate local process (Ollama, LM Studio, llamafile) that hosts the
  model and exposes an HTTP API the game POSTs to. Contrast:
  **in-process LLM**.

- **System prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  The `role: "system"` message in a chat request. Fixed identity, applied
  before any user turn.

- **XRT (Xilinx Runtime)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  The host-side C++ API for talking to an FPGA over PCIe. Provides
  `xrt::device`, `xrt::kernel`, `xrt::bo` (buffer object). The
  five-step pattern: load xclbin → allocate BOs → write inputs + sync to
  device → launch kernel → sync output back. Structurally identical to
  the LlmClient HTTP pattern.

Lesson 0005 is ready. To open on Linux:

## What's in lesson 0005

Every primitive in this lesson is sitting in `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp` already, so the "in this project" section walks through code you've already shipped:

- **§1 Concept** — what threads share (heap, globals, open file descriptors) vs. what's private (stack, registers); a textual timeline of the classic race condition; the three primitives (mutex, condition variable, atomic) and a one-line rule of thumb for when to use each.
- **§2 Minimal example** — the same counter incremented from two threads, in three versions: **no sync** (race, wrong result, marked red), **mutex** (correct but heavy), **atomic** (correct and cheap). Three takeaways including "'works on my machine' is meaningless for thread bugs."
- **§3 In your project** — the four-primitive tour of `LlmClient`:
  - `std::thread` + RAII (ctor starts, dtor joins).
  - Producer side: `nextId_.fetch_add(1)` (atomic counter) + `lock_guard` on `requestMutex_` + `notify_one` — two synchronisation primitives in one short function.
  - Consumer side: `unique_lock` + the **predicate form of `cv.wait`** that handles spurious wakeups and the stop signal in the same expression.
  - Lock released before `processOne()` (would block all submits for seconds otherwise).
  - **Why two mutexes** — a side-by-side timeline showing how splitting `requestMutex_` and `replyMutex_` lets the producer and consumer never block each other.
- **§4 Often confused with** — five contrasts: mutex vs atomic, race condition vs deadlock, `notify_one` vs `notify_all` (thundering herd), CV vs sleep-polling, threads vs processes (callback to lesson 0004).
- **§5 Quiz** — 5 shuffled, including a sneaky `volatile` distractor (it does *not* make things atomic — classic interview trap).
- **§6 Scenarios** — three open-ended, including "describe a sequence where the worker misses the shutdown signal if `stop_` were a plain `bool`."

## Default Thread Stack Size - Linux and Windows

The default size of the stack for threads varies by operating system; on Windows and Linux, the default size is 1MB. However, for the main thread specifically, the situation differs: In many Linux systems, the default stack size is 8 MB per thread.

## SSO (Small String Optimization) in libstdc++

Small String Optimization (or Short String Optimization, SSO) is an optimization applied in the std::basic_string class template that allows avoiding additional dynamic memory allocations for small strings and placing them inside the object itself.

In libstdc++ specifically:
- In g++ (libstdc++) implementation on a 64-bit OS, the basic_string structure is 32 bytes total
- GCC's implementation on Linux has sizeof(std::string) being 32 bytes but only 15 characters can be optimized before going to the heap.

SSO is applied in multiple libraries including Microsoft STL, libstdc++, libc++, Boost, and Folly.

Lesson 0006 · cpp_games / docs / learning

Stack vs. heap

Why this matters: every variable in your three games sits in one of these two places. Earlier lessons told you "stack is fast, heap is slow" without explaining what those are. This is the lesson where memory finally clicks — and where you stop guessing which side of the line a given std::vector, std::string, or Vec3 lives on.

1. The concept

Every running program gets a chunk of memory from the OS. That chunk is organised into three regions a beginner C++ programmer can mostly think about: the static region (your code, your globals, string literals), the stack, and the heap. The stack and the heap are the two areas where your data usually lives, and they behave completely differently.

high addresses +----------------------+ | STACK | <-- grows DOWN as you call functions | (each thread has | | its own; ~8 MB | | for main, ~1 MB | | for worker threads)| | ↓ | | | | ...empty... | | | | ↑ | | HEAP | <-- grows UP as you call new/malloc | (one big arena, | | shared by all | | threads in the | | process) | +----------------------+ | static / globals | +----------------------+ | program code | +----------------------+ low addresses

The stack

The stack is a LIFO region tied to the call chain. When a function is called, a chunk called a stack frame is added on top — it holds that function's local variables and bookkeeping. When the function returns, the chunk is popped. Allocating on the stack is one CPU instruction: subtract from the stack-pointer register. Deallocating is one instruction too: add back. That's why we say stack allocation is "free" — in any meaningful per-frame measurement, it really is.

Properties of stack storage:

  • Tiny cost. Single instruction, no kernel involvement, perfect cache locality.
  • Automatic lifetime. When the function returns, the object is destroyed — destructor runs, memory reclaimed. No delete, no leak.
  • Compile-time-known size. The compiler has to know how big the stack frame is. Variable-length arrays in stack frames are not standard C++.
  • Limited total size. Linux: ~8 MB for the main thread, ~1 MB per worker thread by default. Windows: ~1 MB for everything by default. Overflow it (e.g. deep recursion) and the program crashes.
  • One stack per thread. Your main thread and LlmClient's worker have separate stacks; they never accidentally collide.

The heap

The heap is a free-form arena. You ask the allocator for N bytes and it finds a free spot. You ask it to release them later. The allocator (typically malloc's implementation under new) maintains free lists, tracks fragmentation, and occasionally asks the kernel for more memory via brk or mmap.

Properties of heap storage:

  • Variable cost. Usually a few hundred nanoseconds. Sometimes a syscall (tens of microseconds). Spiky.
  • Manual lifetime. You decide when to release. In modern C++, RAII containers (std::vector, std::unique_ptr, std::string) do this for you in their destructors. Raw new/delete is a foot-gun and you shouldn't use it.
  • Runtime-sized. The size can be a value computed at runtime.
  • Huge. Practically as big as your free RAM — gigabytes.
  • Shared across threads. One heap per process. Allocator code is thread-safe (which makes it slower than a single-threaded allocator would be).

One-paragraph mental model

The stack is a fast scratch pad whose size and lifetime are decided at compile time and tied to function calls. The heap is a flexible long-lived workspace whose size can be decided at runtime, and whose lifetime is decided by your code. C++ pushes you toward the stack by default — locals, parameters, members of locals all live there — and asks you to opt in to the heap by writing a container or new.

2. Minimal example — same data, two storage locations

This program holds three integers in three places.

#include <array>
#include <vector>

struct Point { int x, y, z; };  // 12 bytes

int main() {
    // (A) STACK — the Point object itself sits in this function's frame.
    //     Lifetime: until main() returns. Cost: 12 bytes of stack pointer move.
    Point p1{1, 2, 3};

    // (B) STACK — std::array is a thin wrapper. The 12 bytes live inline.
    //     Same lifetime and cost as (A) — no heap involvement at all.
    std::array<int, 3> p2 = {1, 2, 3};

    // (C) MIXED — the vector OBJECT (3 pointers, 24 bytes on x64) is on the
    //     stack. The 12 bytes of data are on the heap. push_back may call
    //     new to grow. Destructor frees the heap data when main returns.
    std::vector<int> p3 = {1, 2, 3};
    p3.push_back(4);  // might allocate; the vector grows beyond its capacity

    // (D) RAW HEAP — single Point on the heap. unique_ptr cleans up at scope end.
    auto p4 = std::make_unique<Point>(1, 2, 3);
}
// p1, p2, p3, p4 all destroyed here — p3's heap buffer freed by its dtor,
// p4's heap Point freed by unique_ptr's dtor. No "delete" needed.

The case that trips beginners is (C). The std::vector is not "on the heap." Its three internal pointers (begin, end, capacity) live wherever the variable does — on the stack in main, in a member of a class on the heap, etc. The data those pointers point to is on the heap. This split is the secret to why std::vector is fast: small object you can copy/move cheaply, big growable storage when you actually need it.

3. In your project — the line through your real code

Pure stack: Vec3 and std::array

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:36 
struct Vec3 {
    float x = 0.0f;
    float y = 0.0f;
    float z = 0.0f;
};

// And, deep inside the per-frame loop:
const Vec3 playerCenter = game.player.pos + Vec3{0.0f, 2.5f, 0.0f};

Vec3 is 12 bytes of POD. The temporary Vec3{0, 2.5, 0}, the result of operator+, and the local playerCenter all live on the stack. Every frame thousands of these come and go — and zero of them touch the heap. That's why lesson 0003 said "don't allocate in the hot loop" rather than "don't have objects in the hot loop." Locals are free.

cpp_racing_game/src/main.cpp:943 
const std::array<sf::Vector2f, 4> outerQuad = { /* four corners */ };

Four sf::Vector2fs — 32 bytes — sitting in the renderer's stack frame for the duration of the draw call. When the function returns, they're gone. No delete, no allocator, no bookkeeping.

The mixed case: containers and their heap buffers

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:318 
struct GameState {
    Player player;                          // inline — same memory as GameState
    std::vector<Projectile> projectiles;    // 3-pointer struct inline; data on heap
    std::vector<Enemy>      enemies;        // same
    std::vector<Pickup>     pickups;        // same
    std::vector<ImpactEffect> impacts;      // same
    int kills = 0;                       // inline — 4 bytes of GameState
};

int main() {
    GameState game;   // the WHOLE struct is on the stack of main()
}

The GameState variable in main() is on the stack. So are the Player, the four vectors' three-pointer internals, the int kills. But the moment projectiles.push_back(...) happens, the new Projectile goes to a heap buffer that the vector points at. That's where the "vectors as long-lived members" trick from lesson 0003 pays off: the heap buffer grows once and stays put, and per-frame pushes after warmup don't reallocate.

The trap: std::string and SSO

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Npc.hpp 
struct ChatTurn {
    std::string role;     // 32 bytes on libstdc++; might or might not allocate
    std::string content;  // same
};

A std::string looks like a heap allocation. It usually isn't. Modern standard libraries use Small String Optimization (SSO): the string struct itself reserves ~15 bytes for the contents. If the string fits, it's stored inline — no heap allocation at all. role in your ChatTurn is always either "user" or "assistant" (4 and 9 chars). Neither allocates. Wren's replies almost always do.

Why SSO matters for game code

You can sprinkle small std::string labels everywhere without paying for them, but the moment a string grows past ~15 chars you've quietly bought a heap allocation. This is one of the surprising places lesson 0003's rule 1 ("don't allocate in the hot loop") gets violated by accident.

The thread case: another stack appears

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:13 
LlmClient::LlmClient(LlmConfig config) : config_(std::move(config)) {
    worker_ = std::thread(&LlmClient::workerLoop, this);
}

That one line of code allocates an entire second stack — about 1 MB on Linux, dedicated to the worker thread. The two threads share the heap (so requests_ can be touched from both) but each has its own stack (so a local ChatRequest req in workerLoop is private). This is the underlying reason a thread can call functions without disturbing the main thread's call chain — their call chains live in different memory.

4. Often confused with...

Stack vs. heap — the headline

Stack

  • One CPU instruction to (de)allocate
  • Lifetime = scope
  • Size known at compile time
  • Small — megabytes
  • One per thread
  • Pointers/references valid only until scope ends

Heap

  • Hundreds of ns, sometimes a syscall
  • Lifetime = until you (or RAII) free it
  • Size can be runtime-computed
  • Big — gigabytes
  • One per process (shared by threads)
  • Pointers valid until delete/destructor

"On the heap" vs. "is a pointer"

A pointer doesn't imply heap. int x = 42; int* p = &x; — x is on the stack and p points into the stack. What a pointer points to is the question; the pointer itself just holds an address. Inside your game, a reference to game.player.pos is "a pointer into the stack" because game is a stack local.

The program stack vs. std::stack

Two unrelated things sharing a word. The program stack is the OS-managed memory region we've been discussing. std::stack<T> is the C++ container class that stores elements LIFO-style — just like the program stack does — but it's a normal heap-allocated container under the hood (it's a vector or deque with a different interface). Don't confuse "I'm using std::stack" with "I'm on the program stack."

Static / global storage — the forgotten third region

Variables declared at namespace scope or with static inside a function live in neither stack nor heap. They live in a fixed region set up at program start. String literals like "qwen2.5:3b-instruct" in your code live there too — read-only. Lifetime: the whole program run. We won't dwell on this region, but knowing it exists keeps you from getting tripped up by "this isn't on the stack and I didn't new it — where is it?"

Stack overflow vs. heap exhaustion

Both are out-of-memory situations but they fail very differently.

  • Stack overflow. Your call chain grew past the ~1–8 MB stack limit. Usually unbounded recursion, sometimes a giant local array (char buf[10*1024*1024]). The OS sees you walking off your own stack and kills the process. Diagnosis: deep crash with a recursive backtrace.
  • Heap exhaustion. You asked new/malloc for memory and there's none left. new throws std::bad_alloc. Diagnosis: a specific allocation that failed. Much rarer in practice; usually points at a leak or a runaway data structure.

5. Quiz

Where does game.projectiles[0] live, given GameState game; as a local in main()?

  • Entirely on the stack, since game is a local.
  • The element is on the heap; the vector's 3-pointer struct that finds it is on the stack inside game.
  • In static storage, since vectors use a static allocator.
  • In the worker thread's stack, because vectors are thread-local.

Each ChatTurn has two std::strings. The role is always "user" or "assistant"; the content is whatever Wren said. Which strings allocate on the heap?

  • Both, because std::string always uses the heap.
  • Only content usually allocates; the short role stays inline thanks to Small String Optimization.
  • Only role allocates, because string literals always copy to the heap.
  • Neither — the compiler interns both strings at compile time.

A C++ beginner writes Vec3* p = new Vec3{1,2,3}; return p; from a function. Their friend writes Vec3 v{1,2,3}; return v;. Which is the more idiomatic modern C++ and why?

  • The pointer version, because it skips a copy and is faster.
  • The pointer version, because returning a local by value is a dangling-reference bug.
  • The value version. Modern C++ returns by value; NRVO usually eliminates the copy entirely, and there's no leak risk because there's no new.
  • They're equivalent — pick whichever you prefer stylistically.

Your game crashes deep in a recursive collision-test function. Stack overflow vs. heap exhaustion — which is more likely and why?

  • Stack overflow — recursion piles stack frames; if the recursion is unbounded it walks past the stack limit.
  • Heap exhaustion — each call allocates new memory for its parameters.
  • Static exhaustion — the global region fills up after enough function calls.
  • Cross-process memory pressure — another program ate your stack.

In lesson 0005 you saw that the main thread and the worker thread don't share their stacks, but they share the queue at requests_. Why is sharing the queue OK?

  • The mutex copies requests_ into the worker's stack before reading.
  • The queue's nodes live on the heap, which is shared by all threads in the process. Both threads can reach it; the mutex makes that safe.
  • The worker is on a 'shared stack' specifically marked for cross-thread access.
  • std::queue is internally atomic, so cross-thread access is always safe.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. Sketch the rough memory layout of one Npc sitting on main()'s stack. For each field of Npc — the Persona (which contains a vector<string> of traits), the LlmClient& reference, the vector<ChatTurn> history — say whether the field itself is on the stack or the heap, and whether the data it owns or refers to is on the stack or the heap. One sentence each.

Scenario B. A new shooter feature: when an enemy dies it spawns 200 particles. You're about to write std::vector<Particle> spawned; inside the death-handler function and push 200 things into it before passing it to a renderer. Sketch the version that's a problem and the version that isn't. Tie your answer to where each version lives, not just to "is it fast."

Scenario C. You add a deep recursive function for navigating a tree of dialog options. Each frame the tree has at most ~30 levels. Plenty of headroom under an 8 MB stack — why might it still be a problem if you also spawn a worker thread that does the same recursion? (Hint: lesson 0005 + this lesson.)

7. Track your progress

Further reading — cppreference: storage duration · cppreference: std::basic_string · Small String Optimization in libstdc++/libc++ · cppreference: unique_ptr

  • Limited total size. Linux: ~8 MB for the main thread, ~1 MB per worker thread by default. Windows: ~1 MB for everything by default. Overflow it (e.g. deep recursion) and the program crashes.
  • One stack per thread. Your main thread and LlmClient's worker have separate stacks; they never accidentally collide.

The heap

The heap is a free-form arena. You ask the allocator for N bytes and it finds a free spot. You ask it to release them later. The allocator (typically malloc's implementation under new) maintains free lists, tracks fragmentation, and occasionally asks the kernel for more memory via brk or mmap.

Properties of heap storage:

  • Variable cost. Usually a few hundred nanoseconds. Sometimes a syscall (tens of microseconds). Spiky.
  • Manual lifetime. You decide when to release. In modern C++, RAII containers (std::vector, std::unique_ptr, std::string) do this for you in their destructors. Raw new/delete is a foot-gun and you shouldn't use it.
  • Runtime-sized. The size can be a value computed at runtime.
  • Huge. Practically as big as your free RAM — gigabytes.
  • Shared across threads. One heap per process. Allocator code is thread-safe (which makes it slower than a single-threaded allocator would be).

One-paragraph mental model

The stack is a fast scratch pad whose size and lifetime are decided at compile time and tied to function calls. The heap is a flexible long-lived workspace whose size can be decided at runtime, and whose lifetime is decided by your code. C++ pushes you toward the stack by default — locals, parameters, members of locals all live there — and asks you to opt in to the heap by writing a container or new.

2. Minimal example — same data, two storage locations

This program holds three integers in three places.

#include <array>
#include <vector>

struct Point { int x, y, z; };  // 12 bytes

int main() {
    // (A) STACK — the Point object itself sits in this function's frame.
    //     Lifetime: until main() returns. Cost: 12 bytes of stack pointer move.
    Point p1{1, 2, 3};

    // (B) STACK — std::array is a thin wrapper. The 12 bytes live inline.
    //     Same lifetime and cost as (A) — no heap involvement at all.
    std::array<int, 3> p2 = {1, 2, 3};

    // (C) MIXED — the vector OBJECT (3 pointers, 24 bytes on x64) is on the
    //     stack. The 12 bytes of data are on the heap. push_back may call
    //     new to grow. Destructor frees the heap data when main returns.
    std::vector<int> p3 = {1, 2, 3};
    p3.push_back(4);  // might allocate; the vector grows beyond its capacity

    // (D) RAW HEAP — single Point on the heap. unique_ptr cleans up at scope end.
    auto p4 = std::make_unique<Point>(1, 2, 3);
}
// p1, p2, p3, p4 all destroyed here — p3's heap buffer freed by its dtor,
// p4's heap Point freed by unique_ptr's dtor. No "delete" needed.

The case that trips beginners is (C). The std::vector is not "on the heap." Its three internal pointers (begin, end, capacity) live wherever the variable does — on the stack in main, in a member of a class on the heap, etc. The data those pointers point to is on the heap. This split is the secret to why std::vector is fast: small object you can copy/move cheaply, big growable storage when you actually need it.

3. In your project — the line through your real code

Pure stack: Vec3 and std::array

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:36 
struct Vec3 {
    float x = 0.0f;
    float y = 0.0f;
    float z = 0.0f;
};

// And, deep inside the per-frame loop:
const Vec3 playerCenter = game.player.pos + Vec3{0.0f, 2.5f, 0.0f};

Vec3 is 12 bytes of POD. The temporary Vec3{0, 2.5, 0}, the result of operator+, and the local playerCenter all live on the stack. Every frame thousands of these come and go — and zero of them touch the heap. That's why lesson 0003 said "don't allocate in the hot loop" rather than "don't have objects in the hot loop." Locals are free.

cpp_racing_game/src/main.cpp:943 
const std::array<sf::Vector2f, 4> outerQuad = { /* four corners */ };

Four sf::Vector2fs — 32 bytes — sitting in the renderer's stack frame for the duration of the draw call. When the function returns, they're gone. No delete, no allocator, no bookkeeping.

The mixed case: containers and their heap buffers

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:318 
struct GameState {
    Player player;                          // inline — same memory as GameState
    std::vector<Projectile> projectiles;    // 3-pointer struct inline; data on heap
    std::vector<Enemy>      enemies;        // same
    std::vector<Pickup>     pickups;        // same
    std::vector<ImpactEffect> impacts;      // same
    int kills = 0;                       // inline — 4 bytes of GameState
};

int main() {
    GameState game;   // the WHOLE struct is on the stack of main()
}

The GameState variable in main() is on the stack. So are the Player, the four vectors' three-pointer internals, the int kills. But the moment projectiles.push_back(...) happens, the new Projectile goes to a heap buffer that the vector points at. That's where the "vectors as long-lived members" trick from lesson 0003 pays off: the heap buffer grows once and stays put, and per-frame pushes after warmup don't reallocate.

The trap: std::string and SSO

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Npc.hpp 
struct ChatTurn {
    std::string role;     // 32 bytes on libstdc++; might or might not allocate
    std::string content;  // same
};

A std::string looks like a heap allocation. It usually isn't. Modern standard libraries use Small String Optimization (SSO): the string struct itself reserves ~15 bytes for the contents. If the string fits, it's stored inline — no heap allocation at all. role in your ChatTurn is always either "user" or "assistant" (4 and 9 chars). Neither allocates. Wren's replies almost always do.

Why SSO matters for game code

You can sprinkle small std::string labels everywhere without paying for them, but the moment a string grows past ~15 chars you've quietly bought a heap allocation. This is one of the surprising places lesson 0003's rule 1 ("don't allocate in the hot loop") gets violated by accident.

The thread case: another stack appears

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:13 
LlmClient::LlmClient(LlmConfig config) : config_(std::move(config)) {
    worker_ = std::thread(&LlmClient::workerLoop, this);
}

That one line of code allocates an entire second stack — about 1 MB on Linux, dedicated to the worker thread. The two threads share the heap (so requests_ can be touched from both) but each has its own stack (so a local ChatRequest req in workerLoop is private). This is the underlying reason a thread can call functions without disturbing the main thread's call chain — their call chains live in different memory.

4. Often confused with...

Stack vs. heap — the headline

Stack

  • One CPU instruction to (de)allocate
  • Lifetime = scope
  • Size known at compile time
  • Small — megabytes
  • One per thread
  • Pointers/references valid only until scope ends

Heap

  • Hundreds of ns, sometimes a syscall
  • Lifetime = until you (or RAII) free it
  • Size can be runtime-computed
  • Big — gigabytes
  • One per process (shared by threads)
  • Pointers valid until delete/destructor

"On the heap" vs. "is a pointer"

A pointer doesn't imply heap. int x = 42; int* p = &x; — x is on the stack and p points into the stack. What a pointer points to is the question; the pointer itself just holds an address. Inside your game, a reference to game.player.pos is "a pointer into the stack" because game is a stack local.

The program stack vs. std::stack

Two unrelated things sharing a word. The program stack is the OS-managed memory region we've been discussing. std::stack<T> is the C++ container class that stores elements LIFO-style — just like the program stack does — but it's a normal heap-allocated container under the hood (it's a vector or deque with a different interface). Don't confuse "I'm using std::stack" with "I'm on the program stack."

Static / global storage — the forgotten third region

Variables declared at namespace scope or with static inside a function live in neither stack nor heap. They live in a fixed region set up at program start. String literals like "qwen2.5:3b-instruct" in your code live there too — read-only. Lifetime: the whole program run. We won't dwell on this region, but knowing it exists keeps you from getting tripped up by "this isn't on the stack and I didn't new it — where is it?"

Stack overflow vs. heap exhaustion

Both are out-of-memory situations but they fail very differently.

  • Stack overflow. Your call chain grew past the ~1–8 MB stack limit. Usually unbounded recursion, sometimes a giant local array (char buf[10*1024*1024]). The OS sees you walking off your own stack and kills the process. Diagnosis: deep crash with a recursive backtrace.
  • Heap exhaustion. You asked new/malloc for memory and there's none left. new throws std::bad_alloc. Diagnosis: a specific allocation that failed. Much rarer in practice; usually points at a leak or a runaway data structure.

5. Quiz

Where does game.projectiles[0] live, given GameState game; as a local in main()?

  • Entirely on the stack, since game is a local.
  • The element is on the heap; the vector's 3-pointer struct that finds it is on the stack inside game.
  • In static storage, since vectors use a static allocator.
  • In the worker thread's stack, because vectors are thread-local.

Each ChatTurn has two std::strings. The role is always "user" or "assistant"; the content is whatever Wren said. Which strings allocate on the heap?

  • Both, because std::string always uses the heap.
  • Only content usually allocates; the short role stays inline thanks to Small String Optimization.
  • Only role allocates, because string literals always copy to the heap.
  • Neither — the compiler interns both strings at compile time.

A C++ beginner writes Vec3* p = new Vec3{1,2,3}; return p; from a function. Their friend writes Vec3 v{1,2,3}; return v;. Which is the more idiomatic modern C++ and why?

  • The pointer version, because it skips a copy and is faster.
  • The pointer version, because returning a local by value is a dangling-reference bug.
  • The value version. Modern C++ returns by value; NRVO usually eliminates the copy entirely, and there's no leak risk because there's no new.
  • They're equivalent — pick whichever you prefer stylistically.

Your game crashes deep in a recursive collision-test function. Stack overflow vs. heap exhaustion — which is more likely and why?

  • Stack overflow — recursion piles stack frames; if the recursion is unbounded it walks past the stack limit.
  • Heap exhaustion — each call allocates new memory for its parameters.
  • Static exhaustion — the global region fills up after enough function calls.
  • Cross-process memory pressure — another program ate your stack.

In lesson 0005 you saw that the main thread and the worker thread don't share their stacks, but they share the queue at requests_. Why is sharing the queue OK?

  • The mutex copies requests_ into the worker's stack before reading.
  • The queue's nodes live on the heap, which is shared by all threads in the process. Both threads can reach it; the mutex makes that safe.
  • The worker is on a 'shared stack' specifically marked for cross-thread access.
  • std::queue is internally atomic, so cross-thread access is always safe.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. Sketch the rough memory layout of one Npc sitting on main()'s stack. For each field of Npc — the Persona (which contains a vector<string> of traits), the LlmClient& reference, the vector<ChatTurn> history — say whether the field itself is on the stack or the heap, and whether the data it owns or refers to is on the stack or the heap. One sentence each.

Scenario B. A new shooter feature: when an enemy dies it spawns 200 particles. You're about to write std::vector<Particle> spawned; inside the death-handler function and push 200 things into it before passing it to a renderer. Sketch the version that's a problem and the version that isn't. Tie your answer to where each version lives, not just to "is it fast."

Scenario C. You add a deep recursive function for navigating a tree of dialog options. Each frame the tree has at most ~30 levels. Plenty of headroom under an 8 MB stack — why might it still be a problem if you also spawn a worker thread that does the same recursion? (Hint: lesson 0005 + this lesson.)

7. Track your progress

Further reading — cppreference: storage duration · cppreference: std::basic_string · Small String Optimization in libstdc++/libc++ · cppreference: unique_ptr

## A

- **Array decay** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When a C-style array is passed to a function, the parameter is silently
  rewritten to a pointer, losing its size. `void f(int arr[10])` becomes
  `void f(int* arr)`. `std::array` does not decay.

  efficient than the same design on an FPGA, but unchangeable once
  shipped. FPGA is the reprogrammable cousin.

- **Bitstream** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*

  HDL/HLS design through place-and-route. Loading a different bitstream
  reconfigures the chip into a different circuit.

- **C-style array** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*

  another thread signals state change. Always paired with a mutex and a
  predicate (`cv.wait(lock, pred)`) so spurious wakeups are handled
  automatically. Used at
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:52`.

  order. `LlmClient` avoids the risk by never holding both mutexes
  simultaneously.

  fixed circuit.

  C++ kernel into HDL, then through synthesis into a bitstream.

  `llama.cpp`). Contrast: **sidecar process**.

- **Latency vs throughput** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*

  total operations per second (requests). Games optimize for worst-case
  latency, not average throughput.

  implement any boolean function. Combined with flip-flops, DSPs, and

Lesson 0006 is in place. To open on Linux:

```
xdg-open /home/node/work/normal_work/cpp_games/docs/learning/lessons/0006-stack-vs-heap.html
```

## What's in lesson 0006

This pays off the foundation that lessons 0002, 0003, and 0005 kept stepping on without explaining:

- **§1 Concept** — an ASCII memory diagram with stack and heap labeled; then a properties list each. Real numbers: ~8 MB main stack on Linux, ~1 MB worker thread stack, gigabytes of heap. One-paragraph mental model at the end as a callout.
- **§2 Minimal example** — same three integers in four storage locations: (A) inline `Point` on stack, (B) `std::array` on stack, (C) the all-important **mixed case** of `std::vector` (struct on stack, data on heap), (D) `std::make_unique<Point>` for raw heap with RAII cleanup. Explicit "this is the case that trips beginners" callout on (C).
- **§3 In your project** — real-code anchors:
  - **Pure stack**: `Vec3` (`cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:36`), `std::array<sf::Vector2f, 4> outerQuad` (racing).
  - **Mixed**: `GameState` with four vector members — the struct on `main()`'s stack, the data on the heap, calling back to lesson 0003's "vectors as long-lived members" optimization.
  - **The SSO trap**: `ChatTurn::role` ("user"/"assistant") never allocates because Small String Optimization keeps strings ≤15 chars inline in the 32-byte struct; `ChatTurn::content` usually does.
  - **The second stack**: `worker_ = std::thread(...)` allocates ~1 MB of fresh stack for the worker — connecting back to lesson 0005's "threads share heap, not stack."
- **§4 Often confused with** — side-by-side stack/heap cards; *"on the heap" vs "is a pointer"* (a reference into a stack local is still a pointer into the stack); **`std::stack` the container vs the program stack** (different uses of the same word); the static/global third region; **stack overflow vs heap exhaustion** as two different failure modes.
- **§5 Quiz** — 5 shuffled. Includes a question that directly tests whether you know the `std::vector`-as-member-of-stack-local split, and the SSO trap.
- **§6 Scenarios** — three open-ended, including one that asks you to sketch where every field of an `Npc` lives.
