Quiz: 0 / 0
Lesson 0009 · cpp_games / docs / learning

OS fundamentals: what runs your code under the surface

Why this matters: lesson 0005 taught you the concurrency primitives. This lesson teaches you the OS layer they sit on. Your game, Ollama, the worker thread, the localhost HTTP call — every one is an OS abstraction working behind the scenes. Knowing the layer down lets you reason about failure modes lesson 0005 couldn't.

1. The concept — the four jobs of the OS

Strip an operating system down to fundamentals and it does four things on your behalf. Every line of code you've written so far has been quietly riding on them.

Process model

"Multiple programs share one machine, none of them can step on each other." Each program runs in its own isolated address space. Your game and Ollama are two processes.

Virtual memory

Each process sees a private 64-bit address space the OS fakes out of real RAM via page tables and the MMU. Two processes can both use address 0x0040_1234 for completely unrelated data.

System calls

The doorways from your program (user space) into the kernel. Opening a file, allocating memory beyond what you have, sending bytes on a socket — all are syscalls. ~100–200 ns each on modern hardware.

Scheduling

Decides which runnable thread runs on which core, when. A blocked thread (e.g. one in cv.wait) is removed from the scheduler entirely until something wakes it.

The architecture diagram

user space (your code, libraries, Ollama) +------------------------------------------------------------+ | cpp_game_with_llm_npcs Ollama (the model) | | - main thread - one of its threads| | - LlmClient worker thread | | - SFML, libstdc++, httplib... - go runtime... | +------------------------------------------------------------+ | | | system call boundary | v v ====[ syscall: ~100-200 ns ]==== | | +------------------------------------------------------------+ | kernel space | | scheduler virtual memory network stack | | filesystem page tables / MMU TCP loopback | | signal delivery page faults (127.0.0.1) | +------------------------------------------------------------+ | v hardware (CPU, RAM, NIC, GPU, disk)

That syscall boundary is where your program ends and the kernel begins. Calling printf doesn't cross it (it's all library code until the very last write). Calling open does. The cost difference is real: a library call is a function call (~1 ns). A syscall is at least 100x that, and the kernel side may involve disk, the network, or context switching that costs thousands of ns more.

The one-sentence mental model

The OS gives your code two illusions — "you have the whole machine" (virtual memory + scheduling) and "you have safe paths to hardware" (syscalls). Everything else is built on those.

2. A minimal example — tracing one cli.Post() call through the OS

What actually happens when LlmClient::processOne() calls cli.Post("/api/chat", ...)? In your code it's one line. At the OS level it's a half-dozen syscalls.

// Your C++ (one line):
auto res = cli.Post("/api/chat", body.dump(), "application/json");

// What httplib does, library-side only (no syscalls yet):
//   - format the HTTP/1.1 request as a string
//   - check connection state, set timeouts, etc.

// What httplib does that CROSSES INTO THE KERNEL:
fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);              // open a TCP socket
connect(fd, "127.0.0.1:11434");                     // TCP handshake (loopback)
send(fd, requestBytes, requestLen, 0);             // hand the request to the kernel
// — worker thread blocks here, removed from scheduler —
recv(fd, replyBuffer, bufLen, 0);                  // wake when reply bytes arrive
close(fd);                                          // release the socket

Five syscalls highlighted in red, each ~100–200 ns. The cost of the call isn't the syscalls though — it's the second between send and recv while Ollama actually runs the model. During that second, your worker thread is asleep: the scheduler has removed it from the runnable set, freeing the CPU for the main thread (and everything else on the machine). When Ollama writes its reply to the socket, the kernel notes that data is available, marks your thread runnable again, and at the next scheduling opportunity it wakes up inside recv. This is the OS as your silent collaborator.

"localhost" is still networking

People sometimes say "Ollama on localhost isn't really a network call." It is. The data goes through the TCP stack, gets a sequence number, hits the loopback interface, comes back up through the network stack on the other side. It's just that the wire is zero meters long. You skip the NIC, you skip the cable, you skip routing — but you keep socket creation, TCP framing, copy-into-kernel and copy-out, and scheduler latency. That's why a localhost ping is microseconds, not zero.

3. In your project — the OS abstractions hiding in code you've written

Two processes (game and Ollama) and why we needed HTTP

Lesson 0001 picked Ollama as a sidecar without explaining the deeper reason: two processes cannot just share memory. The OS makes sure of it — that's what isolation means. Your game can't access Ollama's std::queue, even though it's on the same machine, because they live in different virtual address spaces. The OS's page tables for each process are different. The only ways across the boundary are:

  • Files — both processes can open the same file (via syscalls).
  • Pipes / sockets — the kernel hands one end to each process. Bytes flow through the kernel.
  • Shared memory regions — the kernel maps the same physical pages into both processes' address spaces, by explicit request.
  • Signals — one-bit notifications like SIGINT (Ctrl-C).

The HTTP call to Ollama is option 2: a TCP socket via the loopback interface. The kernel routes bytes from your game's process to Ollama's process, copying them through kernel buffers on the way. Compared to "two threads sharing a std::queue with a mutex" (lesson 0005), this is dramatically more expensive — but it's also the only way to talk to a separate program.

One process, two threads: why LlmClient works so differently

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:48 (recap from lesson 0005) 
void LlmClient::workerLoop() {
    while (true) {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(requestMutex_);
        requestCv_.wait(lock, [this] {
            return stop_.load() || !requests_.empty();
        });
        // ... dequeue, process ...
    }
}

The main thread and the worker thread are in the same process — one virtual address space — so requests_ is literally the same memory to both. No syscall is needed to "share" it; they already share it. The mutex protects them from racing, but the data itself doesn't have to travel anywhere.

What about cv.wait? That's an OS scheduler call. wait() hands the kernel a request: "remove me from the runnable threads until someone notifies this CV." A blocked thread costs zero CPU until the notify wakes it. The "sleep cheaply" promise from lesson 0005 is literally the OS scheduler doing its job.

Files, the unsung syscall storm

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp:31 
std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string> readKv(const fs::path& path) {
    std::ifstream in(path);   // → open() syscall
    // std::getline calls into read() repeatedly
    while (std::getline(in, line)) { /* ... */ }
    // ifstream destructor calls close()
}

Three syscalls minimum: open, one or more reads, close. The read calls return data that the kernel already buffered (Linux's page cache), so they're fast once the file is cached, but the first read may pull from disk — tens of microseconds on an SSD, milliseconds on a spinning disk. Game code that opens files per frame is one of the classic per-frame-budget destroyers from lesson 0003.

The signals you haven't used yet, but will

Press Ctrl-C while your game is running. The terminal asks the kernel to send your process SIGINT. The kernel interrupts your code — literally yanks the CPU out of whatever it was doing — and runs a handler. By default the handler exits the program. LlmClient never registered a signal handler, so destructors don't run; the worker thread is killed mid-HTTP-call. If you want a clean shutdown via Ctrl-C, you'd register a handler that sets stop_ and notifies the CV — the same pattern as the destructor in lesson 0005. We don't have that today; it's a real follow-up.

4. Often confused with...

Process vs. thread — from the OS angle this time

Lesson 0005 contrasted these from the C++ standpoint: threads share memory, processes don't. From the OS standpoint the distinction is sharper: on Linux, threads and processes are both created by the same syscall (clone), and the difference is just which flags are passed. CLONE_VM says "share the parent's address space" — that's a thread. Without it, you get a separate address space — a process. So at the kernel level there's only one mechanism; "process" and "thread" are user-space labels for two configurations of it.

 ThreadProcess
Address spaceShared with parentOwn copy (via copy-on-write)
Creation costCheap (clone with CLONE_VM)Heavier (clone without it; page tables to copy)
Context switch cost~thousands of ns (no TLB flush)~tens of thousands of ns (TLB flush — softened by PCID on modern x86)
Crash impactKills the whole processJust kills itself
Used for in your codeLlmClient's workergame ↔ Ollama

System call vs. library call

A library call is a regular function call inside your process. std::string::push_back — library call. std::sin — library call. std::ifstream's constructor doing the actual file open? That's a library call that internally makes a system call. The line is fuzzy from your seat but extremely sharp from the CPU's: a syscall flips the CPU into kernel mode, which is a special privileged execution state. Library calls don't. The cost difference (~1 ns vs ~100+ ns) is one consequence.

User space vs. kernel space

Two execution modes the CPU itself supports. User space is where your program runs; it can't touch hardware directly, can't read/write other processes' memory, can't change the page tables. Kernel space can. A syscall is the controlled door between them. The reason this distinction matters: a buggy program in user space can crash itself; a buggy driver in kernel space can crash the whole machine. The OS uses the CPU's mode bit to enforce the boundary.

Blocking vs. non-blocking I/O

When the worker calls recv on the socket, the thread is removed from the scheduler until the reply arrives — that's blocking I/O. The alternative is non-blocking: recv returns immediately with "no data yet" and you poll later. Blocking is simpler and cheaper if you have a thread to spare; non-blocking is what you need when one thread must juggle thousands of connections (a web server). Your worker thread design is blocking by choice — one thread, one job, simple.

Concurrency vs. parallelism (one more time)

Lesson 0003 mentioned this; lesson 0005 hinted at it. Restated here in OS terms: concurrency is a property of the program ("multiple tasks are in flight at the same time"). Parallelism is a property of the hardware ("multiple cores actually execute simultaneously"). The OS scheduler gives you concurrency on a single core by time-slicing; multi-core CPUs let you also have real parallelism. LlmClient's two threads are concurrent always; whether they're parallel depends on the user's CPU.

5. Quiz

Why can't cpp_game_with_llm_npcs just read Ollama's std::queue of pending requests directly — they're on the same machine after all?

  • Ollama doesn't expose a mutex for it.
  • They run in different processes — different virtual address spaces. The same C++ address points to different physical memory in each.
  • It would require the read syscall, which is privileged.
  • std::queue has different sizes in Go (Ollama) and C++ (your game).

A naive estimate: how many syscalls does one cli.Post("/api/chat", ...) from your worker thread minimally cost during the network round-trip itself? (Don't count syscalls inside Ollama's process; just yours.)

  • One — cli.Post bundles everything into a single sendto syscall.
  • Around 5 — socket, connect, send, recv, close at minimum.
  • Hundreds — every byte of the request and reply is its own syscall.
  • Zero — httplib uses memory-mapped I/O internally.

The worker thread calls recv() and blocks for 1.5 seconds waiting for Ollama's reply. During that 1.5 s, what is the worker thread actually doing from the OS's perspective?

  • Polling the socket once per millisecond from inside the kernel.
  • Spinning on a flag in user space waiting for the reply.
  • Nothing — it's marked unrunnable; the scheduler will mark it runnable again when the kernel sees reply data on its socket.
  • Draining the CPU's battery while it waits.

The shooter game reads arial.ttf in loadHudAssets() at startup. The next frame after start, opening the same file would be much faster than the first open. Why?

  • std::ifstream caches the file contents across instances.
  • The kernel cached the file's pages in RAM after the first read; the second access doesn't touch the disk.
  • The OS pre-loaded the font into a global font cache when SFML started up.
  • The filesystem is mounted with noatime, making the second read much faster.

A user runs both your game and Ollama, but only has a single-core CPU (rare in 2026, but pretend). Is concurrency between the worker thread and main thread still useful, or does the single core kill it?

  • Useless — without two cores, both threads are just fighting for the same one and waste each other's time.
  • Useful — while the worker is blocked on the network recv, the OS schedules the main thread, which keeps the game responsive on the one core available.
  • Useful, but you'd need an atomic CAS on every memory access to prevent corruption on a single core.
  • Useful only if the OS automatically merges your two threads into one.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. The user closes the game window via the X button while a request is mid-flight (cli.Post is waiting for Ollama). Walk through what happens to the worker thread — the main thread, the destructor sequence, the syscall the worker is blocked in, all of it. Where does the OS step in?

Scenario B. You want a feature where Ctrl-C in the terminal cleanly stops the game (LlmClient joins, files close, dialog state is saved). Without writing the code, sketch what you'd register with the OS and which existing primitive in LlmClient you'd reuse to make the worker actually exit. Use the words signal handler, atomic, and condition variable.

Scenario C. A teammate says "let's just mmap a shared memory region between the game and Ollama instead of HTTP — it'll be way faster." Argue the technical case for it (one paragraph) and the practical case against (one paragraph). Bring in what you know about the IPC options from §3.

7. Track your progress

OS fundamentals: what runs your code under the surface

Why this matters: lesson 0005 taught you the concurrency primitives. This lesson teaches you the OS layer they sit on. Your game, Ollama, the worker thread, the localhost HTTP call — every one is an OS abstraction working behind the scenes. Knowing the layer down lets you reason about failure modes lesson 0005 couldn't.

1. The concept — the four jobs of the OS

Strip an operating system down to fundamentals and it does four things on your behalf. Every line of code you've written so far has been quietly riding on them.

Process model

"Multiple programs share one machine, none of them can step on each other." Each program runs in its own isolated address space. Your game and Ollama are two processes.

Virtual memory

Each process sees a private 64-bit address space the OS fakes out of real RAM via page tables and the MMU. Two processes can both use address 0x0040_1234 for completely unrelated data.

System calls

The doorways from your program (user space) into the kernel. Opening a file, allocating memory beyond what you have, sending bytes on a socket — all are syscalls. ~100–200 ns each on modern hardware.

Scheduling

Decides which runnable thread runs on which core, when. A blocked thread (e.g. one in cv.wait) is removed from the scheduler entirely until something wakes it.

The architecture diagram

user space (your code, libraries, Ollama) +------------------------------------------------------------+ | cpp_game_with_llm_npcs Ollama (the model) | | - main thread - one of its threads| | - LlmClient worker thread | | - SFML, libstdc++, httplib... - go runtime... | +------------------------------------------------------------+ | | | system call boundary | v v ====[ syscall: ~100-200 ns ]==== | | +------------------------------------------------------------+ | kernel space | | scheduler virtual memory network stack | | filesystem page tables / MMU TCP loopback | | signal delivery page faults (127.0.0.1) | +------------------------------------------------------------+ | v hardware (CPU, RAM, NIC, GPU, disk)

That syscall boundary is where your program ends and the kernel begins. Calling printf doesn't cross it (it's all library code until the very last write). Calling open does. The cost difference is real: a library call is a function call (~1 ns). A syscall is at least 100x that, and the kernel side may involve disk, the network, or context switching that costs thousands of ns more.

The one-sentence mental model

The OS gives your code two illusions — "you have the whole machine" (virtual memory + scheduling) and "you have safe paths to hardware" (syscalls). Everything else is built on those.

2. A minimal example — tracing one cli.Post() call through the OS

What actually happens when LlmClient::processOne() calls cli.Post("/api/chat", ...)? In your code it's one line. At the OS level it's a half-dozen syscalls.

// Your C++ (one line):
auto res = cli.Post("/api/chat", body.dump(), "application/json");

// What httplib does, library-side only (no syscalls yet):
//   - format the HTTP/1.1 request as a string
//   - check connection state, set timeouts, etc.

// What httplib does that CROSSES INTO THE KERNEL:
fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);              // open a TCP socket
connect(fd, "127.0.0.1:11434");                     // TCP handshake (loopback)
send(fd, requestBytes, requestLen, 0);             // hand the request to the kernel
// — worker thread blocks here, removed from scheduler —
recv(fd, replyBuffer, bufLen, 0);                  // wake when reply bytes arrive
close(fd);                                          // release the socket

Five syscalls highlighted in red, each ~100–200 ns. The cost of the call isn't the syscalls though — it's the second between send and recv while Ollama actually runs the model. During that second, your worker thread is asleep: the scheduler has removed it from the runnable set, freeing the CPU for the main thread (and everything else on the machine). When Ollama writes its reply to the socket, the kernel notes that data is available, marks your thread runnable again, and at the next scheduling opportunity it wakes up inside recv. This is the OS as your silent collaborator.

"localhost" is still networking

People sometimes say "Ollama on localhost isn't really a network call." It is. The data goes through the TCP stack, gets a sequence number, hits the loopback interface, comes back up through the network stack on the other side. It's just that the wire is zero meters long. You skip the NIC, you skip the cable, you skip routing — but you keep socket creation, TCP framing, copy-into-kernel and copy-out, and scheduler latency. That's why a localhost ping is microseconds, not zero.

The only ways across the boundary are:

  • Files — both processes can open the same file (via syscalls).
  • Pipes / sockets — the kernel hands one end to each process. Bytes flow through the kernel.
  • Shared memory regions — the kernel maps the same physical pages into both processes' address spaces, by explicit request.
  • Signals — one-bit notifications like SIGINT (Ctrl-C).

The HTTP call to Ollama is option 2: a TCP socket via the loopback interface. The kernel routes bytes from your game's process to Ollama's process, copying them through kernel buffers on the way. Compared to "two threads sharing a std::queue with a mutex" (lesson 0005), this is dramatically more expensive — but it's also the only way to talk to a separate program.

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:48 (recap from lesson 0005) 
void LlmClient::workerLoop() {
    while (true) {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(requestMutex_);
        requestCv_.wait(lock, [this] {
            return stop_.load() || !requests_.empty();
        });
        // ... dequeue, process ...
    }
}

The main thread and the worker thread are in the same process — one virtual address space — so requests_ is literally the same memory to both. No syscall is needed to "share" it; they already share it. The mutex protects them from racing, but the data itself doesn't have to travel anywhere.

What about cv.wait? That's an OS scheduler call. wait() hands the kernel a request: "remove me from the runnable threads until someone notifies this CV." cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp:31 
std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string> readKv(const fs::path& path) {
    std::ifstream in(path);   // → open() syscall
    // std::getline calls into read() repeatedly
    while (std::getline(in, line)) { /* ... */ }
    // ifstream destructor calls close()
}

Three syscalls minimum: open, one or more reads, close. The read calls return data that the kernel already buffered (Linux's page cache), so they're fast once the file is cached, but the first read may pull from disk — tens of microseconds on an SSD, milliseconds on a spinning disk. Game code that opens files per frame is one of the classic per-frame-budget destroyers from lesson 0003.

Press Ctrl-C while your game is running. The terminal asks the kernel to send your process SIGINT. LlmClient never registered a signal handler, so destructors don't run; the worker thread is killed mid-HTTP-call. If you want a clean shutdown via Ctrl-C, you'd register a handler that sets stop_ and notifies the CV — the same pattern as the destructor in lesson 0005.   are ordinary function calls; syscalls flip the CPU into kernel mode.

Lesson 0009 is in place. To open on Linux:

```
xdg-open /home/node/work/normal_work/cpp_games/docs/learning/lessons/0009-os-fundamentals.html
```

## What's in lesson 0009

This lesson sits *underneath* lesson 0005. Where 0005 explained the concurrency primitives (mutex, CV, atomic), this one explains the OS layer that makes those primitives actually work:

- **§1 Four jobs of the OS** — process model, virtual memory, syscalls, scheduling — each in a color-coded card. Plus an ASCII architecture diagram showing your game, Ollama, the syscall boundary, the kernel, and the hardware all stacked up.
- **§2 Minimal example** — a real syscall trace of one `cli.Post("/api/chat", ...)` call: `socket → connect → send → recv → close`, with syscall names highlighted in red. Explicitly calls out the **"localhost is still networking"** misconception in a warning callout.
- **§3 In your project** — three OS anchors hiding in code you already shipped:
  - **Two processes (game ↔ Ollama)** — why HTTP is necessary at all (address-space isolation), with the four IPC options enumerated.
  - **One process, two threads (`LlmClient`)** — why `requests_` doesn't need a syscall to be shared, and why `cv.wait` is literally the OS scheduler dequeueing your thread.
  - **`std::ifstream` as a syscall storm** — the `open/read/close` triple, with a callback to the kernel page cache (relevant to per-frame budget).
  - **Signals you haven't used yet** — the missing Ctrl-C handler in `LlmClient`, flagged as a real follow-up.
- **§4 Often confused with** — five contrasts:
  - **Process vs thread from the OS angle** — both are `clone()` on Linux; `CLONE_VM` is the difference. Full comparison table.
  - **Syscall vs library call** — ~1 ns vs ~100 ns; library call may *internally* make a syscall.
  - **User space vs kernel space** — CPU mode bit.
  - **Blocking vs non-blocking I/O.**
  - **Concurrency vs parallelism, restated in OS terms** — concurrency is program-shaped, parallelism is hardware-shaped.
- **§5 Quiz** — 5 shuffled, including a stab-the-syscall-count question and an "is concurrency useful on a single-core CPU?" question that tests whether you've distinguished concurrency from parallelism for real.
- **§6 Scenarios** — three open-ended, including the **Ctrl-C signal handler** design exercise that uses the existing `LlmClient` `stop_`/CV plumbing.

## Workspace state

- **PROGRESS.md** — lesson 0009 logged.
- **GLOSSARY.md** — promoted: *Context switch*, *IPC*, *Kernel space / user space*, *Page cache*, *Scheduler*, *System call*, *Virtual memory / address space*. Seven new OS terms.

## Knowledge check (let's talk through these)

Three questions to verify the OS layer landed:

1. **You're profiling and see that one frame in 60 takes 18 ms instead of the usual 4 ms.** You strace the process and notice that on the slow frame there are ~200 syscalls and on a normal frame there are ~5. Without seeing the code, what's your *first* hypothesis about what's happening on the slow frame?

2. **In `LlmClient::workerLoop`, two distinct OS mechanisms put the thread to sleep depending on where it's stuck.** Name both, and say what kind of event wakes the thread up from each.

3. **A teammate says** "let's just have the game and Ollama share a `std::queue` via shared memory — it'll be much faster than HTTP." Sketch your reply: name the *one* OS feature that makes this possible in principle, and then list *two* practical reasons it's not what we want to do.

Take a swing at any or all. I'll correct gently and update GLOSSARY (`taught` → `firm`) based on how the answers land.

**Sources used:**
- [man syscalls(2) — full Linux system-call list](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/syscalls.2.html)
- [Eli Bendersky — measuring context switch overhead](https://eli.thegreenplace.net/2018/measuring-context-switching-and-memory-overheads-for-linux-threads/)
- [The cost of context switching — SoByte](https://www.sobyte.net/post/2022-06/ctx-switch/)
- [man clone(2) — thread vs process at the syscall level](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/clone.2.html)

This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. ## Key Smart Pointer Types

Smart pointers are defined in the <memory> header and include types such as std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, and std::weak_ptr.

### unique_ptr
unique_ptr is a smart pointer that provides exclusive ownership of a dynamically allocated object. It ensures that only one pointer can own a resource at a time, and when the unique_ptr goes out of scope, it automatically deletes the resource it manages, preventing memory leaks. std::unique_ptr is the right choice for the vast majority of heap allocations. It enforces exclusive ownership, transfers cleanly with std::move, and has zero runtime overhead. Use it as your default.

### shared_ptr
shared_ptr allows shared ownership with reference counting, enabling multiple pointers to share the same resource. A shared_ptr is a smart pointer that retains shared ownership of an object. The object is destroyed and its memory deallocated when the last remaining shared_ptr pointing to it is destroyed or reset.

### weak_ptr
A weak_ptr provides access to an object that one or more shared_ptr instances own, but doesn't participate in reference counting. Use when you want to observe an object, but don't require it to remain alive. Required in some cases to break circular references between shared_ptr instances.

## Performance Considerations

unique_ptr is faster and has zero overhead, while shared_ptr has the overhead of reference counting but enables shared ownership patterns.

## Best Practices

There is an additional, vital reason to create an std::shared_ptr with std::make_shared, and an std::unique_ptr with std::make_unique: no memory leak. Using two invocations of std::shared_ptr or std::unique_ptr in one expression can cause a memory leak if an exception happens.

When using Shared_Ptr in data structures like trees or graphs, always use Weak_Ptr for back-references to prevent memory leaks.

Lesson 0010 · cpp_games / docs / learning

Smart pointers: unique_ptr, shared_ptr, weak_ptr

Why this matters: lesson 0007 quietly used std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> without ever explaining what it does. Lesson 0006 promised "modern C++ has no manual delete." This is the lesson where you finally learn the type that delivered on that promise — and the two siblings that handle the cases unique_ptr doesn't.

1. The concept — the ownership question

For every heap object in a program, there's a question someone has to answer: who owns this, and who is responsible for freeing it? Pre-modern C++ answered that with a convention — "whoever called new should later call delete" — and the convention failed constantly. Forget to delete: memory leak. Delete twice: undefined behaviour. Delete on the wrong thread: crash. Pass a raw pointer across an API and you don't know whether you're supposed to free it.

Smart pointers replace the convention with a type. Each smart pointer encodes one specific answer to the ownership question, and the compiler enforces it. There are three:

std::unique_ptr<T>

"Exactly one owner." Can be moved, never copied. Destroys the object when it goes out of scope. Zero runtime overhead. Your default.

std::shared_ptr<T>

"Shared by N owners." Reference-counted. Object destroyed when the count reaches zero. The count uses atomics, so it's thread-safe and ~2× slower to copy than a raw pointer.

std::weak_ptr<T>

"I observe but don't own." Doesn't keep the object alive. lock() upgrades to a shared_ptr if the object still exists, else returns null. Required to break shared_ptr cycles.

The decision tree is short:

who needs to keep this alive? one obvious owner ──> std::unique_ptr<T> multiple owners, none demonstrably "last" ──> std::shared_ptr<T> I just want to watch it, I'm fine if it's gone ──> std::weak_ptr<T> nobody needs to free it (it's a stack local, or a container element) ──> no smart pointer; use a reference

The one-sentence mental model

Smart pointers are RAII wrappers around a heap pointer. The destructor of the wrapper does the delete — so as long as the wrapper has the right scope, the heap object is freed exactly once, at exactly the right moment.

2. Minimal example — one heap object, four ways

struct Wren { std::string greeting = "Hi there."; };

// (1) RAW NEW/DELETE — the way that used to be normal. Every error path
// has to remember the delete. Forget it (or throw on the line above) → leak.
Wren* w = new Wren;
useWren(*w);                       // what if this throws? leak.
delete w;                          // have to remember; no compiler help

// (2) UNIQUE_PTR — RAII. delete runs automatically at scope end, even on
// exceptions. Zero overhead vs raw new — just one pointer in size.
auto w = std::make_unique<Wren>();   // allocates and owns
useWren(*w);
// destructor of w runs here → delete is called for us.

// (3) SHARED_PTR — two pointers can both own. Refcount goes up on copy,
// down on destruction. Object freed when count hits zero.
std::shared_ptr<Wren> a = std::make_shared<Wren>();   // refcount = 1
{
    std::shared_ptr<Wren> b = a;                     // refcount = 2
    use(b);
}                                                    // b destroyed → refcount = 1
// a destroyed → refcount = 0 → delete runs

// (4) WEAK_PTR — observes the shared_ptr above without keeping it alive.
std::weak_ptr<Wren> observer = a;                    // refcount UNCHANGED
if (auto locked = observer.lock()) {                // upgrades to shared_ptr if still alive
    useWren(*locked);
} else {
    // the Wren is gone; lock() returned a null shared_ptr.
}

Three things to take away:

  • make_unique and make_shared are the right way to construct. They're exception-safe; bare new in an argument list can leak if a sibling argument throws.
  • unique_ptr isn't slower than new/delete. It's the same heap allocation; the wrapper is sizeof(pointer). The compiler optimises the destructor call away when there's nothing else to do.
  • shared_ptr isn't free. Each copy/destruction touches an atomic counter. ~2× the cost of a raw pointer copy. Fine for occasional copies; surprising in a hot loop.

3. In your project — where smart pointers fit

You're already using them — just inside containers

Every std::vector, std::string, and std::thread you've written is conceptually a smart pointer with extras. A std::vector<Projectile> owns its heap buffer; its destructor frees it. A std::string owns its (possibly heap-allocated) character buffer. A std::thread owns the OS-level thread handle. None of them require you to write delete. They're all RAII wrappers, just specialised to one kind of resource.

This is why your code has zero new and zero delete today. You've been writing modern C++ without thinking about it. Smart pointers are the same idea applied to single heap objects that don't fit any of the specialised containers.

The case you've already seen: unique_ptr for HAL backends

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.hpp (proposed in lesson 0007) 
class LlmClient {
 public:
    explicit LlmClient(std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> backend);
    // ...
 private:
    std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> backend_;
};

Why unique_ptr<LlmBackend> and not a value member or a raw pointer?

  • Can't be a value member. LlmBackend is abstract — you can't instantiate it directly. The member has to be polymorphic: unique_ptr<Base> can hold an OllamaBackend or XrtFpgaBackend derived; a LlmBackend by value cannot.
  • Could be a raw pointer, but why? A raw pointer leaves the question open: who deletes it? With unique_ptr, the answer is unambiguously "LlmClient's destructor does." If you also remember the virtual destructor on LlmBackend (lesson 0007's gotcha), the right derived destructor runs automatically.
  • Can be moved, not copied. Passing std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> into the constructor with std::move transfers ownership. The caller no longer has the backend; LlmClient does. The type system forbids accidentally keeping a second copy.

This is the textbook role for unique_ptr: heap-allocated polymorphic object with one clear owner.

Where shared_ptr would be tempting — and wrong

Imagine a future where multiple Npcs could each hold their own LlmBackend reference: "Jim uses Ollama, Jane uses the FPGA, Bob uses Ollama too." If two NPCs share a backend, you might reach for shared_ptr<LlmBackend> — "we both own it."

Don't. The right model is: LlmClient owns the backend; NPCs borrow it through a reference (or a non-owning raw pointer). One owner, many users is not the same as many owners. Reaching for shared_ptr the moment you see "more than one thing touches it" is the most common abuse of the type. Use it when ownership is genuinely shared and you cannot name the last owner. Most of the time, you can.

Where shared_ptr + weak_ptr would actually fit

A real case is harder to find in this project, but here's a hypothetical: an NPC Quest system where multiple NPCs reference the same quest object ("Jim gave you this quest; Jane comments on it; the journal UI shows it") and the quest dies only when nobody references it anymore.

struct Quest { std::string title; bool complete = false; };

// Each NPC holds a shared_ptr to quests it knows about.
// The quest is alive as long as anyone references it.
struct Npc {
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Quest>> knownQuests;
};

// The UI just wants to observe — if the quest gets removed by the world,
// the UI should NOT keep it alive on its own.
struct QuestLogUI {
    std::vector<std::weak_ptr<Quest>> tracked;

    void render() {
        for (auto& w : tracked) {
            if (auto q = w.lock()) {   // upgrade if still alive
                drawTitle(q->title);
            }
            // else: the quest is gone; we silently skip it.
        }
    }
};

The weak_ptr here would also prevent a cycle. If the UI held shared_ptrs and the quest itself held a shared_ptr back to the UI (say, to push notifications), you'd have a cycle: each end is keeping the other alive, neither will ever destruct, memory is leaked even after the player closes the journal. weak_ptr on one edge breaks the loop.

You don't have a use case for these in your code today

The honest answer: in the current state of your three games, shared_ptr and weak_ptr don't fit anywhere. unique_ptr fits in the lesson-0007 refactor. Smart pointers are the answer to a problem (heap object + ownership question); if you don't have heap objects with ambiguous ownership, you don't need them. The point of learning them is so you recognise the problem when it appears.

4. Often confused with...

unique_ptr vs. shared_ptr

 unique_ptrshared_ptr
Size1 pointer2 pointers (data + control block ptr)
CopyForbidden — compile errorAllowed; increments atomic refcount
MoveCheap, transfers ownershipCheap, same atomic refcount
DestructionAlways; once, at scope endOnly when refcount hits 0
Thread safety of the ptr itselfNone needed (one owner)Refcount is atomic; the pointed-at object is your problem to synchronise
Best whenOne clear owner — the defaultOwnership is genuinely shared and you can't name "last"

shared_ptr vs. raw pointer (or reference)

A shared_ptr owns; a raw pointer or reference observes. If you write void render(Quest& q), you've said "I'm using q for this call; I don't claim ownership." If you write void render(std::shared_ptr<Quest> q), you've said "I'm taking part-ownership; if you destroy your shared_ptr, mine still keeps the quest alive." For most function parameters, the non-owning form is correct. Pass smart pointers only when ownership actually transfers or is shared.

weak_ptr vs. raw pointer

Both observe without owning. The difference is detection. A raw pointer kept around after its target dies becomes a dangling pointer — using it is undefined behaviour with no warning. A weak_ptr kept around after its target dies returns a null shared_ptr when you .lock() — safe, detectable. Use weak_ptr when the observed object might die under you and you need to handle that gracefully. Use a raw pointer or reference when the lifetime is guaranteed by the surrounding code.

Smart pointers vs. garbage collection

Java and Go free memory periodically, scanning to find what's unreachable. The cost: stop-the-world pauses (or background CPU), nondeterministic destruction time. C++'s smart pointers free immediately when ownership ends. The cost: you have to think about ownership; cycles aren't auto-detected. Trade-off in plain English — GC gives you "I never think about it"; smart pointers give you "I know exactly when destructors run." For game code that wants predictable frame budget (lesson 0003), the smart-pointer model is the right one.

std::move(unique_ptr) vs. copy

You can't copy a unique_ptr: the line auto b = a; for two unique_ptrs is a compile error. You can move: auto b = std::move(a);. After the move, a is empty — a.get() == nullptr — and b owns the heap object. The language enforces "exactly one owner at a time" by literally disallowing the operation that would violate it. This is the type system at its best.

5. Quiz

In the lesson 0007 refactor, why is LlmClient's backend field declared as std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> rather than LlmBackend by value?

  • Performance — storing it by value would copy the whole backend on every LlmClient copy.
  • LlmBackend is abstract (pure virtuals) — it can't be instantiated as a value member. Polymorphic ownership requires pointer-to-base.
  • To allow multiple LlmClients to share one backend.
  • C++ doesn't allow inheritance hierarchies as value members in general.

You add std::shared_ptr<Texture> to Projectile in the shooter game so every projectile can show a custom sprite. The shooter's per-frame loop now iterates the projectile vector, copying each Projectile into a temporary for some helper. What's the hidden cost?

  • Every projectile copy deep-copies the underlying texture pixels.
  • Every projectile copy increments an atomic reference count; the temporary's destruction decrements it. In a hot loop, those atomic ops add up.
  • Each access does a null-pointer check, which adds a branch in the hot loop.
  • Each shared_ptr access requires a syscall to update the reference count in the kernel.

Two classes hold std::shared_ptr to each other (a "cycle"). The program exits. What happens to the two objects?

  • Both are correctly freed because std::shared_ptr always cleans up.
  • Both leak — each keeps the other's refcount above zero, so neither destructor runs. Fix: make one side a weak_ptr.
  • The compiler detects the cycle at build time and refuses to compile.
  • The standard library's garbage collector detects the cycle and frees both.

You're writing void renderQuest(Quest& q). Which is the right parameter type, given the function only reads q and the quest's lifetime is guaranteed by the caller?

  • std::shared_ptr<Quest> q — safest by default.
  • const Quest& q — non-owning observation, no refcount cost.
  • Quest* q — matches old C-style APIs.
  • Quest&& q — allows moving the quest out efficiently.

A teammate writes std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> b1 = backend; std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> b2 = backend; hoping to keep backend while also giving it to someone else. What happens?

  • backend ends up with refcount 3 and all three pointers stay valid.
  • b2 is initialised but backend is silently nulled at runtime.
  • Compile error on both lines. unique_ptr's copy constructor is deleted; the only way to transfer ownership is std::move.
  • Both b1 and b2 point at the same backend; the destructor pool handles it.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. Look at DialogUI::transcript_ — a std::deque<TranscriptLine>. The deque is "really" a smart pointer over its data. State the parallel as precisely as you can: what does the deque own (heap-wise), and what destructor frees it?

Scenario B. A teammate proposes std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Enemy>> enemies; in the shooter "so we can pass enemies around safely." Argue against it (one paragraph) using lesson 0003's hot-loop cost and this lesson's "one owner" principle. What container would you keep instead?

Scenario C. Imagine you add quest-tracking like §3 sketched. The journal UI uses std::weak_ptr<Quest> to observe. The player completes a quest; the world destroys its shared_ptr<Quest>. The journal renders on the next frame. Walk through what happens inside render()'s loop — specifically what w.lock() returns and why that's better than a raw pointer.

7. Track your progress

 private:
    std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> backend_;
};

Why unique_ptr<LlmBackend> and not a value member or a raw pointer?

  • Can't be a value member. LlmBackend is abstract — you can't instantiate it directly. The member has to be polymorphic: unique_ptr<Base> can hold an OllamaBackend or XrtFpgaBackend derived; a LlmBackend by value cannot.
  • Could be a raw pointer, but why? A raw pointer leaves the question open: who deletes it? With unique_ptr, the answer is unambiguously "LlmClient's destructor does." If you also remember the virtual destructor on LlmBackend (lesson 0007's gotcha), the right derived destructor runs automatically.
  • Can be moved, not copied. Passing std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> into the constructor with std::move transfers ownership. The caller no longer has the backend; LlmClient does. The type system forbids accidentally keeping a second copy.

This is the textbook role for unique_ptr: heap-allocated polymorphic object with one clear owner.

Where shared_ptr would be tempting — and wrong

Imagine a future where multiple Npcs could each hold their own LlmBackend reference: "Jim uses Ollama, Jane uses the FPGA, Bob uses Ollama too." If two NPCs share a backend, you might reach for shared_ptr<LlmBackend> — "we both own it."

Don't. The right model is: LlmClient owns the backend; NPCs borrow it through a reference (or a non-owning raw pointer). One owner, many users is not the same as many owners. Reaching for shared_ptr the moment you see "more than one thing touches it" is the most common abuse of the type. Use it when ownership is genuinely shared and you cannot name the last owner. Most of the time, you can.

Where shared_ptr + weak_ptr would actually fit

A real case is harder to find in this project, but here's a hypothetical: an NPC Quest system where multiple NPCs reference the same quest object ("Jim gave you this quest; Jane comments on it; the journal UI shows it") and the quest dies only when nobody references it anymore.

struct Quest { std::string title; bool complete = false; };

// Each NPC holds a shared_ptr to quests it knows about.
// The quest is alive as long as anyone references it.
struct Npc {
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Quest>> knownQuests;
};

// The UI just wants to observe — if the quest gets removed by the world,
// the UI should NOT keep it alive on its own.
struct QuestLogUI {
    std::vector<std::weak_ptr<Quest>> tracked;

    void render() {
        for (auto& w : tracked) {
            if (auto q = w.lock()) {   // upgrade if still alive
                drawTitle(q->title);
            }
            // else: the quest is gone; we silently skip it.
        }
    }
};

The weak_ptr here would also prevent a cycle. If the UI held shared_ptrs and the quest itself held a shared_ptr back to the UI (say, to push notifications), you'd have a cycle: each end is keeping the other alive, neither will ever destruct, memory is leaked even after the player closes the journal. weak_ptr on one edge breaks the loop.

You don't have a use case for these in your code today

The honest answer: in the current state of your three games, shared_ptr and weak_ptr don't fit anywhere. unique_ptr fits in the lesson-0007 refactor. Smart pointers are the answer to a problem (heap object + ownership question); if you don't have heap objects with ambiguous ownership, you don't need them. The point of learning them is so you recognise the problem when it appears.

4. Often confused with...

unique_ptr vs. shared_ptr

 unique_ptrshared_ptr
Size1 pointer2 pointers (data + control block ptr)
CopyForbidden — compile errorAllowed; increments atomic refcount
MoveCheap, transfers ownershipCheap, same atomic refcount
DestructionAlways; once, at scope endOnly when refcount hits 0
Thread safety of the ptr itselfNone needed (one owner)Refcount is atomic; the pointed-at object is your problem to synchronise
Best whenOne clear owner — the defaultOwnership is genuinely shared and you can't name "last"

shared_ptr vs. raw pointer (or reference)

A shared_ptr owns; a raw pointer or reference observes. If you write void render(Quest& q), you've said "I'm using q for this call; I don't claim ownership." If you write void render(std::shared_ptr<Quest> q), you've said "I'm taking part-ownership; if you destroy your shared_ptr, mine still keeps the quest alive." For most function parameters, the non-owning form is correct. Pass smart pointers only when ownership actually transfers or is shared.

weak_ptr vs. raw pointer

Both observe without owning. The difference is detection. A raw pointer kept around after its target dies becomes a dangling pointer — using it is undefined behaviour with no warning. A weak_ptr kept around after its target dies returns a null shared_ptr when you .lock() — safe, detectable. Use weak_ptr when the observed object might die under you and you need to handle that gracefully. Use a raw pointer or reference when the lifetime is guaranteed by the surrounding code.

Smart pointers vs. garbage collection

Java and Go free memory periodically, scanning to find what's unreachable. The cost: stop-the-world pauses (or background CPU), nondeterministic destruction time. C++'s smart pointers free immediately when ownership ends. The cost: you have to think about ownership; cycles aren't auto-detected. Trade-off in plain English — GC gives you "I never think about it"; smart pointers give you "I know exactly when destructors run." For game code that wants predictable frame budget (lesson 0003), the smart-pointer model is the right one.

std::move(unique_ptr) vs. copy

You can't copy a unique_ptr: the line auto b = a; for two unique_ptrs is a compile error. You can move: auto b = std::move(a);. After the move, a is empty — a.get() == nullptr — and b owns the heap object. The language enforces "exactly one owner at a time" by literally disallowing the operation that would violate it. This is the type system at its best.

5. Quiz

In the lesson 0007 refactor, why is LlmClient's backend field declared as std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> rather than LlmBackend by value?

  • Performance — storing it by value would copy the whole backend on every LlmClient copy.
  • LlmBackend is abstract (pure virtuals) — it can't be instantiated as a value member. Polymorphic ownership requires pointer-to-base.
  • To allow multiple LlmClients to share one backend.
  • C++ doesn't allow inheritance hierarchies as value members in general.

You add std::shared_ptr<Texture> to Projectile in the shooter game so every projectile can show a custom sprite. The shooter's per-frame loop now iterates the projectile vector, copying each Projectile into a temporary for some helper. What's the hidden cost?

  • Every projectile copy deep-copies the underlying texture pixels.
  • Every projectile copy increments an atomic reference count; the temporary's destruction decrements it. In a hot loop, those atomic ops add up.
  • Each access does a null-pointer check, which adds a branch in the hot loop.
  • Each shared_ptr access requires a syscall to update the reference count in the kernel.

Two classes hold std::shared_ptr to each other (a "cycle"). The program exits. What happens to the two objects?

  • Both are correctly freed because std::shared_ptr always cleans up.
  • Both leak — each keeps the other's refcount above zero, so neither destructor runs. Fix: make one side a weak_ptr.
  • The compiler detects the cycle at build time and refuses to compile.
  • The standard library's garbage collector detects the cycle and frees both.

You're writing void renderQuest(Quest& q). Which is the right parameter type, given the function only reads q and the quest's lifetime is guaranteed by the caller?

  • std::shared_ptr<Quest> q — safest by default.
  • const Quest& q — non-owning observation, no refcount cost.
  • Quest* q — matches old C-style APIs.
  • Quest&& q — allows moving the quest out efficiently.

A teammate writes std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> b1 = backend; std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend> b2 = backend; hoping to keep backend while also giving it to someone else. What happens?

  • backend ends up with refcount 3 and all three pointers stay valid.
  • b2 is initialised but backend is silently nulled at runtime.
  • Compile error on both lines. unique_ptr's copy constructor is deleted; the only way to transfer ownership is std::move.
  • Both b1 and b2 point at the same backend; the destructor pool handles it.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. Look at DialogUI::transcript_ — a std::deque<TranscriptLine>. The deque is "really" a smart pointer over its data. State the parallel as precisely as you can: what does the deque own (heap-wise), and what destructor frees it?

Scenario B. A teammate proposes std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Enemy>> enemies; in the shooter "so we can pass enemies around safely." Argue against it (one paragraph) using lesson 0003's hot-loop cost and this lesson's "one owner" principle. What container would you keep instead?

Scenario C. Imagine you add quest-tracking like §3 sketched. The journal UI uses std::weak_ptr<Quest> to observe. The player completes a quest; the world destroys its shared_ptr<Quest>. The journal renders on the next frame. Walk through what happens inside render()'s loop — specifically what w.lock() returns and why that's better than a raw pointer.

7. Track your progress

Further reading — cppreference: std::unique_ptr · cppreference: std::shared_ptr · cppreference: std::weak_ptr · C++ Core Guidelines: smart pointer rules · Microsoft: smart pointers in modern C++

## What I picked and why

You typed "C++/OS Fundamentals" — essentially the blank/auto case. Rather than write a tour-style retread (we've shipped nine lessons already, and most C++ and OS basics are covered), I followed PROGRESS.md's outstanding suggestion: **smart pointers**. Three reasons it's the highest-value next:

1. **Direct unmet debt** — Lesson 0007 used `std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend>` in your refactor proposal and never explained it.
2. **Concept ready** — You've now seen heap (0006), RAII (0006), inheritance (0007), and containers (0008). Smart pointers sit where those collide.
3. **Modern C++ payoff** — Lesson 0006 promised "no manual `delete` in modern C++." This is the type that delivered on that promise.

## What's in lesson 0010

- **§1 The ownership question** — every heap object needs an answer, and smart pointers turn the answer into a *type*. Color-coded cards for `unique_ptr` / `shared_ptr` / `weak_ptr`, followed by a four-line decision tree.
- **§2 Minimal example** — one heap `Wren` object stored four ways: raw `new`/`delete` (with the exception-safety leak called out in red), `unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr` showing refcount stepping up/down, `weak_ptr` showing `.lock()` upgrade.
- **§3 In your project**:
  - "You're already using them — inside containers" — `std::vector`/`string`/`thread` *are* smart pointers, specialised. That's why your code has zero `new`/`delete` today.
  - **The textbook `unique_ptr` case**: `LlmClient::backend_` from lesson 0007, explained for the first time. Three reasons it can't be a value member, can't be a raw pointer, and shouldn't be `shared_ptr`.
  - **"Where `shared_ptr` would be tempting and wrong"** — a hypothetical multi-NPC-shared-backend setup that explains the most common smart-pointer abuse.
  - **Hypothetical `Quest` system** for `shared_ptr` + `weak_ptr` with cycle-leak gotcha and how `weak_ptr` breaks the loop.
  - **Honest callout**: your code doesn't actually need shared/weak today. They're taught so you recognise the problem when it appears.
- **§4 Often confused with** — five pairs: unique vs shared (with comparison table), shared vs raw (owning vs observing), weak vs raw (detectable vs dangling), smart pointers vs garbage collection (deterministic vs not), `std::move(unique_ptr)` vs copy (compile error).
- **§5 Quiz** — 5 shuffled, including a "teammate copies a `unique_ptr`" question testing whether you understand the type system enforces "exactly one owner" at compile time.
- **§6 Scenarios** — three open-ended, including one that asks you to argue against `vector<shared_ptr<Enemy>>` using lesson 0003's hot-loop reasoning.

## Workspace state

- **PROGRESS.md** — lesson 0010 logged. **New suggested-next: profiling** — three previous lessons (0003, 0005, 0009) all gestured at "measure before you change." You're now ready to actually do it with `std::chrono::steady_clock` instrumentation in the shooter loop.
- **GLOSSARY.md** — promoted: *`std::unique_ptr`*, *`std::shared_ptr`*, *`std::weak_ptr`*, *Reference counting*. Four new entries.

## Knowledge check (let's talk through these)

Three questions to verify the lesson stuck:

1. **In `LlmClient::workerLoop`** the worker dereferences `backend_->request(req)`. The arrow operator on a `unique_ptr` — what is it actually doing, and how does it cost the same as dereferencing a raw pointer?

2. **You write** `void renderQuest(std::shared_ptr<Quest> q)` instead of `void renderQuest(const Quest& q)`. Name the *specific* cost the shared_ptr version pays *on every call site*. (Lesson 0009 vocabulary applies here — describe what the CPU actually does.)

3. **A `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Enemy>>` is legal C++** (vector of unique_ptrs). A `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Enemy>>` that you try to copy is *not* legal — the line won't compile. Why? Tie it back to the rule from this lesson.

This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive comparison of C++20 semaphores and mutexes:

## Key Differences

**Ownership:**
Semaphores can count to more than one, and any thread can decrement or increment the semaphore, whereas mutex can only be unlocked by the thread that locked it. The big difference from a mutex is ownership: any thread can signal (release) and any thread can wait (acquire).

**Purpose:**
Mutexes handle mutual exclusion (protecting shared state), while semaphores handle coordination and ordering (controlling who may proceed and when).

## When to Use Each

**Use a Mutex when:**
If you have a single shared object that must be updated atomically, use a mutex. It guards the object, and the thread that locks it must unlock it.

**Use a Semaphore when:**
If you have a pool of identical resources, or you need to allow a fixed number of concurrent entries, use a semaphore. It tracks permits, not owners.

**Practical guidance:**
If you are going to synchronize threads within the same address space, use mutexes and conditional variables; if you need to synchronize processes, use semaphores.

## C++20 Types

C++20 has introduced a new synchronization mechanism, namely the semaphore. It is accessed via std::counting_semaphore and std::binary_semaphore.

The fundamental difference is that mutexes enforce ownership, making them safer for protecting a single shared resource, while semaphores are more flexible for coordinating access to multiple resources or controlling concurrency limits.

Most C++ devs confuse them because they sometimes look interchangeable. They aren't. This lesson is the rule for picking right.

1. The concept — the ownership question

The single most important difference between a mutex and a semaphore is one word: ownership.

  • A mutex has ownership. Only the thread that locked it can unlock it. The mutex "belongs" to that thread for the duration of the lock. If anyone else tries to unlock it, you have a bug.
  • A semaphore has no ownership. It's just a counter. Any thread can acquire (decrement) and any thread can release (increment). The thread that calls release needn't be the one that called acquire.

That single distinction is enough to explain why they're used so differently. A mutex models "I'm using this thing; everyone else wait." A semaphore models "there are N permits available; take one when you need it, return one when you're done — or hand it to someone else." Different shapes of problem, different tools.

std::mutex

Mutual exclusion of one resource. Lock/unlock by the same thread. RAII-wrapped via lock_guard / unique_lock. Use to protect shared data.

std::counting_semaphore<N>

"At most K things may be in flight at once." Initial count K; acquire decrements, release increments. Any thread can do either. Use for resource pools, rate limits, admission control.

std::binary_semaphore

One-shot signal between threads. Special case of counting semaphore with max=1. Often used as a "wait for done" primitive. Looks like a mutex; semantically different.

The visual model

MUTEX SEMAPHORE (count = 3) ────────────── ────────────────────── +---+---+---+ "the lock" | • | • | • | ← 3 permits available +---+---+---+ Thread A: lock() | ▼ | acquire → count = 2 ┌─────────┐ | │ holding │ Thread B and | acquire → count = 1 │ the │ C wait at the | │ mutex │ door | acquire → count = 0 └─────────┘ | Thread A: unlock() | acquire → BLOCKS | (no permits available) Anyone else trying | to unlock = bug | release (any thread) → count = 1 | (the blocked thread wakes)

Mutex: "I claim this; nobody else touch it until I'm done."
Counting semaphore: "There are N seats; take one and give it back."
Binary semaphore: "Tap me on the shoulder when X is done."

The clearest way to feel the difference is to see each tool solve the problem it is for. Same idea every time: multiple threads, one piece of shared infrastructure.

// PROBLEM 1: One database connection, many threads want to use it.
// Use a MUTEX — exclusion of one resource.
class DbWriter {
    std::mutex m_;
    Connection conn_;
 public:
    void write(const std::string& row) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m_);  // one writer at a time
        conn_.send(row);
    }
};

// PROBLEM 2: A "GPU capacity" of 3 concurrent LLM calls. More requesting threads
// must wait their turn. Use a COUNTING SEMAPHORE — admission control.
std::counting_semaphore<3> gpuSlots{3};  // 3 permits initially available

void handleRequest(const Request& r) {
    gpuSlots.acquire();                  // blocks if all 3 in use
    auto reply = runOnGpu(r);
    gpuSlots.release();                  // any thread releases; not "the owner"
}

// PROBLEM 3: A worker thread does setup, then signals the main thread it's done.
// Use a BINARY SEMAPHORE — one-shot cross-thread signal.
std::binary_semaphore done{0};         // initially: no signal

std::thread t([&] {
    setUpEverything();
    done.release();                      // signal: ready
});

done.acquire();                          // main thread blocks until signal
useTheThing();

3. In your project — mutexes you have, semaphores you might add

Today: two mutexes in LlmClient (recap)

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.hpp:78-82 
std::mutex requestMutex_;
std::condition_variable requestCv_;
std::queue<ChatRequest> requests_;

std::mutex replyMutex_;
std::vector<ChatReply> replies_;

Each mutex protects exactly the data structure it guards. Same thread that locks unlocks (lesson 0005). This is exclusion of a shared resource — the textbook mutex case. No semaphore would fit; the queue isn't a count, it's a structure.

Hypothetical: a counting semaphore for "max N requests in flight"

Today LlmClient has one worker. Suppose you scale up: 5 worker threads, all popping from requests_. But your GPU can only realistically handle 3 LLM calls in flight before VRAM and compute saturate. You want the workers to pop as many requests as they like, but only 3 of them can call processOne at a time.

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp (hypothetical) 
private:
    std::counting_semaphore<8> gpuSlots_{3};   // max=8, start with 3 permits

void LlmClient::workerLoop() {
    while (true) {
        ChatRequest req = dequeueOne();         // existing mutex-protected pop

        gpuSlots_.acquire();                    // block until a GPU slot opens
        ChatReply reply = backend_->request(req);
        gpuSlots_.release();                    // hand the slot to whoever's next

        pushReply(std::move(reply));            // existing mutex-protected push
    }
}

Why a semaphore and not a fourth mutex? Because you're not protecting one resource — you're admitting threads to a pool of three identical resources. A mutex models "one." A semaphore models "K." Notice also that with the semaphore release, any thread can be the one to call it. If you added a feature where the main thread cancels a request mid-flight and needs to release the GPU slot, it can — even though the worker acquired it. A mutex would forbid that ("only the locker may unlock").

Hypothetical: a binary semaphore as a simpler shutdown handshake

Today LlmClient's destructor sets stop_ and calls notify_all on the CV (lesson 0005). The worker checks the predicate, sees stop_, returns. That's fine, but it uses three primitives: atomic, mutex, CV.

An alternative for the simpler "just wait for the worker to finish one specific thing" case is a binary semaphore:

std::binary_semaphore startupReady_{0};   // not yet signalled

LlmClient::LlmClient(...) {
    worker_ = std::thread([this] {
        connectToOllama();
        startupReady_.release();              // signal: I'm ready for traffic
        workerLoop();
    });
    startupReady_.acquire();                  // main thread waits
}

Just like lesson 0010's note about shared_ptr: semaphores don't currently fit your code. They're taught so you recognise the problem when it appears — "I want N things in flight at once" or "I just want a one-shot wait" — and don't reach for a mutex out of habit.

4. Often confused with...

Mutex vs. binary semaphore (THE classic confusion)

Both look like "lock the door, unlock the door." Semantically they're not interchangeable.

Who can unlock?Only the lockerAnyone
Used forProtecting shared dataCross-thread one-shot signal
RAII helperstd::lock_guard / unique_lockNone standard; you call acquire/release by hand
Recursive same-thread relockDeadlocks (unless recursive_mutex)Decrements to 0, next acquire blocks
Best whenYou're protecting stateYou're handing control from one thread to another

Mutex vs. condition variable

You already know this one (lesson 0005), but it's worth restating: a mutex enforces exclusion ("nobody else may touch this"), a CV enables waiting ("sleep until something changes"). They pair: every CV is associated with a mutex. A semaphore folds both ideas (counted admission + waiting) into one primitive.

You could simulate a counting semaphore with an array of K mutexes and a "find the next free one" routine. People sometimes do this in pre-C++20 code. The result is more complex, slower (you scan), and exposes the ownership constraint you don't want (only-locker-can-unlock). A counting semaphore is the right answer for "K equivalent permits."

A spinlock is a mutex-like primitive that busy-loops on an atomic instead of sleeping. Useful when critical sections are extremely short (a few instructions) and the cost of putting the thread to sleep would exceed the lock wait. For your game's locks (which protect non-trivial data structures), std::mutex is the right tool; the sleep is fine.

The same idea as a mutex, but with two modes: many readers OR one writer. Lets concurrent readers all proceed when nobody's writing. Pays off for read-heavy workloads on big data structures. Not used in your code; mentioned here because it's the third major lock variety after mutex and semaphore.
