The word "semaphore" is also used for POSIX named semaphores (sem_open) and SysV semaphores — cross-process primitives the OS provides. Same concept, different scope: those synchronise processes (lesson 0009 IPC), while std::counting_semaphore synchronises threads within one process. If you ever wanted your game and Ollama to coordinate via a counter (you don't), the POSIX version would be the right tool. The C++ one is in-process only.

5. Quiz

You add a feature: a main thread can cancel an in-flight LLM request. When it does, it should release the GPU slot that the worker was holding. Which primitive supports this, and why does the other one not?

  • std::mutex — you just unlock it from whichever thread holds the cancellation handle.
  • std::counting_semaphore — any thread can release a permit; ownership semantics don't apply.
  • std::atomic<int> — decrement and increment as needed.
  • A spinlock — it's faster and any thread can release it.

A junior dev replaces all uses of std::mutex in LlmClient with std::binary_semaphore, reasoning "they both look like locks." The code compiles and passes their tests. What's the most likely real-world bug they've introduced?

  • Performance is dramatically worse because semaphores use a syscall for every acquire.
  • The protection of shared data is now allowed to be 'unlocked' by the wrong thread, breaking the invariant the mutex was enforcing — silently.
  • std::binary_semaphore requires C++23 and the build is now using a degraded fallback.
  • The worker thread crashes with a 'use after release' fault.

You have 5 worker threads and a counting semaphore with max=3 limiting concurrent GPU calls. Thread A and Thread B both acquire() permits and run. Thread C is the third to acquire(). Threads D and E call acquire() and block. Now Thread B finishes and calls release(). What happens?

  • Both D and E wake up and both proceed.
  • One of D or E (implementation-dependent which) wakes up and acquires the permit; the other stays blocked.
  • The release() blocks until a fourth thread tries to acquire, then hands off the permit.
  • D and E both starve; the OS prefers waking newly-arrived threads over already-blocked ones.

For the existing LlmClient shutdown sequence (destructor sets stop_, calls notify_all, joins the worker), why is a binary semaphore a worse fit than the current atomic+CV approach?

  • Binary semaphores don't propagate writes between threads on some platforms.
  • The worker waits for two different events (new work OR shutdown). A binary semaphore is a one-shot signal — it can't cleanly multiplex 'work arrived' and 'shutdown requested' on the same wait.
  • std::binary_semaphore isn't available in the C++ standard the project uses.
  • Binary semaphore wakeups have lower priority than CV notifications, so the worker exits later.

You want a "rate limit Wren's replies to one every 2 seconds" feature. Which primitive cleanly expresses this, and what specifically would release do?

  • A std::mutex — lock during the reply, unlock when done.
  • A std::binary_semaphore — a timer thread releases one permit every 2 seconds; the worker acquires before each reply.
  • A std::this_thread::sleep_for(2s) at the end of every reply.
  • A std::condition_variable with a 2-second timeout on wait_for.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. Your game adds a feature: the dialog UI plays a short audio "thinking" cue while Wren is generating, and a different audio cue when the reply arrives. Only one audio channel exists. Should the audio channel be protected by a mutex or by a binary semaphore? Defend your answer; the right one is not the one that sounds like "exclusion."

Scenario B. Suppose LlmClient grows a worker pool of 8 threads and a counting_semaphore<8> gpuSlots_{3}. Now you decide that on a player's beefier GPU the slot count should be 5 instead of 3. What changes in your code, and what doesn't? (Hint: 3 is the runtime starting value; 8 is something else.)

Scenario C. A teammate proposes "let's replace the two mutexes in LlmClient with two binary_semaphores — binary semaphores are 'the new way to do locking.'" Argue against it in one paragraph, using the words ownership, RAII, and invariant. Reference lesson 0005's reason for picking mutexes if you want.

- **`std::counting_semaphore<MaxN>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0011)*
  C++20 admission-control primitive. Holds a counter; `acquire()`
  decrements (blocks if zero), `release()` increments. **No ownership** —
  any thread can release, even one that didn't acquire. Use for
  resource pools, rate limits, or "max K in flight" patterns.

- **`std::binary_semaphore`** — `taught` *(lesson 0011)*
  Special case of `counting_semaphore` with max=1. One-shot cross-thread
  signal ("tap me when X is done"). Looks like a mutex syntactically;
  semantically different (no ownership, no RAII helper). Use to hand
  control between threads, not to protect data.

- **Semaphore (general)** — `taught` *(lesson 0011)*
  Synchronisation primitive that's a counter of available permits with
  blocking acquire/non-blocking release. Distinct from mutex by having
  **no ownership semantics** — any thread can release. Two C++20
  flavors: `std::counting_semaphore<MaxN>` and `std::binary_semaphore`.

Lesson 0011 is in place. To open on Linux:

```
xdg-open /home/node/work/normal_work/cpp_games/docs/learning/lessons/0011-mutexes-and-semaphores.html
```

## What's in lesson 0011

The headline distinction — **ownership** — is the through-line of the whole lesson. A mutex has it; a semaphore doesn't. That single property explains every place they're not interchangeable.

- **§1 The ownership concept** — stated in one sentence at the top, then unpacked with three color-coded cards for `std::mutex` / `std::counting_semaphore` / `std::binary_semaphore`. Plus an ASCII visual showing the lock model (one door, one occupant) vs the semaphore model (three permits, anyone can take or hand back).
- **§2 Three problems, three primitives** — same shape every time: shared infrastructure, multiple threads. Each problem demands a different tool:
  - **Mutex**: one DB connection, many writers (exclusion).
  - **Counting semaphore**: 3 GPU slots, 5 worker threads (admission control).
  - **Binary semaphore**: worker signals main "I'm done" (one-shot handoff).
  - The asymmetric acquire/release in cases 2 and 3 is the "no ownership" property visible.
- **§3 In your project**:
  - **Recap**: `LlmClient`'s two mutexes (lesson 0005) — textbook mutex case, no semaphore would fit.
  - **Hypothetical counting semaphore**: a 5-worker pool with `counting_semaphore<8>{3}` rate-limiting concurrent GPU calls. Explains *why* a semaphore, not a fourth mutex.
  - **Hypothetical binary semaphore**: a one-shot startup handshake. Also explains why a binary semaphore is *not* the right replacement for the shutdown CV pattern (the CV is genuinely better for "wait for one of N events").
  - Honest callout (same as lesson 0010): you don't need these in your code today; the point is to recognize the problem when it appears.
- **§4 Often confused with** — six contrasts:
  - **Mutex vs binary semaphore** (THE classic — comparison table makes the ownership difference explicit).
  - **Mutex vs CV** (recap from lesson 0005).
  - **Counting semaphore vs mutex pool** (why the array-of-mutexes hack is wrong).
  - **Spinlock vs mutex** (when very short critical sections justify busy-waiting).
  - **`std::shared_mutex` (reader-writer lock)** as the third lock variety.
  - **POSIX semaphores vs `std::` semaphores** — cross-process vs in-process.
- **§5 Quiz** — 5 shuffled, including a rate-limit-Wren question and a "junior dev replaces mutex with binary semaphore" question that tests whether the *invisible* nature of the bug has clicked.
- **§6 Scenarios** — three open-ended, including an audio-channel scenario where the "obviously a mutex" intuition is actually wrong.

## Workspace state

- **PROGRESS.md** — lesson 0011 logged. Suggested-next remains **profiling**.
- **GLOSSARY.md** — promoted: *`std::counting_semaphore<MaxN>`*, *`std::binary_semaphore`*, *Semaphore (general)*. Three new terms; *Mutex* was already in there from lesson 0005.

## Knowledge check (let's talk through these)

Three questions to verify the ownership concept landed:

1. **Why is `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>` a thing but `std::lock_guard<std::binary_semaphore>` isn't?** Tie your answer to the ownership distinction. (Hint: what would `lock_guard`'s destructor have to *do*, and does that make sense for a semaphore?)

2. **Imagine you have one printer that two threads need to share.** A teammate says "use a `counting_semaphore<1>{1}` instead of `std::mutex` — same thing, one permit." Identify the *one* failure mode the semaphore version has that the mutex version doesn't. (Hint: think about exception safety mid-print.)

3. **Scenario B from the lesson** asks about `counting_semaphore<8>{3}` and what changes if you want to bump 3 to 5. Specifically: **what is the template parameter 8 for, and what is the constructor argument 3 for?** They are very different things and conflating them is the most common bug with this type.

Take a swing at any or all. Q1 is the cleanest test of whether the ownership concept generalised in your head — if you can articulate why `lock_guard` doesn't work for semaphores, you really get it.

**Sources used:**
- [cppreference — `std::counting_semaphore`](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/thread/counting_semaphore)
- [cppreference — `std::binary_semaphore`](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/thread/binary_semaphore)
- [Vincent Mayeski — Mutexes vs Semaphores in C++20](http://maye.ski/index.php/2022/10/03/mutexes-vs-semaphores-in-c20/)
- [TheLinuxCode — Mutex vs Semaphore: How I Choose in 2026](https://thelinuxcode.com/mutex-vs-semaphore-how-i-choose-in-2026-with-real-pitfalls-and-patterns/)

The user wants to learn "" (or, if blank, you choose the most valuable concept to teach next based on their progress and this project's code). This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.

Based on the web search results, here's what you need to know about `emplace_back` vs `push_back` with explicit constructors:

## The Explicit Constructor Gotcha

push_back() refuses to invoke explicit constructors; emplace_back() invokes them. Therefore it's easy to accidentally invoke the wrong constructor when using emplace_back().

## The Readability Problem

If you have a choice between push_back() and emplace_back() with the same arguments, your code will tend to be more readable if you choose push_back(), because push_back() expresses your intent more specifically. Because it omits types, emplace_back() can be mystifying.

## Safety Concerns

If you write my_vec.push_back(2<<20), you'll get a compile error and you'll quickly spot the problem. On the other hand, if you write my_vec.emplace_back(2<<20), the code will compile, and you won't notice any problems until run-time.

## When to Prefer Each

**Use `push_back()`** for general cases: Choosing push_back() is also safer and should be your default choice.

**Use `emplace_back()`** when:
- If T has an explicit constructor taking U, emplace_back(u) works, but push_back(u) does not. Use emplace_back here for correctness, not efficiency.
- For in-place construction from arguments, emplace_back(args...) remains optimal.

## Performance Reality

For more expensive types, this may be a reason to use emplace_back() instead of push_back(), despite the readability and safety costs, but then again it may not. Very often the performance difference just won't matter.

**2026 Best Practice**: Prefer `push_back()` by default for clarity and safety, and only switch to `emplace_back()` when you have a specific correctness need (explicit constructors) or have benchmarked a real performance gain.

Quiz: 0 / 0
Lesson 0012 · cpp_games / docs / learning

emplace_back vs. push_back

Why this matters: your code uses push_back in 20+ places and emplace_back in zero. Online lore says "always prefer emplace_back — it's faster." That lore is wrong in 2026, and reaching for it without understanding has a real safety cost. This lesson is the rule for picking right.

1. The concept — one constructs, the other appends

Both add a new element to the end of a vector. The difference is how the element gets there.

  • push_back(t) takes an already-existing T (or something implicitly convertible) and copies or moves it into the vector's storage. The function signature is concrete: void push_back(const T&) and void push_back(T&&).
  • emplace_back(args...) takes any number of constructor arguments and forwards them — perfectly — to T's constructor, building the object directly inside the vector's storage. No temporary is built, no copy or move happens.

The visual step-by-step

push_back(std::string("hello")) emplace_back("hello") ──────────────────────────── ────────────────────── 1. construct temp std::string("hello") 1. forward "hello" as constructor arg on the stack no temp built 2. push_back moves it into vector storage 2. emplace_back constructs std::string (move constructor runs) directly into vector storage 3. destroy the temp 3. ... that's it. Two constructions + one move. One construction. No move.

That sounds like a clear win for emplace_back. The reality in 2026 is more nuanced: for modern types with cheap move constructors (basically everything in your code), the difference is invisible. The cost of "construct then move" a std::string is ~5 ns. You can't measure it from a game loop.

The modern rule of thumb

Prefer push_back by default. Reach for emplace_back when you have a specific reason: you'd construct a temporary anyway, the type has multiple constructor arguments and you want to forward them in place, or there's no move/copy available. The "always emplace" advice you may have seen is older than the language is now — it predates good move semantics and modern compiler optimisation.

2. Minimal example — three patterns side by side

struct ChatTurn { std::string role; std::string content; };

std::vector<ChatTurn> history;

// (A) "I already have a ChatTurn" — push_back is the obvious choice.
ChatTurn t{"user", "hello"};
history.push_back(std::move(t));      // move t into the vector. One move.

// (B) "I want to build a new one inline from arguments."
//     push_back constructs a temp + moves it; emplace_back builds in place.
//     For ChatTurn this is unobservable; for types with no cheap move it matters.
history.push_back({"user", "hello"});       // build temp, move into vector
history.emplace_back("user", "hello");    // build in place

// (C) The DANGEROUS case — explicit constructors.
struct Capacity { explicit Capacity(int n) : value(n) {} int value; };
std::vector<Capacity> caps;

caps.push_back(42);        // COMPILE ERROR — push_back refuses explicit conversions.
caps.emplace_back(42);     // COMPILES — emplace_back DOES invoke explicit constructors.
// If you intended 'a Capacity holding 42', emplace_back was right.
// If you intended 'push the integer 42' (and forgot the type),
// emplace_back silently obliged. push_back would have caught the bug.

Pattern (A) is what your code does already. Pattern (B) is where both are fine and the choice is style. Pattern (C) is the gotcha — emplace_back invokes explicit constructors that push_back refuses. That's a feature when you want it and a silent bug when you don't.

The hidden gotcha — explicit constructors

The Chromium project publishes an internal PSA: "Prefer push_back() over emplace_back() unless you know you need it." The reason is exactly pattern (C). emplace_back is more permissive about what it'll convert to T; push_back is stricter. Sometimes the permissiveness is what you want; usually you don't want a "fast write" function to be slipping in conversions you didn't ask for.

3. In your project — every push_back, audited

The "could be emplace" cases — equivalent in practice

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Npc.cpp:30 
history_.push_back({"user", std::move(pendingUserLine_)});
history_.push_back({"assistant", reply.content});

The brace-init constructs a temporary ChatTurn and push_back moves it in. emplace_back("user", std::move(pendingUserLine_)) would build in place. For a struct of two std::strings with their cheap moves, the difference is unmeasurable. The push_back form is also more readable — the braces make the "I am building a ChatTurn" intent visible, while emplace_back hides the type.

cpp_racing_game/src/main.cpp:285 
pts.push_back(sf::Vector2f(cx + std::cos(a) * r, cy + std::sin(a) * r));

This is the textbook "build a temporary and shove it in" case. pts.emplace_back(cx + std::cos(a) * r, cy + std::sin(a) * r) would forward those two floats straight to sf::Vector2f's constructor. Both compile, both produce the same machine code on modern compilers. emplace_back is arguably cleaner here — no redundant sf::Vector2f(...) spelled out. Either is fine.

The "emplace would be wrong" cases — you're already moving

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:62 
replies_.push_back(std::move(reply));
cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/DialogUI.cpp:98 
transcript_.push_back(std::move(line));

Here you already have an existing object (reply, line) and you're transferring ownership into the vector. push_back(std::move(x)) is exactly the right shape. Writing emplace_back(std::move(reply)) would call ChatReply's move constructor with one argument — same outcome, but the intent ("I'm appending this thing") is muddier. The Abseil style guide says it explicitly: use push_back when you have an existing object to put in.

The "definitely fine as push_back" cases — copies of locals

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:410, 498, 555, 568, 748 
game.impacts.push_back(fx);
game.pickups.push_back(pickup);
game.projectiles.push_back(shot);
game.enemies.push_back(enemy);

Each appends a copy of a local struct. Since these are POD-ish (or close to it — mostly arithmetic types), copy and move are identical. emplace_back(fx) would just call ImpactEffect's copy constructor with one argument — same code. No reason to change anything; push_back is the clearer expression of "append this thing."

Audit summary

Across all 20 push_back calls in your code, zero of them have a meaningful win from converting to emplace_back. The racing game's sf::Vector2f temporary is the closest call — pure style, no perf. The Npc ChatTurn calls would also work as emplace, but the brace-init form is more readable. This is what the modern advice means in practice: your default is fine.

4. Often confused with...

emplace_back vs push_back (the headline)

 push_backemplace_back
Signaturevoid push_back(const T&) + rvalue overloadtemplate<class... Args> void emplace_back(Args&&... args)
TakesAn object of type TConstructor arguments forwarded to T
How element is createdCopy/move the argumentConstruct in place from args
Explicit ctorsRefuses (compile error)Invokes (silent)
Best whenYou have an existing object (the common case)You'd build a temp purely to append it
ReadabilityHigher (type is explicit at call site)Lower (call site shows only args; type is hidden in vector<T> declaration)

emplace_back vs push_back(std::move(x))

These are sometimes presented as identical. They're not. emplace_back(x) forwards x to a one-argument constructor of T — might be a copy constructor, a move constructor, or some other converting constructor that happens to match. push_back(std::move(x)) is concrete: it calls the rvalue-reference overload and the move constructor. The latter expresses intent more clearly when moving an existing object is what you mean.

emplace_back vs make_X functions

Some libraries have factory functions (make_pair, make_tuple, make_unique). These construct and return an object — you'd then push_back the result. emplace_back skips the make step by constructing directly. For std::unique_ptr specifically, vec.emplace_back(std::make_unique<T>(...)) is the standard pattern because unique_ptr isn't copyable; you have to either move it in (push_back(make_unique...)) or emplace it. Both work.

The Abseil/Chromium guidance vs the older "always emplace" advice

Pre-2015 advice was "emplace_back can skip a move, so prefer it." That advice predates the language's full move-semantics maturity and modern compilers' RVO/copy-elision. The current consensus among industry style guides (Abseil, Chromium, Google C++ Style) is the inverse: prefer push_back; reach for emplace_back when you have a specific reason. If you read an older tutorial, calibrate accordingly.

emplace_back vs emplace (with no _back)

Different operation. emplace_back is vector/deque-specific and adds at the end. emplace on std::vector takes an iterator and inserts in the middle (O(n) for vector). emplace on std::map/std::set inserts into the tree. Different containers, different return types — don't conflate the names.

5. Quiz

Look at replies_.push_back(std::move(reply)); in LlmClient.cpp. If you change it to replies_.emplace_back(std::move(reply));, what happens at runtime?

  • emplace_back avoids the move constructor and is meaningfully faster here.
  • Identical behaviour — both forms end up calling ChatReply's move constructor. push_back is clearer for an existing object.
  • emplace_back resets reply.id to zero as a side effect.
  • It fails to compile on older compilers because emplace_back requires C++23.

You define struct Bytes { explicit Bytes(size_t n) : count(n) {} size_t count; }; and write std::vector<Bytes> bufs; bufs.emplace_back(1024);. A teammate "improves" the code to bufs.push_back(1024);. What happens?

  • The push_back version compiles and is faster.
  • Compile error on the push_back line — Bytes's constructor is explicit, so 1024 won't implicitly convert. emplace_back was correct.
  • Both compile and produce a Bytes with count == 1024.
  • Both compile; push_back(1024) silently truncates if 1024 is larger than what size_t holds.

A "modern C++ tutorial" written in 2019 says "always prefer emplace_back — it's faster and idiomatic." What's the most accurate critique in 2026?

  • It's outdated; emplace_back was deprecated in C++23.
  • The advice is out of date. Current style guides prefer push_back as the default; emplace_back can bypass explicit constructors and hide types at the call site.
  • It's wrong because C++23 changed emplace_back to make a copy first.
  • Compilers now emit a warning when you write emplace_back.

Look at the racing game's pts.push_back(sf::Vector2f(cx + std::cos(a) * r, cy + std::sin(a) * r));. Of the rewrites below, which is the only one that compiles and means the same thing?

  • pts.emplace_back(sf::Vector2f(cx + ..., cy + ...));
  • pts.emplace_back(cx + std::cos(a) * r, cy + std::sin(a) * r);
  • pts.back() = sf::Vector2f(cx + ..., cy + ...);
  • pts.reserve(pts.size() + 1); pts[pts.size()] = sf::Vector2f(cx + ..., cy + ...);

You have a vector of std::unique_ptr<Backend>. Which line adds a new OllamaBackend to it?

  • backends.push_back(std::unique_ptr<Backend>(new OllamaBackend(host, port, model)));
  • backends.push_back(std::make_unique<OllamaBackend>(host, port, model));
  • backends.emplace_back(host, port, model);
  • backends[0] = std::make_unique<OllamaBackend>(host, port, model);

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. The racing game's pts.push_back(sf::Vector2f(...)) would be equally valid as pts.emplace_back(...). Pick the one you'd prefer for new code in this codebase and defend it in two sentences. (There's no objectively right answer — the point is the reasoning.)

Scenario B. Imagine you're refactoring Npc::onReplyArrived to use emplace_back instead of push_back({"user", std::move(line)}). Rewrite the two relevant lines. Then identify one tiny thing that becomes less clear in the emplace version. (Hint: where is the type "ChatTurn" mentioned now?)

Scenario C. You define struct Damage { explicit Damage(float v) : value(v) {} float value; }; and write code like damages.emplace_back(player.health * 0.1f);. Six months later a teammate accidentally writes damages.emplace_back(3); — an int, not a float, meant as "3 hits worth." Walk through what would have happened with push_back(Damage(3)), and explain why a push_back-by-default style would have caught the bug earlier.

7. Track your progress

Further reading — Abseil Tip #112 — emplace vs. push_back · Arthur O'Dwyer — Don't blindly prefer emplace_back · Chromium PSA — prefer push_back unless you know you need emplace · cppreference: std::vector::emplace_back

  • The advice is out of date. Current style guides prefer push_back as the default; emplace_back can bypass explicit constructors and hide types at the call site.
  • It's wrong because C++23 changed emplace_back to make a copy first.
  • Compilers now emit a warning when you write emplace_back.

Look at the racing game's pts.push_back(sf::Vector2f(cx + std::cos(a) * r, cy + std::sin(a) * r));. Of the rewrites below, which is the only one that compiles and means the same thing?

  • pts.emplace_back(sf::Vector2f(cx + ..., cy + ...));
  • pts.emplace_back(cx + std::cos(a) * r, cy + std::sin(a) * r);
  • pts.back() = sf::Vector2f(cx + ..., cy + ...);
  • pts.reserve(pts.size() + 1); pts[pts.size()] = sf::Vector2f(cx + ..., cy + ...);

You have a vector of std::unique_ptr<Backend>. Which line adds a new OllamaBackend to it?

  • backends.push_back(std::unique_ptr<Backend>(new OllamaBackend(host, port, model)));
  • backends.push_back(std::make_unique<OllamaBackend>(host, port, model));
  • backends.emplace_back(host, port, model);
  • backends[0] = std::make_unique<OllamaBackend>(host, port, model);

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. The racing game's pts.push_back(sf::Vector2f(...)) would be equally valid as pts.emplace_back(...). Pick the one you'd prefer for new code in this codebase and defend it in two sentences. (There's no objectively right answer — the point is the reasoning.)

Scenario B. Imagine you're refactoring Npc::onReplyArrived to use emplace_back instead of push_back({"user", std::move(line)}). Rewrite the two relevant lines. Then identify one tiny thing that becomes less clear in the emplace version. (Hint: where is the type "ChatTurn" mentioned now?)

Scenario C. You define struct Damage { explicit Damage(float v) : value(v) {} float value; }; and write code like damages.emplace_back(player.health * 0.1f);. Six months later a teammate accidentally writes damages.emplace_back(3); — an int, not a float, meant as "3 hits worth." Walk through what would have happened with push_back(Damage(3)), and explain why a push_back-by-default style would have caught the bug earlier.

7. Track your progress

## What's in lesson 0012

The headline is the inverted 2026 consensus: **prefer `push_back` by default**, not `emplace_back`. Online tutorials still teach the older "always emplace_back" advice, and following it has a real safety cost.

- **§2 Three-pattern example** — the same operation in three shapes:
  - (A) Existing object → `push_back` is obvious.
  - (B) Building a new one inline → both work; for modern movable types, the difference is unmeasurable.
  - (C) **The dangerous case**: a `struct Capacity { explicit Capacity(int) ... };` where `emplace_back(42)` silently compiles and `push_back(42)` correctly refuses. Red callout: *the explicit-constructor gotcha*.
- **§3 In your project** — **audit of every push_back in your repo**:
  - "Could be emplace" (Npc.cpp brace-init, racing's `sf::Vector2f` temp) — equivalent in practice.

- **§4 Often confused with** — five contrasts including:
  - `emplace_back` vs `push_back(std::move(x))` (subtly different semantics).
  - `emplace_back` vs `make_X` factories (the `std::make_unique` interaction).

This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of C++ standards and compiler support:

## C++ Standards Overview

The latest standard version was ratified and published by ISO in October 2024 as ISO/IEC 14882:2024 (C++23), with C++29 as the next planned standard on a three-year release schedule.

## Key Features by Standard

**C++11:** GCC 4.8.1 was the first feature-complete implementation of the 2011 C++ standard.

**C++14:** C++14 was released as a small extension to C++11, featuring mainly bug fixes and small improvements.

**C++17:** A major revision C++17 was completed by the ISO C++ committee in mid July 2017 and was approved and published in December 2017.

**C++20:** C++20 introduced major features including concepts, modules, and coroutines.

**C++23:** C++23 added the named standard library modules std and std.compat.

## Compiler Support

**GCC:** C++23 features are available since GCC 11. C++26 features are available since GCC 14. To enable C++26 support, add the command-line parameter -std=c++26.

**Clang:** Clang has partial C++20 support that can be enabled with the option -std=c++20 (version 10 and later) or -std=c++2a (version 9 and earlier).

**MSVC:** MSVC achieved full C++17 conformance in Visual Studio 2017 15.7. C++23 support is under active development. As of MSVC Build Tools 14.50 (VS 2026 18.0), C++23 features are supported.

Quiz: 0 / 0
Lesson 0013 · cpp_games / docs / learning

A tour of C++11 / 14 / 17 / 20 / 23

Why this matters: your CMakeLists pin CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17. That number is doing real work — it decides which features you can use. Across the twelve lessons so far you've touched features from every standard from C++11 to C++20. This is the map that tells you which version gave you what, and what bumping the number would unlock.

1. The concept — C++ has a release train

Since 2011, ISO C++ releases on a three-year cadence: C++11, C++14, C++17, C++20, C++23, with C++26 in progress. Each release adds language features and library functions; older code keeps working. The number you set in your build system (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD, -std=c++17) controls which features the compiler will accept.

C++11 (2011)

Theme: "modern C++" begins.

  • auto, lambdas
  • range-for
  • nullptr
  • move semantics
  • smart pointers
  • <thread>, <atomic>
  • enum class

C++14 (2014)

Theme: polishing C++11.

  • std::make_unique
  • generic lambdas (auto params)
  • variable templates
  • binary/digit literals

C++17 (2017)

Theme: "comfortable" modern C++.

  • structured bindings
  • if constexpr
  • std::optional/variant
  • std::string_view
  • std::filesystem
  • [[nodiscard]]
  • CTAD

C++20 (2020)

Theme: language overhaul.

  • concepts
  • ranges
  • modules
  • coroutines
  • std::span
  • std::jthread
  • semaphores
  • <=> spaceship
  • designated initializers

C++23 (2024)

Theme: the long tail.

  • std::expected
  • std::print/println
  • std::flat_map/set
  • std::mdspan
  • <stacktrace>
  • if consteval

The mental model

C++11 is where "modern C++" begins; if you have that, you have 80% of what you write day-to-day. C++17 fills in usability gaps. C++20 is the next big language overhaul. C++23 is incremental but useful (especially std::expected and std::print).

2. A minimal example — the same loop, four ways

Read the same idea evolving across versions to feel how each one cleans the language up.

// C++03 (pre-modern): verbose, manual iterator types.
std::vector<std::string> names;
names.push_back("alice");
for (std::vector<std::string>::iterator it = names.begin();
     it != names.end(); ++it) {
    std::cout << *it << "\n";
}

// C++11: auto + range-for + initializer list = legible.
std::vector<std::string> names = {"alice", "bob"};
for (const auto& n : names) std::cout << n << "\n";

// C++17: structured bindings make iterating maps clean.
std::unordered_map<std::string, int> counts = {{"alice", 1}};
for (const auto& [name, count] : counts) {
    std::cout << name << ": " << count << "\n";
}

// C++23: std::print replaces <iostream> for many cases.
std::print("{}: {}\n", name, count);  // type-safe, no <<, no manual newlines

Every C++03 line still compiles in C++23. The new versions don't remove anything (mostly); they give you cleaner ways to express the same intent.

3. In your project — every feature you use, audited by standard

Your codebase is on CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17. Here's what each standard gave you of what's actually in your source.

StandardFeature you useWhere in your code
C++11 auto, range-for Everywhere — e.g. for (auto& projectile : game.projectiles) in the shooter
C++11 Lambdas LlmClient::workerLoop — requestCv_.wait(lock, [this] { return ... })
C++11 Brace initialization Vec3{0.0f, 2.5f, 0.0f} in shooter, {"user", std::move(line)} in Npc.cpp
C++11 Move semantics + std::move LlmClient::submit, drainReplies, your whole "by-value+std::move" pattern (lesson 0003)
C++11 std::unique_ptr / std::shared_ptr Lesson-0007 refactor's unique_ptr<LlmBackend> (lesson 0010)
C++11 std::thread, std::mutex, std::condition_variable, std::atomic LlmClient — the whole concurrency layer from lesson 0005
C++11 std::array, std::unordered_map Racing's quad corners + matrix, both games' config readers (lessons 0002, 0008)
C++11 override, final In the proposed HAL refactor (lesson 0007)
C++11 enum class TranscriptLine::Kind in DialogUI.hpp
C++14 std::make_unique Lesson-0007 refactor: std::make_unique<OllamaBackend>(...)
C++14 Generic lambdas ([](auto& x)) Used implicitly in the shooter's erase-remove lambdas
C++17 std::filesystem cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp — fs::path, fs::exists, fs::current_path
C++17 std::optional Npc::onReplyArrived returns std::optional<std::string>
C++17 Nested namespace syntax You could write namespace llm_npc nested if needed (you currently don't)
C++17 Structured bindings (potential) You could iterate kv map with for (auto& [key, value] : kv) — currently using .first/.second

What bumping to C++20 would give you

If you change CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17 to 20, these become available:

FeatureWhat it'd buy you
std::jthreadAuto-joining thread. Your LlmClient destructor wouldn't need the explicit join() — jthread's destructor does it.
std::counting_semaphore / std::binary_semaphoreLesson 0011's hypothetical GPU rate-limiter would actually be writable in standard C++.
std::span<T>Non-owning view over a contiguous range. Cleaner function signatures than const std::vector<T>& when you don't care if the source is a vector or array.
Designated initializersPersona{.name = "Wren", .role = "..."} — brace-init that names the fields. Catches misordered arguments at compile time.
Three-way operator<=>Define one comparison operator and get all six. Useful when you add ordered NPC types.
ConceptsConstrain template parameters (template <Integer T>). Better error messages, expresses intent.

What bumping to C++23 would give you

FeatureWhat it'd buy you
std::print / std::printlnType-safe formatted output without <iostream>. Cleaner than streams, faster than printf, and you don't have to repeatedly type std::cout << ... << "\n".
std::expected<T, E>ChatReply could be std::expected<std::string, std::string> — "either a reply or an error" in one type instead of the ok/content/errorMessage trio.
std::flat_mapMap with vector-of-pairs storage — cache-friendly for small maps. Faster than unordered_map for <100 entries.
<stacktrace>Get the call stack from inside the program. Useful for error messages and crash diagnostics.

Compiler support reality check (mid-2026)

You can bump CMake to 20 today on any reasonably current compiler (GCC 11+, Clang 14+, MSVC 19.30+). C++23 also works on GCC 14+, Clang 17+, and MSVC 2026 Build Tools 18.0+. Your MSYS2 UCRT64 toolchain almost certainly supports both. The headline features (jthread, semaphores, span, expected, print) are all there.

4. Often confused with...

Language standard vs library version

"C++17" refers to both the language (new syntax: structured bindings, if constexpr) and the library (std::optional, std::filesystem). They were standardised together but they're implemented separately: the compiler does the language parts; the standard library implementation (libstdc++, libc++, MSVC STL) does the library parts. Some compiler versions support the language but not the full library yet, or vice versa.

-std=c++17 vs compiler version

-std=c++17 sets the dialect — what the compiler accepts. The compiler version sets how completely that dialect is implemented. GCC 6 will accept -std=c++17 but doesn't fully implement it; GCC 11 does. When something "doesn't compile", the question is which: dialect not enabled, or version too old to have the feature.

"Modern C++"

The phrase is fuzzy. The Bjarne-coined meaning is "C++ written in the C++11 idiom or later": auto, smart pointers, range-for, no manual new/delete. Doesn't necessarily mean C++23. Your code is modern C++ in the original sense even though it's pinned to C++17.

Forward and backward compatibility

Backward compatibility: C++17 code compiles in C++20 mode (almost always). Forward compatibility: C++17 code does not use C++20 features. The standards committee tries hard not to break old code; the corollary is that "old features that aged poorly" stay in the language (e.g. printf, raw new).

Compiler-specific extensions vs standard features

GCC and Clang offer extensions that aren't standard C++ — nested functions, variable-length arrays, designated initializers (which became standard in C++20). If you write code that uses an extension without realising, you may be locked to that compiler. The -pedantic flag tells GCC/Clang to warn about extensions; CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF in your CMakeLists.txt does the equivalent — you have this set, which is why your code is portable.

5. Quiz

Your CMakeLists.txt has set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17). You write std::span<int> v in a new file. What happens?

  • Compiles fine — std::span is a C++17 feature.
  • Compile error — std::span is C++20; you need to bump CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD to 20.
  • Compiles and works — the compiler automatically detects you need C++20.
  • Compiles, but crashes at runtime on the first access.

Which of these is the oldest standard that gave you the syntax for (const auto& x : container)?

  • C++03 — range-for has been there since the beginning.
  • C++11 — range-for was a headline 'modern C++' feature.
  • C++14 — introduced as part of C++14's quality-of-life pass.
  • C++17 — came with structured bindings.

The lesson 0007 refactor uses std::make_unique<OllamaBackend>(host, port, model). The user's CMake is on C++17. Which earlier standard introduced this function (and when would you not be able to use it)?

  • C++11 — alongside std::unique_ptr itself.
  • C++14 — make_unique was famously omitted from C++11 and added later.
  • C++17 — came with the smart-pointer overhaul.
  • C++20 — alongside std::span.

Your cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp uses fs::path, fs::exists, fs::current_path. Which standard first made these portable across compilers?

  • C++03 — the standard library has always shipped a filesystem API.
  • C++11 — alongside std::thread.
  • C++17 — std::filesystem finalised the long-running TS.
  • C++20 — along with std::span and concepts.

A teammate says "let's add std::expected to ChatReply; it'd clean up the ok/errorMessage pair." You agree the design is nicer. What's the one change to make this concretely possible in your code?

  • Vendor a header-only tl::expected — no compiler change needed.
  • Bump CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD from 17 to 23 (and check the toolchain supports it).
  • Switch the include to <experimental/expected>, since the type isn't yet standardised.
  • Pass -fstdlib-extensions to the compiler to opt in.

6. Check your understanding (scenario)

Scenario A. You bump CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD from 17 to 20 in cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/CMakeLists.txt. Name two concrete features in lesson 0011 (the semaphores lesson) that go from "hypothetical, can't write in real code" to "now writable as a one-line change." Then name one change in lesson 0005's code that std::jthread would simplify.

Scenario B. A teammate writes auto [key, value] : kv in the racing game's config reader. The CMake says CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17. The PR compiles for them on Windows but fails for you on Linux. Two distinct possible causes that have nothing to do with the language standard — both have to do with the distinction in §4.

Scenario C. You're considering bumping to C++23 to use std::print across your three games. What's the case against? Think about contributors, CI machines, and the C++17-era libraries you depend on (SFML, cpp-httplib, nlohmann/json). One paragraph.

7. Track your progress

Further reading — cppreference: compiler support tables · GCC C++ standards status · Calandra: modern C++ features cheatsheet · Wikipedia: C++20

## What's in lesson 0013

- **§3 In your project**:
  - **Audit table with colored badges** — every C++ feature you actually use, tagged by which standard introduced it. Covers `auto`/range-for/lambdas/move/atomic/thread/array/unordered_map (C++11), `make_unique` (C++14), `std::filesystem`/`std::optional` (C++17).

This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.

# Plan: LLM-Powered NPC Companion Game

## Context

You have two completed C++ games (`cpp_shooter_game/`, `cpp_racing_game/`) and an empty `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/` directory waiting for content. The goal of this third project is a small game where the player can hold a conversation with NPCs whose dialogue is generated by a **single local LLM**, shared across every NPC. Each NPC contributes only a persona prompt and its own short conversation history; the LLM does the talking.

The first milestone is intentionally tiny: a single **companion** NPC you can chat with via a text box. Storyline, world, and other NPC personas come later, once the dialogue loop feels good.

Key constraints from our discussion:
- **Hardware:** 6GB+ NVIDIA VRAM — comfortable up to ~7-8B parameter models at 4-bit quantization.
- **Integration:** Start with **Ollama as a sidecar** (HTTP on localhost), plan a future migration to embedded `llama.cpp` once the design stabilizes.
- **Platform:** **Cross-platform from day one** (Linux + Windows). The existing games are MSYS2/Windows only, so this is a deliberate departure — we'll keep build scripts and paths portable.
- **No new dependencies** in the existing two games. All new deps live under `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/`.

---

## LLM choice

### Recommended starting model: **Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct** (`qwen2.5:3b-instruct`)
- ~2 GB on disk at Q4_K_M, ~3 GB VRAM at runtime — leaves plenty of headroom.
- Strong instruction-following at small size; good at staying in a persona when given a clear system prompt.
- Fast on a 6GB GPU (30+ tokens/sec typical), so replies feel snappy.
- Permissive license (Apache 2.0–compatible terms for the open weights).

### Honorable mentions (try after Qwen feels limiting)
- **Llama 3.2 3B Instruct** (`llama3.2:3b-instruct`) — comparable size, slightly different writing style. Easy A/B swap.
- **Nous Hermes 3 8B** (`hermes3:8b`) — 8B Llama-3.1 fine-tune explicitly tuned for roleplay and persona consistency. Fits your VRAM at Q4_K_M (~5 GB). This is the upgrade target once you want richer characters.
- **Phi-3.5 Mini 3.8B** (`phi3.5:3.8b-mini-instruct`) — Microsoft's small model; strong reasoning but somewhat stiffer dialogue. Worth trying for contrast.

What we are **not** picking and why:
- Anything under 1B (TinyLlama, SmolLM) — too prone to breaking character mid-reply.
- 13B+ models — overkill for "blacksmith small talk," and slower iteration during development.

### Why a sidecar via Ollama (for now)
- One install (`curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh` on Linux, installer on Windows) gives you model download, quantization, GPU acceleration, and a stable HTTP API.
- `ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct` is the entire "get the model" step.
- The C++ game just needs an HTTP client — no CMake gymnastics for CUDA/CMake/llama.cpp yet.
- You can swap models with one config line, with no rebuild.
- Migration path to embedded `llama.cpp` later is clean because the `LlmClient` interface will hide the transport.

---

## Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────────┐
│  cpp_game_with_llm_npcs      │  HTTP   │  Ollama (sidecar)      │
│  (SFML + OpenGL)             │ ──────► │  qwen2.5:3b-instruct   │
│                              │  JSON   │  localhost:11434       │
│  ┌────────────────────────┐  │         └────────────────────────┘
│  │ LlmClient (singleton)  │  │
│  │  - async request queue │  │
│  │  - HTTP via cpp-httplib│  │
│  └─────────▲──────────────┘  │
│            │                 │
│  ┌─────────┴──────────────┐  │
│  │ Npc                    │  │
│  │  - Persona (system     │  │
│  │    prompt template)    │  │
│  │  - ConversationHistory │  │
│  │  - askAsync(playerLine)│  │
│  └─────────▲──────────────┘  │
│            │                 │
│  ┌─────────┴──────────────┐  │
│  │ DialogUI (SFML)        │  │
│  │  - text input          │  │
│  │  - scrolling transcript│  │
│  │  - "thinking..." state │  │
│  └────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────┘
```

### Key design points
- **One `LlmClient` for the whole game.** NPCs don't each open their own connection — they all call `LlmClient::chat(personaSystemPrompt, history, userMsg, onReply)`. This matches your "centralized" intent.
- **Async by default.** The game loop never blocks on an LLM call. We use a worker thread + a thread-safe reply queue drained on the main thread (SFML is single-threaded for rendering).
- **Per-NPC history, capped.** Each `Npc` keeps its own conversation as a `vector<Turn>`. We cap it to N most-recent turns (e.g. 10) and prepend the persona system prompt every request. Simple, predictable token usage.
- **Persona template, not hardcoded NPCs.** `Persona { name, role, traits, speakingStyle, knowledgeBoundaries }` rendered into a system prompt string at construction. "Jim the pharmacist" and "Jane the random pedestrian #47" are two `Npc` instances built from the same template — exactly what you described.
- **Streaming optional.** Ollama supports streaming token-by-token; for the first milestone we ignore it and just wait for the full reply (simpler). Add streaming later if reply latency feels long.

---

## New C++ dependencies (only inside `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/`)

All header-only / vendored to keep cross-platform builds easy. No package manager required.

| Dep | Why | How to add |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **cpp-httplib** | Single-header HTTPS/HTTP client. POST to Ollama. | Vendor `httplib.h` into `external/` |
| **nlohmann/json** | Build/parse Ollama JSON requests and responses. | Vendor `json.hpp` into `external/` |
| **SFML 2.6** | Already used by the other games; reuse for window + text UI. | Same install path as existing games (apt / brew / vcpkg) |

No new runtime libs beyond what SFML already pulls in. Cross-platform "just works" because both vendored libs are header-only.

---

## Proposed directory layout

```
cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── README.md
├── config/
│   └── llm.cfg                 # ollama host, model name, temperature, max tokens
├── external/
│   ├── httplib.h
│   └── json.hpp
├── personas/
│   └── companion.txt           # system prompt template for the first NPC
├── src/
│   ├── main.cpp                # window + game loop + DialogUI glue
│   ├── LlmClient.hpp/.cpp      # HTTP + async queue
│   ├── Npc.hpp/.cpp            # persona + history + askAsync
│   ├── Persona.hpp             # struct + prompt renderer
│   └── DialogUI.hpp/.cpp       # SFML text box + transcript
└── run.sh / run.ps1            # cross-platform launch scripts
```

This mirrors the single-folder-per-game pattern of the other two but adds `src/` subfiles (the other games are single-file; we need more structure here because the LLM glue earns its own modules).

---

## First milestone: "the companion"

A vertical slice you can run end-to-end:

1. **Window** — single SFML window, 1280×720, dark background.
2. **The companion** — one `Npc` loaded from `personas/companion.txt`. Suggested starting persona: a curious traveling companion who knows nothing about real-world topics but lots about the (yet-undefined) game world. Keeps replies short (1-3 sentences).
3. **Dialog UI** — bottom-of-screen text input, scrolling transcript above. Press Enter to send; UI shows "*\<Companion\> is thinking...*" while the LLM call is in flight.
4. **Centralized client** — even with one NPC, the `LlmClient` is built as a singleton from day one so adding NPC #2, #3, etc. requires no refactor.
5. **No game world yet** — no 3D, no movement, no combat. Just the chat. This proves the dialogue loop in isolation before you wire it into anything more ambitious.

---

## Files to create (representative — not exhaustive)

- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/CMakeLists.txt` — finds SFML, adds `src/*.cpp`, includes `external/`. Same CMake 3.20+ baseline as your other games.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.hpp/.cpp` — public interface `chat(systemPrompt, history, userMsg, callback)`; internal worker thread and `std::queue<Reply>` drained from main thread.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Persona.hpp` — struct + `renderSystemPrompt()` that produces the final string Ollama receives.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Npc.hpp/.cpp` — owns a `Persona` and a bounded `vector<Turn>`; exposes `askAsync(playerLine, onReply)`.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/DialogUI.hpp/.cpp` — SFML text input + transcript rendering + "thinking" indicator.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp` — wires it all together; ~150 lines.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/config/llm.cfg` — key/value (same style as racing game's `track.cfg`): `host=localhost`, `port=11434`, `model=qwen2.5:3b-instruct`, `temperature=0.8`, `max_history_turns=10`.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/personas/companion.txt` — plain-text system prompt template.
- `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/run.sh` and `run.ps1` — cross-platform launchers (check Ollama is running, build, run).

---

## Setup steps the user runs once

1. **Install Ollama** — Linux: `curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh`. Windows: installer from ollama.com.
2. **Pull the model** — `ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct` (~2 GB download).
3. **Confirm it runs** — `ollama run qwen2.5:3b-instruct "say hi"` should reply in a couple of seconds with GPU usage visible in `nvidia-smi`.
4. **Install SFML 2.6** — Linux: `sudo apt install libsfml-dev` (or distro equivalent). Windows: keep the existing MSYS2 path.
5. **Build** — `cmake -S cpp_game_with_llm_npcs -B cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/build && cmake --build cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/build`.
6. **Run** — `./cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/run.sh` (Ollama must be running; the script checks).

---

## Verification (manual test plan for milestone 1)

- `ollama list` shows `qwen2.5:3b-instruct`.
- `curl http://localhost:11434/api/chat -d '{"model":"qwen2.5:3b-instruct","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"stream":false}'` returns a JSON reply with a non-empty `message.content`.
- Game window opens, shows transcript area and input box.
- Typing "hi" and pressing Enter shows the user line in the transcript, then "*Companion is thinking...*", then the reply within a few seconds.
- The reply respects the persona (e.g., refuses to answer real-world questions in character; stays short).
- Sending 15+ messages exercises the history cap — no crash, no slowdown beyond steady state.
- Killing Ollama mid-game produces a graceful in-transcript error like *"\[Companion seems distracted...\]"* rather than a crash.
- Build runs cleanly on at least one Linux box (since cross-platform is a stated goal — if Windows is the only available test target, note that as a follow-up).

---

## Future work (explicitly out of scope for milestone 1)

- **Embed llama.cpp** — once dialogue feels right, swap `LlmClient`'s implementation from cpp-httplib → llama.cpp's C API. The public interface stays the same; only `LlmClient.cpp` changes.
- **Streaming replies** — show tokens as they arrive for a less "frozen" feel.
- **Multiple NPCs in a world** — the architecture already supports this; just instantiate more `Npc`s and add a way to choose who you're talking to (proximity, click, etc.).
- **Persistent memory** — write `vector<Turn>` per NPC to disk between sessions.
- **Game world** — once chat is fun on its own, layer it onto a 3D or 2D world (potentially borrowing rendering patterns from the shooter game).

The user wants to learn "functions" (or, if blank, you choose the most valuable concept to teach next based on their progress and this project's code). This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.
