Lesson 0012 · cpp_games / docs / learning
158

emplace_back vs. push_back

159

Why this matters: your code uses push_back in 20+ places and emplace_back in zero. Online lore says "always prefer emplace_back — it's faster." That lore is wrong in 2026, and reaching for it without understanding has a real safety cost. This lesson is the rule for picking right.

160
161 162

1. The concept — one constructs, the other appends

163 164

Both add a new element to the end of a vector. The difference is how the element gets there.

165 166
    167
  • push_back(t) takes an already-existing T (or something implicitly convertible) and copies or moves it into the vector's storage. The function signature is concrete: void push_back(const T&) and void push_back(T&&).
    • 168
  • emplace_back(args...) takes any number of constructor arguments and forwards them — perfectly — to T's constructor, building the object directly inside the vector's storage. No temporary is built, no copy or move happens.
    • 169
170 171

The visual step-by-step

172 173
push_back(std::string("hello")) emplace_back("hello") 174 ──────────────────────────── ────────────────────── 175 1. construct temp std::string("hello") 1. forward "hello" as constructor arg 176 on the stack no temp built 177 2. push_back moves it into vector storage 2. emplace_back constructs std::string 178 (move constructor runs) directly into vector storage 179 3. destroy the temp 3. ... that's it. 180 181 Two constructions + one move. One construction. No move.
182 183

That sounds like a clear win for emplace_back. The reality in 2026 is more nuanced: for modern types with cheap move constructors (basically everything in your code), the difference is invisible. The cost of "construct then move" a std::string is ~5 ns. You can't measure it from a game loop.

184 185
186

The modern rule of thumb

187

Prefer push_back by default. Reach for emplace_back when you have a specific reason: you'd construct a temporary anyway, the type has multiple constructor arguments and you want to forward them in place, or there's no move/copy available. The "always emplace" advice you may have seen is older than the language is now — it predates good move semantics and modern compiler optimisation.

188
189 190

2. Minimal example — three patterns side by side

191 192 
struct ChatTurn { std::string role; std::string content; };
193	
194	std::vector<ChatTurn> history;
195	
196	// (A) "I already have a ChatTurn" — push_back is the obvious choice.
197	ChatTurn t{"user", "hello"};
198	history.push_back(std::move(t));      // move t into the vector. One move.
199	
200	// (B) "I want to build a new one inline from arguments."
201	//     push_back constructs a temp + moves it; emplace_back builds in place.
202	//     For ChatTurn this is unobservable; for types with no cheap move it matters.
203	history.push_back({"user", "hello"});       // build temp, move into vector
204	history.emplace_back("user", "hello");    // build in place
205	
206	// (C) The DANGEROUS case — explicit constructors.
207	struct Capacity { explicit Capacity(int n) : value(n) {} int value; };
208	std::vector<Capacity> caps;

Function-call nuances for low-latency C++

Why this matters: your shooter calls dot() and the Vec3 operators hundreds of times per frame, and DialogUI::render calls wrap() every frame. Whether those calls cost ~0 ns or ~5 ns each is decided by four things you control at the call site: how arguments travel, how the return value travels, how the callable is dispatched, and whether the compiler can inline it. This lesson is those four decisions.

1. What a function call actually costs

When the compiler can't (or won't) inline a call, the machine does real work that has nothing to do with your function's logic:

caller callee ────── ────── 1. place arguments 4. prologue: save registers it - small/trivial args → CPU registers will clobber, set up stack frame - big or non-trivial args → memory 5. ...your actual logic... 2. `call` — push return address, jump 6. epilogue: restore registers (branch predictor must guess right) 7. `ret` — pop address, jump back 3. after return: result arrives in a register (small) or memory (big) Hidden costs: instruction-cache pressure (jumping to cold code), lost optimization across the boundary (the compiler must assume the callee could do anything), register spills around the call.

Two consequences worth internalizing:

  • The call overhead itself is tiny — a handful of cycles, low single-digit nanoseconds. One un-inlined call per frame is nothing against your 16.7 ms budget (lesson 0003).
  • But it multiplies. A 3 ns call inside a loop that runs 10,000 times per frame is 30 µs/frame — and the bigger loss is usually the missed optimization: an inlined dot() lets the compiler keep all six floats in registers and vectorize the surrounding loop; an opaque call forces everything through memory.

Inlining is the whole ballgame

When the compiler inlines a call, steps 1–7 above all disappear — the callee's body is pasted into the caller and optimized as one unit. Most of this lesson is really about not accidentally preventing inlining, and making un-inlinable calls (virtual, std::function, cross-library) cheap to pass through.

The inline keyword does NOT mean "inline this"

Modern compilers ignore inline as an optimization hint. Its real meaning today is about linkage: "this definition may appear in multiple translation units, merge them." That's why functions defined inside headers (like Persona::renderSystemPrompt() in Persona.hpp) are implicitly inline — otherwise including the header twice would break the build. Actual inlining is the optimizer's call, driven by function size, call frequency, and optimization level (-O2).

2. Decision 1 — how arguments travel

This is the choice you make most often. The rule set (matching the C++ Core Guidelines "F" rules) is small:

Parameter situationPass it asWhy
Cheap to copy (a few words: int, float, pointers, small structs like Vec3) By value — f(Vec3 v) Fits in registers. No indirection, no aliasing worries for the optimizer.
Expensive or unknown-size, read only (std::string, std::vector, big structs) const& — f(const std::string& s) One pointer travels instead of a deep copy.
The function will keep the value (store it in a member, push it into a queue) — a "sink" By value, then std::move into place Caller decides: pass an lvalue → one copy; pass a temporary or std::move(x) → zero copies. One signature handles both.
Read-only view of string data that might be a literal, a substring, or a std::string std::string_view (C++17, lesson 0013) 16 bytes by value (pointer + length). No allocation, accepts anything string-shaped.

The nuance: "cheap to copy" beats "avoid the copy"

Beginners overuse const& because "references avoid copies." But for a small trivially-copyable type, the reference is the slow path when the call isn't inlined:

// By value: x, y, z arrive in three registers. The callee reads registers.
float dot(Vec3 a, Vec3 b);

// By const&: a POINTER arrives in a register. The callee must load from
// memory through it — and the optimizer must assume a and b might alias
// (point at) other memory the function touches, blocking reorderings.
float dot(const Vec3& a, const Vec3& b);

The crossover point is roughly "two or three machine words" (~16–24 bytes). Vec3 is 12 bytes of plain floats — squarely in by-value territory. A std::string is 32 bytes plus a possible heap allocation on copy (lesson 0006's SSO) — squarely in const& territory.

Does your shooter get this "wrong"?

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:42-58 passes const Vec3& everywhere. By the table, by-value would be the textbook choice. In practice it makes zero difference here: these operators are tiny, defined in the same file, and called at -O2 — the compiler inlines every one of them, and after inlining, by-value and by-reference compile to identical code. The rule matters at calls the compiler can't see through: across .cpp files without LTO, virtual calls, library boundaries. This is the recurring theme: the guideline picks the better default; inlining usually erases the difference; profile before "fixing" anything.

3. Decision 2 — how the return value travels

Old C++ folklore says "returning big objects by value is slow — they get copied." That's been wrong for years, and since C++17 it's guaranteed wrong in the common case:

  • RVO (mandatory since C++17): return std::string{"hi"}; — returning a temporary constructs the result directly in the caller's storage. No copy, no move. Not an optimization anymore — the standard requires it ("guaranteed copy elision").
  • NRVO (allowed, near-universal): std::string out; ...; return out; — returning a named local usually also builds in place. Not guaranteed, but every major compiler does it when there's a single return object. Worst case: one cheap move.
// DialogUI.cpp:25 — wrap() returns a vector BY VALUE every frame.
// NRVO: `out` is constructed directly in the caller. Returning it is free.
std::vector<std::string> wrap(const std::string& s, std::size_t maxChars) {
    std::vector<std::string> out;
    // ... fill out ...
    return out;   // NRVO — no copy of the vector or its strings
}

// ANTI-PATTERN: don't "help" with std::move on a local return —
// it DISABLES NRVO and forces an actual move. Compilers warn about this.
return std::move(out);   // pessimization, never do this for locals

So return by value, plainly. The out-parameter style (void wrap(const std::string&, std::vector<std::string>& out)) only wins when the caller can reuse one buffer across calls to avoid repeated allocation — which is exactly the deferred DialogUI::render fix from lesson 0003, and a profiling decision, not a default.

4. Decision 3 — how the callable is dispatched

"Call a function" can mean four mechanically different things. Sorted from transparent to opaque:

MechanismDispatchInlinable?You use it in
Direct call / lambda passed to a template Resolved at compile time; the lambda's exact type is baked into the instantiation Yes — usually fully std::remove_if(..., [](const Projectile& p){...}) — shooter main.cpp:686
Function pointer Indirect jump through a pointer Only if the compiler can prove which function it points to (none currently — C-style callbacks, e.g. GLFW APIs)
Virtual call Load vptr → load vtable slot → indirect jump (lesson 0007) Only with devirtualization (compiler proves the dynamic type) The HAL design from lesson 0007
std::function Type erasure: indirect call through an internal pointer, + possible heap allocation to store a large captured lambda Practically no (none currently — and that's good for hot paths)

The big trap is std::function. It's wonderfully flexible — it can hold any callable with a matching signature — and that flexibility is bought with type erasure: the concrete callable's type is hidden behind an indirect call, and if the captures don't fit in the small internal buffer (typically ~2–3 words), it heap-allocates. Compare:

// (A) Template parameter — the shooter's actual pattern. Zero overhead:
// remove_if is stamped out for THIS lambda; the body inlines.
game.projectiles.erase(
    std::remove_if(game.projectiles.begin(), game.projectiles.end(),
                   [](const Projectile& p) { return p.lifetime <= 0.0f; }),
    game.projectiles.end());

// (B) Same logic through std::function — type-erased, indirect call per
// element, possible allocation when constructed. Fine for "call once per
// click", wasteful for "call per projectile per frame".
std::function<bool(const Projectile&)> pred =
    [](const Projectile& p) { return p.lifetime <= 0.0f; };
game.projectiles.erase(
    std::remove_if(game.projectiles.begin(), game.projectiles.end(), pred),
    game.projectiles.end());

Rule: in hot paths, take callables as template parameters (like the STL does) or call them directly. Reserve std::function for places that genuinely need to store heterogeneous callbacks — UI event tables, a reply-callback registry — where the call happens rarely.

5. Decision 4 — hints that unlock optimization

  • noexcept — promises "this never throws." Two payoffs: the compiler drops exception-path bookkeeping around calls, and (the big one, from lesson 0012's world) std::vector only moves elements during reallocation if the move constructor is noexcept — otherwise it copies to stay exception-safe. Your structs get noexcept moves implicitly; hand-written move constructors must say it explicitly.
  • constexpr — "callable at compile time." Your kPadding/kLineHeight constants (DialogUI.cpp:9-12) are constexpr values; a constexpr function with constant arguments costs zero at runtime because the answer is computed during compilation.
  • static / anonymous namespace — internal linkage (your colorFor() and wrap() live in an anonymous namespace in DialogUI.cpp). The compiler can see every caller, so it inlines aggressively and may delete the standalone function entirely.
  • [[likely]] / [[unlikely]] (C++20, lesson 0013) — tells the compiler which branch to lay out as the fall-through hot path. Use sparingly and only with evidence; mispredicting yourself is worse than letting the compiler guess.

6. In this project

The sink parameter, done right

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:23-34 
std::uint64_t LlmClient::submit(std::string systemPrompt,          // by VALUE
                                std::vector<ChatTurn> history,     // by VALUE
                                std::string userMessage) {         // by VALUE
    ChatRequest req;
    req.systemPrompt = std::move(systemPrompt);   // steal, don't copy
    req.history     = std::move(history);
    req.userMessage  = std::move(userMessage);
    ...
    requests_.push(std::move(req));               // move all the way in
}

submit() keeps everything it's given — it's a sink. By-value + std::move means: a caller passing a temporary pays zero copies (the temporary is moved into the parameter, then moved into the queue); a caller passing a variable it still needs pays exactly one copy (into the parameter), then moves. A const& signature would force a copy in both cases. Latency-wise this also matters for the right reason: the copy/move happens on the main thread before queuing, so the worker thread never touches caller-owned memory — passing by reference here wouldn't just be slower to reason about, it would be a use-after-free waiting to happen (lesson 0005).

The read-only heavyweight

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/DialogUI.cpp:25 
std::vector<std::string> wrap(const std::string& s, std::size_t maxChars)

Textbook row 2: s is big and only read → const&. And row "size_t": maxChars is one machine word → by value. Note the upgrade path: std::string_view s would also accept literals and substrings without allocating — but the caller at line 134 builds prefix + line.text (a fresh std::string) anyway, so string_view wouldn't remove the per-frame allocation flagged in lesson 0003. Fixing the caller is the profiling-gated work; changing the signature alone is cosmetic.

The lambda the compiler eats for free

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/DialogUI.cpp:29-41 · cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:686 
auto flushWord = [&]() {            // captures by reference: out, current,
    if (word.empty()) return;       // word, maxChars — costs 0 to create
    ...
};

flushWord is a local lambda called directly — the compiler sees the exact closure type, inlines it, and the "lambda" dissolves into straight-line code. Same story for the remove_if predicates in the shooter: they travel as template parameters, never as std::function. Your codebase already has zero std::function in hot paths — keep it that way.

The return-by-value pair

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Persona.hpp:19 · DialogUI.cpp:64 
std::string renderSystemPrompt() const {   // returns by value — NRVO,
    std::string out; ... return out;       // constructed in caller's slot
}

Both renderSystemPrompt() and wrap() build a named local and return it. NRVO makes the return itself free. No out-parameters needed until a profiler says the repeated allocation inside the function (not the return) is the problem.

7. Often confused

inline keyword vs. actual inlining

inline keywordInlining (the optimization)
What it isA linkage property: "definition may repeat across translation units"The optimizer pasting a callee's body into the caller
Who decidesYou, in sourceThe compiler, at -O2, by cost heuristics
RelationshipAlmost none today. Header-defined functions need inline (or get it implicitly, like methods defined in-class) just to link; whether they're inlined is a separate decision the keyword barely influences.

Pass-by-value vs. pass-by-const&

Share: both give the callee read access to the caller's data. Diverge: by-value copies (registers for small types — fast; deep copy for big types — slow); const& passes a pointer (one word — but adds indirection and aliasing pessimism). Pick: by size and intent — small-and-trivial or sink → value; big-and-read-only → const&.

Lambda vs. std::function

Share: both are "a callable thing you can pass around." Diverge: a lambda is a unique, concrete, compiler-known type (zero-cost when passed to templates); std::function is a type-erasing container that can hold any matching callable, paying an indirect call and possibly a heap allocation for the privilege. A lambda often gets stored in a std::function — that's the moment the cost appears, not when the lambda is written.

8. Quiz

1. dot(const Vec3& a, const Vec3& b) in your shooter uses const& for a 12-byte struct. Why is this not hurting your frame time?

  • const& is always faster than by-value, so it's optimal
  • The compiler inlines these calls, and after inlining the passing convention doesn't exist anymore
  • References have no runtime representation, so they're always free
  • Vec3's small-size optimization keeps it off the heap, making copies free

2. LlmClient::submit takes std::string systemPrompt by value and then does std::move(systemPrompt). A caller passes a string variable it still needs afterward. How many copies of the string data are made?

  • Zero — std::move never copies
  • Two — one into the parameter, one into the queue
  • One — copied into the parameter, then moved the rest of the way
  • It's undefined — the caller's string was moved-from and can't be used

3. wrap() ends with return out; where out is a local std::vector<std::string>. Your teammate "optimizes" it to return std::move(out);. What happened?

  • A genuine speedup — moves are faster than copies
  • A pessimization — it disabled NRVO and forced a real move
  • A compile error — you can't move a local out of a function
  • Undefined behavior — the local is destroyed before the caller reads it

4. You're adding a per-projectile filter that the player can hot-swap at runtime. A teammate proposes storing it as std::function<bool(const Projectile&)> and calling it inside updateProjectiles for every projectile, every frame. What's the honest cost assessment?

  • Zero cost — std::function is a thin wrapper the compiler sees through
  • It heap-allocates on every call, so it will stutter visibly
  • An indirect, non-inlinable call per projectile — probably affordable at this scale, but it's real overhead the template version wouldn't pay
  • It can't store a capturing lambda, so the design doesn't work

5. What does the inline keyword actually guarantee in modern C++?

  • The compiler must paste the function body into every caller
  • Multiple identical definitions across translation units are allowed and merged
  • The function is evaluated at compile time
  • The function cannot throw exceptions

9. Check your understanding — scenarios

Scenario A. You're writing Npc::setPersona(...) — it stores the persona in a member and is called once per NPC at startup. Which signature do you pick: const Persona&, Persona by value + move, or Persona&&? Does "called once at startup" change how much you should care?
Scenario B. Profiling (someday) shows wrap() is hot, and most calls pass a string that already exists unmodified. Walk the upgrade path: what changes first — the const std::string& parameter, the std::vector<std::string> return, or the caller's prefix + line.text concatenation — and why that order?
Scenario C. For the future HAL (lesson 0007), every render call goes through virtual void drawBox(...). A forum post tells you "virtual calls killed our frame rate, devirtualize everything." Using this lesson's cost model (~ns per indirect call, lost inlining), estimate whether ~500 virtual draw calls per frame threatens your 16.7 ms budget, and name the case where virtual dispatch in a loop would actually hurt.

10. Lesson progress

Further reading — C++ Core Guidelines F.16 — pass cheaply-copied types by value · F.15 — conventional parameter passing (incl. sink = by value + move) · cppreference: copy elision (RVO/NRVO) · cppreference: std::function · Agner Fog — software optimization manuals (calling conventions, call cost)

flushWord is a local lambda called directly — the compiler sees the exact closure type, inlines it, and the "lambda" dissolves into straight-line code. Same story for the remove_if predicates in the shooter: they travel as template parameters, never as std::function. Your codebase already has zero std::function in hot paths — keep it that way.

The return-by-value pair

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Persona.hpp:19 · DialogUI.cpp:64 
std::string renderSystemPrompt() const {   // returns by value — NRVO,
    std::string out; ... return out;       // constructed in caller's slot
}

Both renderSystemPrompt() and wrap() build a named local and return it. NRVO makes the return itself free. No out-parameters needed until a profiler says the repeated allocation inside the function (not the return) is the problem.

7. Often confused

inline keyword vs. actual inlining

inline keywordInlining (the optimization)
What it isA linkage property: "definition may repeat across translation units"The optimizer pasting a callee's body into the caller
Who decidesYou, in sourceThe compiler, at -O2, by cost heuristics
RelationshipAlmost none today. Header-defined functions need inline (or get it implicitly, like methods defined in-class) just to link; whether they're inlined is a separate decision the keyword barely influences.

Pass-by-value vs. pass-by-const&

Share: both give the callee read access to the caller's data. Diverge: by-value copies (registers for small types — fast; deep copy for big types — slow); const& passes a pointer (one word — but adds indirection and aliasing pessimism). Pick: by size and intent — small-and-trivial or sink → value; big-and-read-only → const&.

Lambda vs. std::function

Share: both are "a callable thing you can pass around." Diverge: a lambda is a unique, concrete, compiler-known type (zero-cost when passed to templates); std::function is a type-erasing container that can hold any matching callable, paying an indirect call and possibly a heap allocation for the privilege. A lambda often gets stored in a std::function — that's the moment the cost appears, not when the lambda is written.

8. Quiz

1. dot(const Vec3& a, const Vec3& b) in your shooter uses const& for a 12-byte struct. Why is this not hurting your frame time?

  • const& is always faster than by-value, so it's optimal
  • The compiler inlines these calls, and after inlining the passing convention doesn't exist anymore
  • References have no runtime representation, so they're always free
  • Vec3's small-size optimization keeps it off the heap, making copies free

2. LlmClient::submit takes std::string systemPrompt by value and then does std::move(systemPrompt). A caller passes a string variable it still needs afterward. How many copies of the string data are made?

  • Zero — std::move never copies
  • Two — one into the parameter, one into the queue
  • One — copied into the parameter, then moved the rest of the way
  • It's undefined — the caller's string was moved-from and can't be used

3. wrap() ends with return out; where out is a local std::vector<std::string>. Your teammate "optimizes" it to return std::move(out);. What happened?

  • A genuine speedup — moves are faster than copies
  • A pessimization — it disabled NRVO and forced a real move
  • A compile error — you can't move a local out of a function
  • Undefined behavior — the local is destroyed before the caller reads it

4. You're adding a per-projectile filter that the player can hot-swap at runtime. A teammate proposes storing it as std::function<bool(const Projectile&)> and calling it inside updateProjectiles for every projectile, every frame. What's the honest cost assessment?

  • Zero cost — std::function is a thin wrapper the compiler sees through
  • It heap-allocates on every call, so it will stutter visibly
  • An indirect, non-inlinable call per projectile — probably affordable at this scale, but it's real overhead the template version wouldn't pay
  • It can't store a capturing lambda, so the design doesn't work

5. What does the inline keyword actually guarantee in modern C++?

  • The compiler must paste the function body into every caller
  • Multiple identical definitions across translation units are allowed and merged
  • The function is evaluated at compile time
  • The function cannot throw exceptions

9. Check your understanding — scenarios

Scenario A. You're writing Npc::setPersona(...) — it stores the persona in a member and is called once per NPC at startup. Which signature do you pick: const Persona&, Persona by value + move, or Persona&&? Does "called once at startup" change how much you should care?
Scenario B. Profiling (someday) shows wrap() is hot, and most calls pass a string that already exists unmodified. Walk the upgrade path: what changes first — the const std::string& parameter, the std::vector<std::string> return, or the caller's prefix + line.text concatenation — and why that order?
Scenario C. For the future HAL (lesson 0007), every render call goes through virtual void drawBox(...). A forum post tells you "virtual calls killed our frame rate, devirtualize everything." Using this lesson's cost model (~ns per indirect call, lost inlining), estimate whether ~500 virtual draw calls per frame threatens your 16.7 ms budget, and name the case where virtual dispatch in a loop would actually hurt.

10. Lesson progress

Further reading — C++ Core Guidelines F.16 — pass cheaply-copied types by value · F.15 — conventional parameter passing (incl. sink = by value + move) · cppreference: copy elision (RVO/NRVO) · cppreference: std::function · Agner Fog — software optimization manuals (calling conventions, call cost)

Lesson 0014 · docs/learning/lessons/0014-function-call-cost-and-low-latency.html

lastPrompt: /teach nuanced functions calls for cpp low latency efficiency

6	> conversation or aced the quiz item about it.
7	
8	> Status legend:
9	> `taught` = explained in a lesson  ·
10	> `firm` = used correctly unprompted  ·
11	> `shaky` = needs revisit
12	
13	## A
14	
15	- **Abstract class** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
16	  A C++ class containing at least one pure virtual method (`= 0`).
17	  Cannot be instantiated directly; you instantiate derived classes that
18	  implement the pure virtuals. The base of every HAL.
19	
20	- **Abstraction (vs encapsulation)** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
21	  Hiding *which of several implementations* is in use behind one
22	  interface. Distinct from encapsulation, which hides the internals of
23	  *one* class. A HAL is abstraction; private fields are encapsulation.
24	
25	- **Array decay** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
26	  When a C-style array is passed to a function, the parameter is silently
27	  rewritten to a pointer, losing its size. `void f(int arr[10])` becomes
28	  `void f(int* arr)`. `std::array` does not decay.
29	
30	- **ASIC** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
31	  Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. A chip fabricated for one
32	  fixed job (e.g. NVIDIA H100, phone neural engine). Faster and more
33	  efficient than the same design on an FPGA, but unchangeable once
34	  shipped. FPGA is the reprogrammable cousin.
35	
36	## B
37	
38	- **Bitstream** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
39	  The binary file that programs an FPGA. Produced by synthesizing an
40	  HDL/HLS design through place-and-route. Loading a different bitstream
41	  reconfigures the chip into a different circuit.
42	
43	## C
44	
45	- **C++ language standard** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
46	  Three-year-cadence ISO release that defines what features the compiler
47	  accepts. Current standards: C++11/14/17/20/23 (C++26 in progress).
48	  Controlled via `CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD` / `-std=c++17`. Distinct from
49	  compiler version, which controls how completely a standard is
50	  implemented.
51	
52	- **Context switch** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
53	  The OS suspending one thread/process and resuming another on a CPU
54	  core. Thread-to-thread switches in the same process are cheap (~few
55	  thousand ns); process-to-process switches require a TLB flush and are
56	  ~10× more expensive (softened by PCID on modern x86).
57	
58	- **Container adapter** — `taught` *(lesson 0008)*
59	  Thin wrapper around a real container that restricts the exposed API.
60	  `std::queue`/`std::stack`/`std::priority_queue` are adapters. They're
61	  not containers themselves and can't be iterated. Used in `LlmClient`
62	  via `std::queue<ChatRequest> requests_` to document FIFO discipline.
63	
64	- **C-style array** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
65	  Raw `T arr[N]` from C. Fixed size, stack storage, decays to pointer on
66	  function call. Still appears at
67	  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp:72`.
68	
69	- **Condition variable (`std::condition_variable`)** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
70	  Synchronisation primitive that lets a thread sleep cheaply until
71	  another thread signals state change. Always paired with a mutex and a
72	  predicate (`cv.wait(lock, pred)`) so spurious wakeups are handled
73	  automatically. Used at
74	  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:52`.
75	
76	## D
77	
78	- **Deadlock** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
79	  Two threads each holding a lock the other needs; both wait forever.
80	  Cardinal prevention rule: always acquire multiple locks in the same
81	  order. `LlmClient` avoids the risk by never holding both mutexes
82	  simultaneously.
83	
84	## D
85	
86	- **`std::deque`** — `taught` *(lesson 0008)*
87	  Segmented sequence container — array of fixed-size blocks, blocks
88	  themselves separate heap allocations. O(1) push/pop at *both* ends.
89	  Random access is two pointer dereferences (block table, then block).
90	  Used in `DialogUI::transcript_` for the push_back/pop_front pattern.
91	
92	## E
93	
94	- **`emplace_back(args...)`** — `taught` *(lesson 0012)*
95	  Vector member that forwards args to T's constructor, building the
96	  element directly in the vector's storage with no temporary. Invokes
97	  explicit constructors (push_back refuses), which is its main safety
98	  trap. Modern (Chromium/Abseil/Google) advice: prefer `push_back` by
99	  default; reach for `emplace_back` only when you have a specific reason.
100	
101	- **Embedded LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
102	  A language model whose output is consumed by the running game process,
103	  regardless of whether the model lives in the same binary or in a sidecar
104	  process on `localhost`.
105	
106	- **Erase-remove idiom** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
107	  Pattern for deleting elements from a `std::vector` that match a
108	  predicate without shrinking capacity. `v.erase(std::remove_if(b, e,
109	  pred), e)`. Used in `cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:686` to clean up
110	  dead projectiles per frame.
111	
112	## F
113	
114	- **FPGA** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
115	  Field-Programmable Gate Array. A chip whose internal wiring is
116	  reconfigured at boot by loading a bitstream — the chip *becomes* the
117	  custom circuit you described, rather than executing instructions on a
118	  fixed circuit.
119	
120	- **Frame budget** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
121	  The wall-clock time available for one game-loop iteration before the
122	  next vsync. 16.67 ms at 60 Hz, 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. Exceeding it once
123	  produces visible stutter regardless of average speed.
124	
125	## H
126	
127	- **HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer)** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
128	  Software layer that hides "where the work physically happens" behind a
129	  single interface. Arduino's `digitalWrite`, Linux device drivers,
130	  SFML's `window.draw`, and the proposed `LlmBackend` interface are all
131	  HALs. Implemented in C++ via an abstract base class + per-hardware
132	  derived classes + virtual dispatch.
133	
134	- **Heap** — `taught` *(lesson 0006)*
135	  Free-form memory arena shared by all threads in a process. Variable-
136	  cost allocation (typically a few hundred ns; sometimes a syscall),
137	  runtime-decided lifetime, gigabytes available. RAII containers like
138	  `std::vector` and `std::unique_ptr` manage the lifetime for you.
139	
140	- **HLS (High-Level Synthesis)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
141	  A flow that lets you write FPGA logic in C/C++ instead of Verilog/VHDL.
142	  Vitis HLS is the current AMD/Xilinx tool. The compiler converts your
143	  C++ kernel into HDL, then through synthesis into a bitstream.
144	
145	- **Hot loop / hot path** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
146	  Code that runs many times per frame — per-entity update loops,
147	  per-line render code. Allocations and copies that would be invisible
148	  elsewhere are budget-eaters here.
149	
150	## I
151	
152	- **IPC (Inter-Process Communication)** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
153	  Mechanisms for processes (separate address spaces) to exchange data.
154	  The four common ones: shared files, pipes/sockets, shared memory
155	  regions, signals. Your game ↔ Ollama uses option two (TCP socket over
156	  loopback).
157	
158	- **Iterator invalidation** — `taught` *(lesson 0008)*
159	  Modifying a container can invalidate iterators (and raw pointers /
160	  references) that point into it. `std::vector::push_back` that
161	  triggers a realloc moves the buffer to a new address — every iterator
162	  into the old buffer is now garbage. Each container has its own rules.
163	
164	- **In-process LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
165	  Model linked into the game binary, called via a C/C++ API (e.g.
166	  `llama.cpp`). Contrast: **sidecar process**.
167	
168	## K
169	
170	- **Kernel space / user space** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
171	  Two execution modes the CPU itself enforces via a mode bit. User
172	  space (where your program runs) cannot touch hardware, other
173	  processes' memory, or page tables. Kernel space can. A system call
174	  is the controlled door between them.
175	
176	## L
177	
178	- **Latency vs throughput** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
179	  Latency = time for a single operation (a game frame). Throughput =
180	  total operations per second (requests). Games optimize for worst-case
181	  latency, not average throughput.
182	
183	- **LUT (Look-Up Table)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
184	  The fundamental cell of an FPGA. A 4- or 6-input table you fill in to
185	  implement any boolean function. Combined with flip-flops, DSPs, and
186	  BRAM blocks via programmable routing, LUTs build the user's circuit.
187	
188	## M
189	
190	- **Mutex (`std::mutex`)** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
191	  Mutual-exclusion primitive: only one thread holds it at a time.
192	  Used with RAII via `std::lock_guard` or `std::unique_lock` so the
193	  release is automatic. `LlmClient` uses two independent mutexes
194	  (`requestMutex_`, `replyMutex_`) so producer and consumer don't
195	  contend on unrelated data.
196	
197	- **`std::move`** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
198	  A cast that marks a value as "you may steal from this." Whether
199	  anything is actually stolen depends on the destination's move
200	  constructor. For `std::string`/`std::vector` it steals the heap buffer
201	  in O(1); for trivial types it falls back to a copy.
202	
203	## N
204	
205	- **NRVO (Named Return Value Optimization)** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
206	  Compiler optimization that builds a returned local directly in the
207	  caller's slot, eliminating the return copy/move entirely.
208	  `LlmClient::drainReplies()` relies on this.
209	
210	## O
211	
212	- **`override`** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
213	  C++11 specifier on derived methods that asks the compiler to verify
214	  the method is actually overriding a base virtual. Catches silent
215	  signature drift (e.g. base changes its parameter type and the derived
216	  method becomes a *new unrelated* method). Use on every override.
217	
218	## P
219	
220	- **Page cache** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
221	  Linux kernel cache of file pages in RAM. The first `read()` of a file
222	  may hit disk; subsequent reads of the same pages are served from RAM
223	  with no disk I/O. Shared across all processes, not per-program.
224	
225	- **Persona prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
226	  Static system-prompt text rendered from a `Persona` struct, prepended to
227	  every chat request to keep the NPC in character. See
228	  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Persona.hpp::renderSystemPrompt`.
229	
230	- **Predicate form of `cv.wait`** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
231	  `cv.wait(lock, pred)` — sleeps if `pred()` is false, re-checks on
232	  every wakeup, ignores spurious wakeups for free. Strictly safer than
233	  the no-predicate form. Used at `LlmClient.cpp:52`.
234	
235	- **Pure virtual method (`= 0`)** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
236	  A virtual method declared with `= 0` and no body. Derived classes
237	  *must* implement it. A class with any pure virtual is abstract and
238	  cannot be instantiated.
239	
240	## R
241	
242	- **RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)** — `taught` *(lesson 0006)*
243	  C++ pattern where a resource's lifetime is tied to a stack object: the
244	  constructor acquires (memory, mutex, thread, file), the destructor
245	  releases. `std::vector`, `std::unique_ptr`, `std::lock_guard`,
246	  `std::thread` all use it. Why modern C++ has no manual `delete`.
247	
248	- **Reference counting** — `taught` *(lesson 0010)*
249	  Memory-management technique used by `std::shared_ptr`. Each copy of
250	  the pointer increments a counter; each destruction decrements. The
251	  object is freed when the counter hits zero. The counter is atomic, so
252	  thread-safe but not free (~2× a raw pointer copy).
253	
254	- **Race condition** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
255	  Two or more threads accessing the same data without synchronisation,
256	  with at least one writer. Behaviour becomes nondeterministic and
257	  usually wrong. Not the same as a deadlock — race conditions produce
258	  bad data, deadlocks freeze.
259	
260	- **Reallocation (vector growth)** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
261	  When `std::vector::push_back` exceeds capacity, a new heap buffer is
262	  allocated, all existing elements are moved/copied across, and the old
263	  buffer is freed. `reserve()` ahead of time avoids the storm.
264	
265	## S
266	
267	- **Scheduler (OS scheduler)** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
268	  Kernel subsystem that decides which runnable thread runs on which
269	  core when. Blocked threads (e.g. those in `cv.wait`, blocking
270	  `recv`) are removed from the runnable set entirely until something
271	  wakes them — that's why "sleep cheaply" actually works.
272	
273	- **System call (syscall)** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
274	  Controlled crossing from user space into the kernel. ~100–200 ns on
275	  modern hardware. Examples: `open`, `read`, `write`, `socket`,
276	  `connect`, `send`, `recv`, `mmap`, `clone`. Library calls (~1 ns)
277	  are ordinary function calls; syscalls flip the CPU into kernel mode.
278	
279	- **Small String Optimization (SSO)** — `taught` *(lesson 0006)*
280	  Implementation technique where `std::string` reserves ~15 bytes of
281	  inline storage in its struct (libstdc++ 64-bit). Strings up to that
282	  length stay inline — no heap allocation. Above it, the string spills
283	  to a heap buffer. Why `ChatTurn::role` ("user"/"assistant") never
284	  allocates but `ChatTurn::content` usually does.
285	
286	- **Stack (program stack)** — `taught` *(lesson 0006)*
287	  LIFO memory region tied to the call chain. Allocate by moving a
288	  register; free on function return. ~8 MB for the main thread, ~1 MB
289	  per worker thread on Linux. One per thread. Fast, automatic, but
290	  size-limited.
291	
292	- **Spurious wakeup** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
293	  A condition-variable wait that returns without anyone calling notify.
294	  Permitted by the standard and by real OS-level CVs. The predicate form
295	  of `wait` handles them transparently.
296	
297	- **`std::atomic<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
298	  A variable whose read-modify-write is uninterruptible by other
299	  threads, implemented in hardware. Cheaper than a mutex for single
300	  values. `LlmClient` uses `std::atomic<bool>` for `stop_`/`inFlight_`
301	  and `std::atomic<uint64_t>` for the request-id counter.
302	
303	- **`std::array<T, N>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
304	  Fixed-size, compile-time-known array wrapper. Stack-allocated, doesn't
305	  decay, carries its size in the type. Used in the racing/shooter games
306	  for quad corners, matrices, and font candidate lists.
307	
308	- **`std::unordered_map<K,V>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0008)*
309	  Hash-table associative container. Contiguous bucket array, scattered
310	  chain nodes per bucket. O(1) average lookup/insert; O(n) worst case
311	  on bad hash. Used in both games' config readers
312	  (`std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string>`).
313	
314	- **`std::shared_ptr<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0010)*
315	  Smart pointer for shared ownership. Refcount goes up on copy, down on
316	  destruction; object freed when count hits zero. Refcount is atomic
317	  (~2× a raw pointer copy). Cycles between `shared_ptr`s leak — break
318	  them with `weak_ptr`. Use only when ownership is genuinely shared.
319	
320	- **`std::unique_ptr<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0010)*
321	  Smart pointer for exclusive ownership. One owner; movable but never
322	  copyable. Zero runtime overhead. The default for "heap object with one
323	  clear owner." Used at `LlmClient::backend_` in the lesson-0007 HAL
324	  refactor.
325	
326	- **`std::vector<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
327	  Dynamic-size, heap-backed sequence container. Use when count varies at
328	  runtime. Used throughout: shooter `projectiles`/`enemies`/`pickups`/
329	  `impacts`, racing's `buildRoundedRectLoop` return, NPC `history_`.
330	
331	- **`std::counting_semaphore<MaxN>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0011)*
332	  C++20 admission-control primitive. Holds a counter; `acquire()`
333	  decrements (blocks if zero), `release()` increments. **No ownership** —
334	  any thread can release, even one that didn't acquire. Use for
335	  resource pools, rate limits, or "max K in flight" patterns.
336	
337	- **`std::binary_semaphore`** — `taught` *(lesson 0011)*
338	  Special case of `counting_semaphore` with max=1. One-shot cross-thread
339	  signal ("tap me when X is done"). Looks like a mutex syntactically;
340	  semantically different (no ownership, no RAII helper). Use to hand
341	  control between threads, not to protect data.
342	
343	- **Semaphore (general)** — `taught` *(lesson 0011)*
344	  Synchronisation primitive that's a counter of available permits with
345	  blocking acquire/non-blocking release. Distinct from mutex by having
346	  **no ownership semantics** — any thread can release. Two C++20
347	  flavors: `std::counting_semaphore<MaxN>` and `std::binary_semaphore`.
348	
349	- **`std::weak_ptr<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0010)*
350	  Non-owning observer of a `shared_ptr`-managed object. `lock()`
351	  upgrades to a `shared_ptr` if the object still exists; returns null
352	  otherwise. Required to break `shared_ptr` cycles.
353	
354	- **`std::filesystem`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
355	  Portable file path / directory / file-info library, added in C++17.
356	  Used in `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp` for `fs::path`,
357	  `fs::exists`, `fs::current_path`. Replaces Boost.Filesystem and
358	  hand-rolled platform code.
359	
360	- **`std::optional<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
361	  C++17 type holding either a `T` or no value. Used at
362	  `Npc::onReplyArrived` return type. Modern replacement for "magic
363	  values" (-1, null pointers) signaling absence.
364	
365	- **`std::expected<T, E>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
366	  C++23 type holding either a `T` (success) or an `E` (error). Not
367	  yet usable in this project (CMake pinned to C++17). Would replace
368	  `ChatReply`'s `ok`/`content`/`errorMessage` trio with one type.
369	
370	- **`std::jthread`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
371	  C++20 thread that auto-joins on destruction. Would simplify
372	  `LlmClient`'s destructor — no explicit `join()` needed. Not yet
373	  usable in this project.
374	
375	- **`std::span<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
376	  C++20 non-owning view over a contiguous range. Cleaner function
377	  signatures than `const std::vector<T>&` when the caller has a
378	  vector, array, or C-array equivalently.
379	
380	- **`std::print` / `std::println`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
381	  C++23 type-safe formatted output. Replaces `std::cout << ...`
382	  chains and `printf` family in most cases.
383	
384	- **Sequence / associative / adapter (container families)** — `taught` *(lesson 0008)*
385	  STL containers group into three families. **Sequence**: ordered,
386	  indexable by position (`vector`, `array`, `deque`, `list`).
387	  **Associative**: indexable by key (`map`, `unordered_map`, `set`).
388	  **Adapter**: restricted API over an underlying container (`queue`,
389	  `stack`, `priority_queue`).
390	
391	- **Sidecar process** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
392	  A separate local process (Ollama, LM Studio, llamafile) that hosts the
393	  model and exposes an HTTP API the game POSTs to. Contrast:
394	  **in-process LLM**.
395	
396	- **System prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
397	  The `role: "system"` message in a chat request. Fixed identity, applied
398	  before any user turn.
399	
400	## T
401	
402	- **Thundering herd** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
403	  Anti-pattern where `notify_all` wakes many waiters even though only
404	  one can make progress; they all contend for the lock, find nothing to
405	  do, and go back to sleep. Use `notify_one` when only one waiter can
406	  consume the event.
407	
408	## V
409	
410	- **Virtual memory / address space** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
411	  Per-process abstraction: each process sees a private 64-bit address
412	  space, mapped to real RAM by the OS via page tables and the MMU. The
413	  same numeric address means different physical memory in different
414	  processes — the reason your game can't directly see Ollama's queue.
415	
416	- **`virtual` (function)** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
417	  Base-class keyword that enables dynamic dispatch: calls through a
418	  base-class pointer/reference look up the actual derived class's
419	  implementation at runtime via a vtable. ~1 ns indirection.
420	
421	- **`virtual` destructor** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
422	  Required on every base class that may be deleted through a
423	  base-class pointer (e.g. via `std::unique_ptr<Base>`). Without it,
424	  only the base destructor runs and derived-class cleanup is silently
425	  skipped — the #1 HAL bug.
426	
427	- **Virtual dispatch / vtable** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
428	  Mechanism by which C++ resolves a virtual call at runtime. Each
429	  polymorphic object carries a hidden pointer to a per-class table of
430	  function pointers (the vtable). Cost per call is roughly one
431	  indirect-load instruction.
432	
433	## X
434	
435	- **XRT (Xilinx Runtime)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
436	  The host-side C++ API for talking to an FPGA over PCIe. Provides
437	  `xrt::device`, `xrt::kernel`, `xrt::bo` (buffer object). The
438	  five-step pattern: load xclbin → allocate BOs → write inputs + sync to
439	  device → launch kernel → sync output back. Structurally identical to
440	  the LlmClient HTTP pattern.
441	
442	## Pending promotion
443	
444	(Terms used in lessons but not yet confirmed grasped in conversation —
445	once the user demonstrates understanding, move them above.)
446	
447	- Async drain pattern (worker thread + thread-safe reply queue)
448	- Bounded conversation history
449	- Dialogue tree (the pre-LLM baseline being contrasted)
450	- GGUF (quantized model file format)
451	- llama.cpp (the embedded-inference library)
452	- Ollama (the sidecar we're using)
453	- Quantization
454	- RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
455	- Streaming inference (`"stream": true`)
456	- Structured output (grammar-constrained JSON)
457	- Concurrency vs parallelism
458	- eFPGA / soft core (FPGA fabric inside an SoC; CPU built from LUTs)
459	- HBM (high-bandwidth memory on FPGA cards like VHK158, VCU128)
460	- Vitis HLS / Verilog / VHDL (the FPGA programming toolchain)
461	- LUT-LLM (the 2025 paper that put Qwen 3 1.7B on an Alveo V80)

> the lesson it was introduced in, and where it lives in the codebase.
> Only promote a term here once the user has used it correctly in

> Status legend:
> `taught` = explained in a lesson  ·
> `firm` = used correctly unprompted  ·
> `shaky` = needs revisit

## A

- **Abstract class** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
  A C++ class containing at least one pure virtual method (`= 0`).
  Cannot be instantiated directly; you instantiate derived classes that
  implement the pure virtuals. The base of every HAL.

- **Abstraction (vs encapsulation)** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
  Hiding *which of several implementations* is in use behind one
  interface. Distinct from encapsulation, which hides the internals of
  *one* class. A HAL is abstraction; private fields are encapsulation.

- **Array decay** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When a C-style array is passed to a function, the parameter is silently
  rewritten to a pointer, losing its size. `void f(int arr[10])` becomes
  `void f(int* arr)`. `std::array` does not decay.

- **ASIC** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. A chip fabricated for one
  fixed job (e.g. NVIDIA H100, phone neural engine). Faster and more
  efficient than the same design on an FPGA, but unchangeable once
  shipped. FPGA is the reprogrammable cousin.

## B

- **Bitstream** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  The binary file that programs an FPGA. Produced by synthesizing an

  reconfigures the chip into a different circuit.

## C

- **C++ language standard** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
  Three-year-cadence ISO release that defines what features the compiler
  accepts. Current standards: C++11/14/17/20/23 (C++26 in progress).
  Controlled via `CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD` / `-std=c++17`. Distinct from
  compiler version, which controls how completely a standard is
  implemented.

- **Context switch** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
  The OS suspending one thread/process and resuming another on a CPU
  core. Thread-to-thread switches in the same process are cheap (~few
  thousand ns); process-to-process switches require a TLB flush and are
  ~10× more expensive (softened by PCID on modern x86).

- **Container adapter** — `taught` *(lesson 0008)*
  Thin wrapper around a real container that restricts the exposed API.
  `std::queue`/`std::stack`/`std::priority_queue` are adapters. They're
  not containers themselves and can't be iterated. Used in `LlmClient`
  via `std::queue<ChatRequest> requests_` to document FIFO discipline.

- **C-style array** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Raw `T arr[N]` from C. Fixed size, stack storage, decays to pointer on
  function call. Still appears at
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp:72`.

- **Condition variable (`std::condition_variable`)** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
  Synchronisation primitive that lets a thread sleep cheaply until
  another thread signals state change. Always paired with a mutex and a
  predicate (`cv.wait(lock, pred)`) so spurious wakeups are handled
  automatically. Used at
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/LlmClient.cpp:52`.

## D

- **Deadlock** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
  Two threads each holding a lock the other needs; both wait forever.
  Cardinal prevention rule: always acquire multiple locks in the same
  order. `LlmClient` avoids the risk by never holding both mutexes
  simultaneously.

## D

- **`std::deque`** — `taught` *(lesson 0008)*
  Segmented sequence container — array of fixed-size blocks, blocks
  themselves separate heap allocations. O(1) push/pop at *both* ends.
  Random access is two pointer dereferences (block table, then block).
  Used in `DialogUI::transcript_` for the push_back/pop_front pattern.

## E

- **`emplace_back(args...)`** — `taught` *(lesson 0012)*
  Vector member that forwards args to T's constructor, building the
  element directly in the vector's storage with no temporary. Invokes
  explicit constructors (push_back refuses), which is its main safety
  trap. Modern (Chromium/Abseil/Google) advice: prefer `push_back` by
  default; reach for `emplace_back` only when you have a specific reason.

- **Embedded LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  A language model whose output is consumed by the running game process,
  regardless of whether the model lives in the same binary or in a sidecar
  process on `localhost`.

- **Erase-remove idiom** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Pattern for deleting elements from a `std::vector` that match a
  predicate without shrinking capacity. `v.erase(std::remove_if(b, e,
  pred), e)`. Used in `cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:686` to clean up
  dead projectiles per frame.

## F

- **FPGA** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  Field-Programmable Gate Array. A chip whose internal wiring is
  reconfigured at boot by loading a bitstream — the chip *becomes* the
  custom circuit you described, rather than executing instructions on a
  fixed circuit.

- **Frame budget** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  The wall-clock time available for one game-loop iteration before the
  next vsync. 16.67 ms at 60 Hz, 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. Exceeding it once
  produces visible stutter regardless of average speed.

## H

- **HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer)** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
  Software layer that hides "where the work physically happens" behind a
  single interface. Arduino's `digitalWrite`, Linux device drivers,
  SFML's `window.draw`, and the proposed `LlmBackend` interface are all
  HALs. Implemented in C++ via an abstract base class + per-hardware
  derived classes + virtual dispatch.

- **Heap** — `taught` *(lesson 0006)*
  Free-form memory arena shared by all threads in a process. Variable-
  cost allocation (typically a few hundred ns; sometimes a syscall),
  runtime-decided lifetime, gigabytes available. RAII containers like
  `std::vector` and `std::unique_ptr` manage the lifetime for you.

- **HLS (High-Level Synthesis)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  A flow that lets you write FPGA logic in C/C++ instead of Verilog/VHDL.
  Vitis HLS is the current AMD/Xilinx tool. The compiler converts your
  C++ kernel into HDL, then through synthesis into a bitstream.

- **Hot loop / hot path** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Code that runs many times per frame — per-entity update loops,
  per-line render code. Allocations and copies that would be invisible
  elsewhere are budget-eaters here.

## I

- **IPC (Inter-Process Communication)** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
  Mechanisms for processes (separate address spaces) to exchange data.
  The four common ones: shared files, pipes/sockets, shared memory
  regions, signals. Your game ↔ Ollama uses option two (TCP socket over
  loopback).

- **Iterator invalidation** — `taught` *(lesson 0008)*
  Modifying a container can invalidate iterators (and raw pointers /
  references) that point into it. `std::vector::push_back` that
  triggers a realloc moves the buffer to a new address — every iterator
  into the old buffer is now garbage. Each container has its own rules.

- **In-process LLM** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  Model linked into the game binary, called via a C/C++ API (e.g.
  `llama.cpp`). Contrast: **sidecar process**.

## K

- **Kernel space / user space** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
  Two execution modes the CPU itself enforces via a mode bit. User
  space (where your program runs) cannot touch hardware, other
  processes' memory, or page tables. Kernel space can. A system call
  is the controlled door between them.

## L

- **Latency vs throughput** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Latency = time for a single operation (a game frame). Throughput =
  total operations per second (requests). Games optimize for worst-case
  latency, not average throughput.

- **LUT (Look-Up Table)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  The fundamental cell of an FPGA. A 4- or 6-input table you fill in to
  implement any boolean function. Combined with flip-flops, DSPs, and
  BRAM blocks via programmable routing, LUTs build the user's circuit.

## M

- **Mutex (`std::mutex`)** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
  Mutual-exclusion primitive: only one thread holds it at a time.
  Used with RAII via `std::lock_guard` or `std::unique_lock` so the
  release is automatic. `LlmClient` uses two independent mutexes
  (`requestMutex_`, `replyMutex_`) so producer and consumer don't
  contend on unrelated data.

- **`std::move`** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  A cast that marks a value as "you may steal from this." Whether
  anything is actually stolen depends on the destination's move
  constructor. For `std::string`/`std::vector` it steals the heap buffer
  in O(1); for trivial types it falls back to a copy.

## N

- **NRVO (Named Return Value Optimization)** — `taught` *(lesson 0003)*
  Compiler optimization that builds a returned local directly in the
  caller's slot, eliminating the return copy/move entirely.
  `LlmClient::drainReplies()` relies on this.

## O

- **`override`** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
  C++11 specifier on derived methods that asks the compiler to verify
  the method is actually overriding a base virtual. Catches silent
  signature drift (e.g. base changes its parameter type and the derived
  method becomes a *new unrelated* method). Use on every override.

## P

- **Page cache** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
  Linux kernel cache of file pages in RAM. The first `read()` of a file
  may hit disk; subsequent reads of the same pages are served from RAM
  with no disk I/O. Shared across all processes, not per-program.

- **Persona prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  Static system-prompt text rendered from a `Persona` struct, prepended to
  every chat request to keep the NPC in character. See
  `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/Persona.hpp::renderSystemPrompt`.

- **Predicate form of `cv.wait`** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
  `cv.wait(lock, pred)` — sleeps if `pred()` is false, re-checks on
  every wakeup, ignores spurious wakeups for free. Strictly safer than
  the no-predicate form. Used at `LlmClient.cpp:52`.

- **Pure virtual method (`= 0`)** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
  A virtual method declared with `= 0` and no body. Derived classes
  *must* implement it. A class with any pure virtual is abstract and
  cannot be instantiated.

## R

- **RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)** — `taught` *(lesson 0006)*
  C++ pattern where a resource's lifetime is tied to a stack object: the
  constructor acquires (memory, mutex, thread, file), the destructor
  releases. `std::vector`, `std::unique_ptr`, `std::lock_guard`,
  `std::thread` all use it. Why modern C++ has no manual `delete`.

- **Reference counting** — `taught` *(lesson 0010)*
  Memory-management technique used by `std::shared_ptr`. Each copy of
  the pointer increments a counter; each destruction decrements. The
  object is freed when the counter hits zero. The counter is atomic, so
  thread-safe but not free (~2× a raw pointer copy).

- **Race condition** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
  Two or more threads accessing the same data without synchronisation,
  with at least one writer. Behaviour becomes nondeterministic and
  usually wrong. Not the same as a deadlock — race conditions produce
  bad data, deadlocks freeze.

- **Reallocation (vector growth)** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  When `std::vector::push_back` exceeds capacity, a new heap buffer is
  allocated, all existing elements are moved/copied across, and the old
  buffer is freed. `reserve()` ahead of time avoids the storm.

## S

- **Scheduler (OS scheduler)** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
  Kernel subsystem that decides which runnable thread runs on which
  core when. Blocked threads (e.g. those in `cv.wait`, blocking
  `recv`) are removed from the runnable set entirely until something
  wakes them — that's why "sleep cheaply" actually works.

- **System call (syscall)** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
  Controlled crossing from user space into the kernel. ~100–200 ns on
  modern hardware. Examples: `open`, `read`, `write`, `socket`,
  `connect`, `send`, `recv`, `mmap`, `clone`. Library calls (~1 ns)
  are ordinary function calls; syscalls flip the CPU into kernel mode.

- **Small String Optimization (SSO)** — `taught` *(lesson 0006)*
  Implementation technique where `std::string` reserves ~15 bytes of
  inline storage in its struct (libstdc++ 64-bit). Strings up to that
  length stay inline — no heap allocation. Above it, the string spills
  to a heap buffer. Why `ChatTurn::role` ("user"/"assistant") never
  allocates but `ChatTurn::content` usually does.

- **Stack (program stack)** — `taught` *(lesson 0006)*
  LIFO memory region tied to the call chain. Allocate by moving a
  register; free on function return. ~8 MB for the main thread, ~1 MB
  per worker thread on Linux. One per thread. Fast, automatic, but
  size-limited.

- **Spurious wakeup** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
  A condition-variable wait that returns without anyone calling notify.
  Permitted by the standard and by real OS-level CVs. The predicate form
  of `wait` handles them transparently.

- **`std::atomic<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
  A variable whose read-modify-write is uninterruptible by other
  threads, implemented in hardware. Cheaper than a mutex for single
  values. `LlmClient` uses `std::atomic<bool>` for `stop_`/`inFlight_`
  and `std::atomic<uint64_t>` for the request-id counter.

- **`std::array<T, N>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Fixed-size, compile-time-known array wrapper. Stack-allocated, doesn't
  decay, carries its size in the type. Used in the racing/shooter games
  for quad corners, matrices, and font candidate lists.

- **`std::unordered_map<K,V>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0008)*
  Hash-table associative container. Contiguous bucket array, scattered
  chain nodes per bucket. O(1) average lookup/insert; O(n) worst case
  on bad hash. Used in both games' config readers
  (`std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string>`).

- **`std::shared_ptr<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0010)*
  Smart pointer for shared ownership. Refcount goes up on copy, down on
  destruction; object freed when count hits zero. Refcount is atomic
  (~2× a raw pointer copy). Cycles between `shared_ptr`s leak — break
  them with `weak_ptr`. Use only when ownership is genuinely shared.

- **`std::unique_ptr<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0010)*
  Smart pointer for exclusive ownership. One owner; movable but never
  copyable. Zero runtime overhead. The default for "heap object with one
  clear owner." Used at `LlmClient::backend_` in the lesson-0007 HAL
  refactor.

- **`std::vector<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0002)*
  Dynamic-size, heap-backed sequence container. Use when count varies at
  runtime. Used throughout: shooter `projectiles`/`enemies`/`pickups`/
  `impacts`, racing's `buildRoundedRectLoop` return, NPC `history_`.

- **`std::counting_semaphore<MaxN>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0011)*
  C++20 admission-control primitive. Holds a counter; `acquire()`
  decrements (blocks if zero), `release()` increments. **No ownership** —
  any thread can release, even one that didn't acquire. Use for
  resource pools, rate limits, or "max K in flight" patterns.

- **`std::binary_semaphore`** — `taught` *(lesson 0011)*
  Special case of `counting_semaphore` with max=1. One-shot cross-thread
  signal ("tap me when X is done"). Looks like a mutex syntactically;
  semantically different (no ownership, no RAII helper). Use to hand
  control between threads, not to protect data.

- **Semaphore (general)** — `taught` *(lesson 0011)*
  Synchronisation primitive that's a counter of available permits with
  blocking acquire/non-blocking release. Distinct from mutex by having
  **no ownership semantics** — any thread can release. Two C++20
  flavors: `std::counting_semaphore<MaxN>` and `std::binary_semaphore`.

- **`std::weak_ptr<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0010)*
  Non-owning observer of a `shared_ptr`-managed object. `lock()`
  upgrades to a `shared_ptr` if the object still exists; returns null
  otherwise. Required to break `shared_ptr` cycles.

- **`std::filesystem`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
  Portable file path / directory / file-info library, added in C++17.
  Used in `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs/src/main.cpp` for `fs::path`,
  `fs::exists`, `fs::current_path`. Replaces Boost.Filesystem and
  hand-rolled platform code.

- **`std::optional<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
  C++17 type holding either a `T` or no value. Used at
  `Npc::onReplyArrived` return type. Modern replacement for "magic
  values" (-1, null pointers) signaling absence.

- **`std::expected<T, E>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
  C++23 type holding either a `T` (success) or an `E` (error). Not
  yet usable in this project (CMake pinned to C++17). Would replace
  `ChatReply`'s `ok`/`content`/`errorMessage` trio with one type.

- **`std::jthread`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
  C++20 thread that auto-joins on destruction. Would simplify
  `LlmClient`'s destructor — no explicit `join()` needed. Not yet
  usable in this project.

- **`std::span<T>`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
  C++20 non-owning view over a contiguous range. Cleaner function
  signatures than `const std::vector<T>&` when the caller has a
  vector, array, or C-array equivalently.

- **`std::print` / `std::println`** — `taught` *(lesson 0013)*
  C++23 type-safe formatted output. Replaces `std::cout << ...`
  chains and `printf` family in most cases.

- **Sequence / associative / adapter (container families)** — `taught` *(lesson 0008)*
  STL containers group into three families. **Sequence**: ordered,
  indexable by position (`vector`, `array`, `deque`, `list`).
  **Associative**: indexable by key (`map`, `unordered_map`, `set`).
  **Adapter**: restricted API over an underlying container (`queue`,
  `stack`, `priority_queue`).

- **Sidecar process** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  A separate local process (Ollama, LM Studio, llamafile) that hosts the
  model and exposes an HTTP API the game POSTs to. Contrast:
  **in-process LLM**.

- **System prompt** — `taught` *(lesson 0001)*
  The `role: "system"` message in a chat request. Fixed identity, applied
  before any user turn.

## T

- **Thundering herd** — `taught` *(lesson 0005)*
  Anti-pattern where `notify_all` wakes many waiters even though only
  one can make progress; they all contend for the lock, find nothing to
  do, and go back to sleep. Use `notify_one` when only one waiter can
  consume the event.

## V

- **Virtual memory / address space** — `taught` *(lesson 0009)*
  Per-process abstraction: each process sees a private 64-bit address
  space, mapped to real RAM by the OS via page tables and the MMU. The
  same numeric address means different physical memory in different
  processes — the reason your game can't directly see Ollama's queue.

- **`virtual` (function)** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
  Base-class keyword that enables dynamic dispatch: calls through a
  base-class pointer/reference look up the actual derived class's
  implementation at runtime via a vtable. ~1 ns indirection.

- **`virtual` destructor** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
  Required on every base class that may be deleted through a
  base-class pointer (e.g. via `std::unique_ptr<Base>`). Without it,
  only the base destructor runs and derived-class cleanup is silently
  skipped — the #1 HAL bug.

- **Virtual dispatch / vtable** — `taught` *(lesson 0007)*
  Mechanism by which C++ resolves a virtual call at runtime. Each
  polymorphic object carries a hidden pointer to a per-class table of
  function pointers (the vtable). Cost per call is roughly one
  indirect-load instruction.

## X

- **XRT (Xilinx Runtime)** — `taught` *(lesson 0004)*
  The host-side C++ API for talking to an FPGA over PCIe. Provides
  `xrt::device`, `xrt::kernel`, `xrt::bo` (buffer object). The
  five-step pattern: load xclbin → allocate BOs → write inputs + sync to
  device → launch kernel → sync output back. Structurally identical to
  the LlmClient HTTP pattern.

## Pending promotion

(Terms used in lessons but not yet confirmed grasped in conversation —
once the user demonstrates understanding, move them above.)

- Async drain pattern (worker thread + thread-safe reply queue)
- Bounded conversation history
- Dialogue tree (the pre-LLM baseline being contrasted)
- GGUF (quantized model file format)
- llama.cpp (the embedded-inference library)
- Ollama (the sidecar we're using)
- Quantization
- RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
- Streaming inference (`"stream": true`)
- Structured output (grammar-constrained JSON)
- Concurrency vs parallelism
- eFPGA / soft core (FPGA fabric inside an SoC; CPU built from LUTs)
- HBM (high-bandwidth memory on FPGA cards like VHK158, VCU128)
- Vitis HLS / Verilog / VHDL (the FPGA programming toolchain)
- LUT-LLM (the 2025 paper that put Qwen 3 1.7B on an Alveo V80)

## What's in it

**Function-call nuances for low-latency C++** — the four decisions you make at every call site:

1. **How arguments travel** — the decision table: by-value for small trivially-copyable types (`Vec3`), `const&` for heavyweights (`wrap()`'s string), **by-value + `std::move` for sinks** (your `LlmClient::submit` is the headline anchor — and it's already textbook-perfect), `string_view` for read-only string views.
2. **How returns travel** — RVO is *guaranteed* since C++17, NRVO is near-universal, and `return std::move(local)` is the classic pessimization that disables it.
3. **How callables dispatch** — the ladder from lambda-as-template-parameter (your `remove_if` predicates, zero cost) down to `std::function` (type erasure, indirect call, possible heap allocation). Your repo has zero `std::function` in hot paths — the lesson explains why to keep it that way.
4. **Hints** — `noexcept` (including the vector-realloc tie-in to lesson 0012), `constexpr`, internal linkage, `[[likely]]`.

The recurring honest note: your shooter's `const Vec3&` operators are "textbook-suboptimal" yet cost nothing, because inlining erases the difference — guidelines pick better defaults, but profile before touching working code. (One caveat: live web search was unavailable this session, so the footer cites canonical stable sources rather than freshly verified ones — these are standards-level facts, not fast-moving lore.)

For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Lesson 0015 · cpp_games / docs / learning

Debugging runtime spikes

Why this matters: lessons 0003, 0005, 0009, and 0014 all ended with "measure before you change" — this is the lesson where you finally get the measuring kit. A game that averages 60 FPS but hitches for 80 ms once a second feels broken; a game that averages 45 FPS steadily feels fine. Spikes are a different beast from slowness, and they're hunted differently.

1. The concept — spikes are not slowness

Two performance diseases, two different treatments:

Slow (chronic)Spiky (acute)
SymptomEvery frame takes too long; FPS uniformly lowMost frames are fine; occasional frames take 3–30× longer
What the player feelsSluggish but consistentStutter, hitching, "the game froze for a moment"
What reveals itAverage frame timeWorst frame / 99th percentile — the average actively hides it
Typical causeToo much work per frame (algorithmic)Rare-event work landing on one frame: allocation storms, lock waits, blocking I/O, OS preemption
Typical fixDo less work / better algorithmMove the rare event off the hot path, amortize it, or pre-do it

Why the average lies

1000 frames: 999 take 10 ms, one takes 100 ms. Average = 10.09 ms — "smooth 99 FPS!" But the player saw a visible hitch. The only numbers that catch it: max (100 ms) and p99 (the time the worst 1% of frames exceed). Rule: report frame times as worst/p99/median, never as average FPS. This is lesson 0003's latency-vs-throughput distinction with teeth.

The four-step spike hunt

1. CONFIRM Record per-frame times into a ring buffer. Is there a spike at all, how big, how often? (No tooling yet — 20 lines of code.) 2. LOCATE Split the frame into sections (events / update / render / display). Time each. When a spike frame happens, which section ate the budget? 3. CLASSIFY Match the guilty section against the usual-suspects table (section 4): allocation? lock? syscall? GPU? OS? 4. FIX + RE-MEASURE Apply the matching fix, then rerun step 1. If the worst frame didn't improve, revert — the suspicion was wrong.

The discipline matters more than the tools: never skip from symptom to fix. Every lesson so far that said "profile first" was protecting you from optimizing the wrong thing — lesson 0014's wrap() suspicion is exactly the kind of claim step 2 confirms or kills.

2. Minimal example — a 30-line spike detector

This is self-contained instrumentation you can paste into any of your three games today. Two pieces: the right clock, and spike-triggered logging.

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>

// ALWAYS steady_clock for intervals. system_clock is wall-clock time and
// can jump (NTP sync, DST) — a "frame" could measure negative.
using Clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;

struct SectionTimer {                       // RAII: times a scope (lesson 0006)
    Clock::time_point start = Clock::now();
    double& sink;                          // where to record milliseconds
    explicit SectionTimer(double& s) : sink(s) {}
    ~SectionTimer() {
        sink = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(Clock::now() - start).count();
    }
};

// In the game loop:
double msUpdate = 0, msRender = 0;
auto frameStart = Clock::now();

{ SectionTimer t(msUpdate);  updateEverything(dt); }   // destructor records
{ SectionTimer t(msRender);  renderScene(window);  }

double msFrame = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(Clock::now() - frameStart).count();

// SPIKE-TRIGGERED logging: only speak when something is wrong.
// Logging every frame would itself allocate/IO and distort the measurement
// (the observer effect). 25 ms = 1.5x the 60 Hz budget.
if (msFrame > 25.0) {
    std::printf("SPIKE %.1fms (update %.1f, render %.1f)\n",
                msFrame, msUpdate, msRender);
}
  • steady_clock, never system_clock — steady is monotonic (only moves forward, at a constant rate). System clock is "what time is it," adjustable by the OS at any moment.
  • RAII timer — the destructor records the time, so early returns and exceptions are timed correctly for free. Same pattern as lock_guard (lesson 0005).
  • Spike-triggered output — the conditional printf runs ~never, so the instrumentation's own cost stays out of the numbers. This matters: instrumentation that's heavier than the thing measured produces fiction.
  • Measure in release (-O2, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release) — debug builds are 5–30× slower in different *proportions* per function, so debug-build spikes often point at the wrong suspect entirely.

3. In this project

The spike defense you already shipped

cpp_shooter_game/src/main.cpp:1093 
const float dt = std::min(0.03f, frameClock.restart().asSeconds());

This clamp says: "even if the last frame took 200 ms, pretend at most 30 ms passed." Without it, a single spike would feed a huge dt into the physics — projectiles tunneling through enemies, the player launched by one integration step. Understand what this is: mitigation, not cure. It stops a spike from corrupting the simulation, but the player still sees the hitch. (Side effect worth knowing: during a spike the game world runs slower than real time, because clamped dt < real elapsed time.)

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>

// can jump (NTP sync, DST) — a "frame" could measure negative.
using Clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;

struct SectionTimer {                       // RAII: times a scope (lesson 0006)
    Clock::time_point start = Clock::now();
    double& sink;                          // where to record milliseconds
    explicit SectionTimer(double& s) : sink(s) {}
    ~SectionTimer() {
        sink = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(Clock::now() - start).count();
    }
};

// In the game loop:
double msUpdate = 0, msRender = 0;
auto frameStart = Clock::now();

{ SectionTimer t(msUpdate);  updateEverything(dt); }   // destructor records

double msFrame = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(Clock::now() - frameStart).count();

// Logging every frame would itself allocate/IO and distort the measurement
// (the observer effect). 25 ms = 1.5x the 60 Hz budget.

  the OS adjusts it (NTP/DST) — capable of measuring a negative frame.
  SFML's `sf::Clock` is also monotonic.
